articles.title: CELEBRATING 100 YEARS

paras.en: MEDINA, OH (January 6, 2025) – Carlisle Brake & Friction (CarlisleCBF), a global leader in brake and friction technology and part of the CentroMotion family of brands, has reached a momentous milestone – its 100th anniversary.
Since its founding in 1925, the company has lived up to its tagline, "Braking New Ground," by consistently pioneering innovative solutions that have propelled industries forward.

"For 100 years, Carlisle has been synonymous with groundbreaking innovation and unwavering reliability in the braking industry," says Tom Vanderlaan, Chief Commercial Officer (CCO) of CentroMotion. "This milestone is a testament to the dedication of our employees, the trust of our customers, and the enduring strength of our products. As we celebrate our centennial, we reaffirm our commitment to continuous innovation, strong partnerships, and giving back to the communities we serve."
paras.zh: CentroMotion 首席商务官 (CCO) Tom Vanderlaan 表示：“100 年来，Carlisle 一直是制动行业突破性创新和坚定可靠性的代名词。” “这一里程碑证明了我们员工的奉献、客户的信任以及我们产品的持久实力。在庆祝我们百年华诞之际，我们重申我们对持续创新、强有力的合作伙伴关系以及回馈我们所服务的社区的承诺。”

paras.en: A Century of Innovation in Motion Control

For a century, CarlisleCBF has been at the forefront of motion control, pushing the boundaries of performance with its industry-leading brakes and friction materials. Through unwavering commitment to R&D, the company has earned the trust of customers worldwide, establishing itself as a cornerstone of reliability.
paras.zh: 一个世纪以来，CarlisleCBF 一直处于运动控制领域的前沿，凭借其行业领先的制动器和摩擦材料突破了性能界限。通过坚定不移地致力于研发，该公司赢得了全球客户的信任，奠定了其可靠性的基石。

paras.en: Celebrating 100 Years of Braking New Ground: A Digital Celebration
paras.zh: 庆祝开拓新天地 100 周年：数字庆典

paras.en: To commemorate this historic milestone, CarlisleCBF is launching a comprehensive digital celebration. This virtual experience will allow customers, employees and industry partners to delve into the company’s rich history, groundbreaking innovations and commitment to excellence through historical photographs and stories.
paras.zh: 为了纪念这一历史性里程碑，CarlisleCBF 推出了全面的数字庆祝活动。这种虚拟体验将使客户、员工和行业合作伙伴能够通过历史照片和故事深入了解公司丰富的历史、突破性的创新和对卓越的承诺。

paras.en: A core aspect of the celebration is fostering a sense of community. CarlisleCBF invites customers, employees and industry partners to join the journey by visiting their dedicated anniversary webpage, www.CarlisleCBF.com, and following their story on social media.
paras.zh: 庆祝活动的一个核心方面是培养社区意识。 CarlisleCBF 邀请客户、员工和行业合作伙伴通过访问其专门的周年纪念网页 www.CarlisleCBF.com 并在社交媒体上关注他们的故事来加入这一旅程。

paras.en: The webpage and social media channels will serve as a virtual time capsule, showcasing CarlisleCBF's rich history, ground-breaking milestones and product innovations.
paras.zh: 网页和社交媒体渠道将充当虚拟时间胶囊，展示 CarlisleCBF 丰富的历史、突破性的里程碑和产品创新。

paras.en: To encourage participation and celebrate the impact CarlisleCBF has had, a social media campaign is launching with the hashtag #CarlisleCBF100. Participants are encouraged to share stories, photos and memories that illustrate how CarlisleCBF products have impacted their lives or businesses. The most engaging submissions will be featured on the company's social media channels and website.

paras.en: By combining digital storytelling with interactive social media, CarlisleCBF aims to create a lasting legacy for its first century of service, while fostering a spirit of community and appreciation.

articles.title: Collision Safety Consultants Opens Oregon, Massachusetts Offices
articles.author: Jason Stahl

paras.en: Billy Walkowiak, founder and CEO of Collision Safety Consultants, LLC, announced two new locations in Oregon and Massachusetts. The newest locations will be led by Corinna Rowland – Oregon and John Hayduk – Massachusetts
These additions bring Collision Safety Consultants to 32 locations worldwide, including 30 in the U.S., one in Canada and one in Australia.

Collision Safety Consultants is an international automotive appraisal and motor vehicle damage assessment company specializing in total loss disputes, diminished value recovery and post-collision repair inspections safety inspections.
With a network of licensed adjusters, appraisers and inspectors, the company is committed to protecting vehicle owners’ interests and helping ensure fair and accurate insurance claim settlements.
“Our continued growth is a testament to the reputation we’ve built, the professionals who represent our company and the trust our customers place in us,” said Walkowiak.

Having celebrated its 17th anniversary in March 2026, Collision Safety Consultants continues to expand its reach while maintaining the principles upon which it was founded: integrity, professionalism, independence and consumer advocacy.

“Thirty-two locations across three countries is something we’re extremely proud of, but our mission remains the same as it was on day one: protecting vehicle owners and making sure they receive what they’re rightfully owed.”
For more information on Collision Safety Consultants, visit collisionsafetyconsultants.us.

articles.title: AkzoNobel Launches Modern Vintage Refinish Line
articles.author: Jason Stahl

paras.en: AkzoNobel has announced the launch of Modern Vintage, a groundbreaking refinish product line that gives vehicle owners, professional builders, restoration shops and refinish professionals access to an extensive library of authentic OEM colors spanning more than 140 years of automotive history — all recreated using proven, premium Sikkens refinish technology.

Developed in partnership with renowned custom vehicle builder and television personality Dave Kindig of Kindig-it Design, Modern Vintage bridges the gap between automotive color heritage and the performance demands of today’s refinish market. The full product line is available exclusively through TCP Global, whose Auto Color Library supplies the historic color reference behind every formula and whose color lab mixes, fills and ships each order direct to the customer’s door.

Modern Vintage gives restorers and builders the ability to search by year, make, model and OEM paint code to find and recreate the precise factory color of virtually any vehicle — from legendary American classics to rare international models.

TCP Global’s Auto Color Library, the largest online automotive paint color reference library in the world, holds OEM chips and formulas reaching back to the early 1900s, and its color lab is equipped to mix, fill and ship those colors to order.

While the colors are historic, the paint technology is anything but. Sikkens, founded in 1792 and one of the world’s most respected refinish brands, underpins every Modern Vintage formulation — delivering the modern performance, durability and finish quality expected from a premium paint system.

Dave Kindig brings authentic credibility to Modern Vintage. As the founder of Kindig-It Design and a leading voice in the custom and vintage vehicle world, Kindig’s passion for period-correct color and craftsmanship aligns directly with the product’s mission. Modern Vintage also connects naturally with the established Modern Classikk color collection, giving customers a complete ecosystem for both vintage restoration and custom builds.

“We’re bringing exciting announcements to our customers at SEMA,” said Maximilien Schréder, commercial director, AkzoNobel North American Automotive & Specialty Coatings. “Modern Vintage completes our portfolio of Sikkens refinish technology for custom and OEM matching colors to distributors, shops and restorers.”

“I’ve always believed every great build starts with the right color,” said Dave Kindig, founder and creative director, Kindig-It Design. “Modern Vintage brings the right color, every time, with state-of-the-art Sikkens paint technology.”

“Restorers don’t want a modern interpretation of an old color — they want the color that was on the car when it left the production line,” said Dean Faucett, president, TCP Global. “We have spent decades building an archive that can answer that question, and pairing it with Sikkens technology and Dave’s eye is the first time the history and the performance have come together in one product.”
- 140+ years of OEM color history — domestic and international makes and models
- Search by year, make, model and OEM paint code for precise color matching
- Premium Sikkens refinish technology for modern performance and finish quality
- Available through TCP Global with fast direct-to-door shipping
- Backed by Dave Kindig — trusted builder, restorer and automotive creative authority

Modern Vintage is available now through TCP Global at https://tcpglobal.com, where customers can search by year, make, model and OEM code and order paint mixed to that code. For professional inquiries, existing Sikkens customers and refinish facilities can contact their local Sikkens representative or visit sikkensvr.com/en-us. More details on Modern Vintage are available at modernvintagepaint.com.
For more information on AkzoNobel’s Vehicle Refinish business, visit akzonobel.com.

articles.title: BodyShop Business Hands Out Executive of the Year Awards at 2026 SEMA Show
articles.author: Jason Stahl

paras.en: BodyShop Business handed out their annual Executive of the Year awards sponsored by Autel at the Collision Industry Red Carpet Awards Night at Westgate Las Vegas Resort & Casino at the 2026 SEMA Show.
Bob Knodel of Silver Creek Auto Body won the Single-Shop award, and Eric McKenzie of Asbury Automotive Group won the Multi-Shop award.

BodyShop Business has been honoring collision repairers with this award since 1984. The winners of this prestigious award are true collision repair “visionaries” who have experienced great success through innovative thinking, overcoming challenges and persevering.
This Collision Industry Red Carpet Awards continues a tradition of honoring excellence, leadership and lasting contributions across the collision repair industry.
Knodel has been in the collision repair industry for 34 years. Under his leadership, Silver Creek Auto Body has grown from approximately $700,000 in annual sales to nearly $4 million.

What distinguishes him from the average successful shop owner is his willingness to invest his time and experience outside the walls of his own business. He has become an active advocate for independent collision repairers in Oregon, working to educate shops, encourage collaboration and address industry challenges that individual repairers often struggle to tackle on their own.

Knodel is a founding board member and president of the Oregon Collision Repair Association, and an industry representative of the Oregon Collision Repair Legislative Workgroup — where he identifies industry concerns and explores legislative solutions that can create positive change for Oregon collision repair businesses and consumers.

McKenzie has been in the collision repair industry for 29 years. He started with Sewell Collision as an estimator in 1997, then production manager and senior estimator/assistant manager. He helped design and set up an 83,000 square foot collision center and helped grow monthly sales from $300,000 to over $1,000,000. His next stop was Park Place Bodywerks as body shop director, where he helped design and set up a 110,000-square-foot collision center and grow monthly sales from $500,000 to over $4,000,000. At Park Place dealerships, he helped design and start up two 35,000-square-foot collision centers and grew monthly sales in one location to $1,500,000 and another location to $850,000.

articles.title: MSO CEOs on the right people for the right jobs, and some industry misconceptions
articles.author: Lurah Lowery

paras.en: This year’s MSO Symposium brought together “the Four Aces” — the CEOs of Boyd Group, Caliber, Classic Collision, and Crash Champions —in Las Vegas on Monday, who ultimately landed on a simple conclusion: the collision repair industry depends on the right people fitting into the right roles.

When moderator Dan Risley asked what they’re hearing from investors and other stakeholders about the industry today, Boyd Group CEO Brian Kaner responded that the industry isn’t “recession-proof, but it is recession-resilient.”

“There are plenty of opportunities for us to continue to grow our businesses,” he said. “It all comes down to making sure you have the right people in the right roles with the right capabilities. And if you have that and you know how to keep score and you can win with the insurance carriers and you can take care of their customers and really be the extension of what they’re looking for, this is a great business to be in, and it’s something that we can continue to all thrive in.”

However, in response to a different question Risley posed about the “temperature” of each MSO’s team leaders, Crash Champions CEO Matt Ebert and Kaner agreed it’s a tense, stressful time for them, and made some important points about estimators.
Ebert said being an estimator, or as Crash Champions calls them, a service advisor, “has to be one of the most miserable spots.”

“You’ve got technicians bitching at you, you’ve got management or ownership bitching at you, you’ve got insurance companies bitching at you,” he said. “Everything you do gets criticized. Everything you do gets reviewed and sent back, and you have to do it again. I wouldn’t last a week. I would quit that job and tell you to shove it up your a**. If you want to know the temperature of our people, that is the truth.”

Ebert added that general managers also face pressure to keep customers, employees, and insurance companies happy while trying to make money and handle the safety, legal, and logistical pieces of their jobs.
Kaner said the industry has a “compelling opportunity” to invest in people.

“You’ve got to make investments in estimators,” he said. “We all make investments in technicians. I think one of the bigger gaps we have as an industry right now is in estimators. There’s not enough of them. There’s not enough of them that understand the metrics. There’s not enough of them that are salespeople that can go help actually go sell a consumer-paid job. …it’s a tense time and anytime when you’re in an environment where volume is tight, it just ups the pressure of the organization.”
Brad Anderson, who joined the collision repair industry in June to take over as CEO of Classic Collision, said he believes all jobs in the industry are hard.

“We put a lot on them, and I think all of us as an industry and ecosystem have to consider that it all crashes down to the people at the shop,” he said. “The small changes we make up here get really big when there’s 20 changes happening to the individual, whether it’s a tech, a GM, a service advisor, so we’ve got to simplify the work.”
During the discussion, Ebert also noted that 40-50% of MSO employees don’t touch a car, which he said “presents huge administrative opportunity,” another point he and Kaner agreed on.

“We have 15,000 people in our organization, and half of them are technicians and the other half are the people that are just trying to get the car to the back and do all the administrative things that they need to do to get it there,” Kaner said.
The conversation also touched on declining repairable claims volume, with Risley asking what’s missing from that narrative.

Caliber CEO David Simmons said the overall picture on repairable claims is probably a little more positive than the data that’s often quoted, “even though it is bad.” The primary misleading point, he said, is repairable claims data being viewed as representative of the market.

“If you allow yourself to be defined by repairable claims volumes, you have 30 years of history of insurance premium inflation in one year followed by claims frequency 12 to 18 months later,” he said. “And the pattern recognition in that 30-year data set would show that when you get into mid- to low-single-digit insurance premium inflation, which we’ve been in for several quarters now, you have a lag to low- to mid-single-digit claims frequency increase. There’s reasons for optimism that the old pattern holds, kind of offset by a structural shift with consumers because of the shock factor of insurance premium inflation.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: However, outside of insurance claims, one point remains: people are still getting their cars repaired, but they’re paying out of pocket, he said.

“We don’t track the juxtaposition of [the] increase in the dollar value of direct customer pay against the decrease in repairable claims and the dollar value of that,” Simmons said. “If you look at that, the total market has come down, but it’s a lot different dynamic. Now we’re built to service the insurance carrier, so it requires some adaptation to get at this customer pay. But if you want, we have to adapt, but if one’s willing to adapt, that market segment is there, and it’s growing, it’s growing robustly.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Simmons said he would love to see Mitchell and CCC “come together with a combined audited data set that is as close to accurate as possible on what’s really going on with claims, total losses, repairable claims, and segments of claims.”
Kaner said he thinks one thing people miss is that what’s happening in the industry isn’t all that different from what’s been happening.
“It’s like any ecosystem; something that happens can have a negative effect downstream, and this industry has the same thing,” he said.

In this case, “a very precipitous increase in premiums that then put consumers on heightened alert,” Kaner said, causing them to raise their deductibles, drop coverage, or not file a claim for fear of a large premium increase.

“But if you look at what’s happening in the environment, the underlying claims themselves, i.e., we call for a claims environment to be down 2%,” he said. “I think the claims environment driven by the ADAS systems, collision avoidance systems, is probably just that. What’s happened is the propensity to file a claim over that two-year period of time is really what’s driven much of the negative in the industry. And as that starts to work itself out of the system, you’re starting to see the claims environment come back again.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Kaner added that too much is ascribed to collision avoidance systems.

“We as an industry have to do a really good job of making sure people don’t hear things like, ‘Oh, well, front-end collisions are down 40%.’ Well, front-end collisions are down 40% in the cars that actually have that technology in them,” he said. “The reality is, for that technology to bleed through the system takes quite a while… Anything that happens new in a car takes 20 years to get all the way through the system.”
Risley also asked the group what the biggest threat to the collision repair industry is. Three out of the four responded, “ourselves.” Anderson’s take was technology.

articles.title: Annual Red Carpet Awards recognize excellence in leadership, education, and advocacy
articles.author: Lurah Lowery

paras.en: The Collision Industry Red Carpet Awards, held Tuesday during SEMA Week in Las Vegas, honored several individuals in the collision repair industry for their dedication to safe and proper repairs; education and training; consumer advocacy; and doing the right thing.

The Society of Collision Repair Specialists (SCRS) honored Petra Schroeder, known to the industry as “Collisionista,” with the 2026 Humanitarian Award for a relentlessness never to stop giving to the industry.

“There are people who talk about giving back, and there are people who just quietly get to work, people who answer the phone when someone needs help, who encourage someone who’s trying to find their place in the industry, and who remind us that sometimes the most meaningful thing we can do for another person is simply show up,” said SCRS Board Member Kena Dacus, when co-presenting the award. “Our recipient has spent a lifetime doing exactly that.”
Past SCRS Chair and co-presenter Amber Alley added that Schroeder’s mentoring, advocacy, and generosity have never stopped, and her impact has kept growing with a genuine love for the industry.

“I truly love this industry,” Schroeder said when accepting the award. “I truly love the people even more. And everything, every person that I ever met means a lot to me. …I just want to cry and just say thank you so much for your love, for your passion that you returned to this industry as much as I have returned to this industry.”

SCRS also awarded the March Taylor Kina’Ole Award to Jason Bartanen in celebration of March Taylor, who passed away in 2007. SCRS says Taylor’s commitment to technical excellence, mentorship, and service to others left a lasting impression on the collision repair community and around the SCRS table.

Taylor was a master technician, owner of Auto Body Hawaii, and an industry leader who spearheaded the idea of a centralized service that repairers could use to submit inquiries challenging estimating systems’ data based on real-world repairs. That idea became the Data Enhancement Gateway (DEG).

“March was a technician first,” said Aaron Schulenburg, SCRS executive director. “He was somebody who believed in the work that was being done behind the front office in the bays of our shops. He lived and breathed and taught the culture of doing the right thing, the right way, for the right reasons, and that’s what kina’ole means.

“I think March understood something that can get lost in conversations about this industry: that the greatest responsibility lies with the men and women who perform repairs; the people who go home at the end of the day with busted knuckles and calloused hands; the people who straighten the structures, and repair the damage, and put vehicles back together. They’re the ones whose work determines how vehicles will protect our families.”
Barry Dorn added that Taylor “stood for the people whose voices weren’t always heard — the technicians, the people doing the work.”

Dorn said Bartanen never loses sight of his “why,” and has spent his career advocating for technicians, investing in their success, and making sure they have someone in their corner. Bartanen has spent years working with SkillsUSA students and now helps build technicians’ careers through his business, Collision ProAssist.

“I’ve always wanted to do the right thing,” Bartanen said. “Our technicians are the reason we’re here today; the men and women who are fixing cars each and every day. I want all of us to lift them up, recognize their accomplishments, and support them.”

In honor of another collision repair industry leader, the Collision Repair Education Foundation (CREF) presented the first annual Clark Plucinski Legacy Award to Chris Evans of State Farm. Evans is a former collision technician and collision center manager who previously served as CREF’s chair and on I-CAR’s Board of Directors.
The award recognizes an individual who embodies the spirit, dedication, and commitment that defined Plucinski’s life and career.
Plucinski dedicated more than 50 years to the collision repair industry, receiving numerous honors and recognitions throughout his career, including induction into the Hall of Eagles in 1993.
From 2012 until his retirement in 2020, Plucinski served as CREF’s executive director.

“Those of you who knew Clark will remember hearing him say time and time again, ‘It’s all about the kids,'” shared Stacy Bartnik, CREF Board of Trustees member. “Those words were more than just a phrase. They reflected his passion, his purpose, his unwavering belief that the future of our industry depends on investing in the next generation. Clark dedicated his career to creating opportunities for students, supporting collision repair education and ensuring that young people had a path to successful careers in our industry.”

articles.title: What Treadwear Grades and Traction Ratings Mean
articles.author: Christian Hinton

paras.en: You’ve probably seen numbers and letters on a tire sidewall. But what do tire treadwear ratings and traction grades actually tell you?

The treadwear grade compares how quickly a tire wore during controlled testing. Generally, a higher grade means the tread wore more slowly during that test. However, the grade is not a mileage guarantee.
Driving habits, tire maintenance, road conditions and climate all affect how long the tread will actually last.

The traction rating measures a tire’s ability to stop on wet pavement during controlled, straight-line braking tests. These ratings can help when comparing tires. However, they do not provide a complete picture of handling, cornering or performance in every condition.
Use treadwear and traction ratings as one part of the decision, along with the vehicle, the driver and how the tire will be used.

articles.title: Don’t Forget Lubrication During an Oil Change
articles.author: Andrew Markel

paras.en: Back in my day at the service station, when a customer came in for an oil change, they pulled it into a grease pit and we would grease up everything on the vehicle—ball joints, universal joints, and then we would do the oil changes. Today, it’s different. Vehicles are a lot more low maintenance.

However, the aftermarket has not abandoned the message that lubrication is required for certain repair components to make that repair just that much better. In other words, we have ball joints that have grease nipples that need to be lubricated every so often, like during an oil change. It’s also written in the vehicle service information that doors and lift hatches need to be lubricated every so often.
Your shop probably has an oil change and you probably call it an LOF. So let’s put that L back in LOF: lubrication, oil, filter.

articles.title: Six Tips for Building and Selling a Better Timing Belt Job
articles.author: Andrew Markel

paras.en: Although timing chains offer maintenance advantages, timing belts can provide benefits for engine efficiency and noise, vibration and harshness (NVH). With many engines having timing belt replacement intervals of more than 100,000 miles, it is very important to recommend a complete service designed to last until the next replacement interval. When preparing the estimate and presenting it to the customer, keep the following six tips in mind.

The labor times for replacing a timing belt found in your shop management system are typically based on ideal conditions. Account for additional labor when corrosion, damaged fasteners or other complications are likely. Labor for servicing the cooling system, front cover or water pump may not be included in the published time.

Also, include the necessary labor to remove and reinstall wheel-well liners, splash shields and other components. If these parts are missing or damaged, replacements may be available and should be included in the estimate.

If the water pump is driven by the timing belt, be aware that a new pump may exhibit a small amount of seepage through the weep hole during its initial break-in period. Changes in water-pump designs can also mean that limited seepage during initial operation may be considered normal. Always consult the pump manufacturer’s service information before determining whether leakage indicates a problem.
On timing-belt-driven water pumps, the weep-hole passage may discharge behind the front cover, making the source of the coolant difficult to identify.
3. Don’t Forget the Other Belts and Tensioners

Whether the engine is mounted longitudinally or transversely, the serpentine belt will usually be removed during the timing belt service. If the customer has not previously replaced the belt, this is the ideal time to recommend replacement.

On many applications, replacing the automatic belt tensioner is also recommended. Some engines may have an additional belt that drives a balance shaft or another component. Inspect these belts and replace them as needed.

Because the camshaft and crankshaft sprockets may already be exposed, consider recommending replacement of the related seals. With some timing belt replacement intervals reaching 120,000 miles, these seals may be prime candidates for replacement because of the age and deterioration of their soft materials and sealing lips.

Some camshaft seals may be subjected to increased pressure from variable valve timing actuators. These seals can be exposed to full engine oil pressure as oil is routed through the camshaft to the actuator. Some timing belt kits include new camshaft and crankshaft seals. When included, these seals should not be treated as optional parts.

If the valve cover gasket is allowing even a small amount of oil to enter the timing belt area, recommend replacing the gasket. This can prevent oil from contaminating the belt and causing premature failure.
6. Don’t Forget the Oil Change and Other Mileage-Based Maintenance

Timing belt replacement is typically part of a larger scheduled maintenance service that may include an oil change, filters, fluids and other service items. Consult the manufacturer’s maintenance schedule and recommend any services due at the vehicle’s current mileage.

articles.title: Dipstick Replacement Sensors: How They Work
articles.author: Andrew Markel

paras.en: GM has taken a lot of guff recently for eliminating the dipstick on some of their newer V8 engines and replacing it with a sensor. Let’s talk about how those sensors actually work, and how and when they measure the oil level.

It’s not like, for example, a brake master cylinder that has a float and a level that turns on the light on the dash when it reaches a certain level. These sensors are ultrasonic. In other words, it’s sending out a sound wave into the oil pan and determining the oil level that way.

How does it know when to measure the level of oil in the oil pan? If you’re using a dipstick, the vehicle would be parked, it probably wouldn’t be running, and that’s when you’re checking the oil level. The sensor works the same way: It’s only measuring the oil level at certain instances. Let’s say it’s in Park when you first start up. Let’s say you’re sitting at a traffic light; that is when it’s measuring the level.
For more on sensors and how they work, including oxygen and TPMS sensors, watch the video above.

articles.title: AISIN Announces New Product Program
articles.author: Alex Crissey

paras.en: AISIN Corp. announced that it will introduce a new product line at the Automotive Aftermarket Products Expo (AAPEX) in Las Vegas.

To support the rollout, AISIN vetted and established a pilot program with a China-based global supply chain partner. The pilot enabled AISIN to maintain its OE-quality standards while expanding into new, high-volume maintenance-related categories, the company said.
Parts available through this program include products in cooling systems, drivetrain, steering, suspension, chemicals and fluids.

The new AISIN product range has begun rolling out through online sellers first, including Amazon, and will expand into offline channels by the end of the year. Following the pilot, the company has a pending joint venture in the works, with additional details to be announced at completion.
The new line of products will be on display at booth V3261 in The Venetian Expo at AAPEX, Nov. 3-5, 2026.

articles.title: Worldpac to Open Automated Distribution Center
articles.author: Alex Crissey

paras.en: Worldpac announced plans to open its first automated distribution center, a new 413,000-square-foot facility in Forest Park, Georgia. Scheduled to begin operations in the first half of 2027, the facility will feature AutoStore robotic storage and retrieval technology.

The facility will support Worldpac branches and customers across the Southeast and surrounding markets, while providing more than 250,000 additional square feet compared with the current Norcross distribution center, the company said.

AutoStore is an automated storage and retrieval system that uses robotics to store, retrieve, and process inventory within a highly efficient storage grid. Rather than team members traveling through warehouse aisles to locate parts, inventory is automatically delivered to workstations for picking, replenishment, and processing.
The facility will be located at 2160 Anvil Block Road, Suite 200 Forest Park, GA 30297.

“We are excited to expand Worldpac’s distribution presence in the Atlanta metro market and strengthen our ability to serve customers throughout the Southeastern United States. The Forest Park facility represents a major step forward in our use of robotics and automation, helping us improve speed, accuracy, and efficiency,” said Rich Tannenbaum, chief operating officer of Worldpac.

articles.title: AACF Elects Marc Blackman President of Board of Trustees
articles.author: Jeff White

paras.en: The Automotive Aftermarket Charitable Foundation (AACF) announced the election of Marc Blackman as president of its board of trustees, effective Jan. 1, 2027. Blackman, chairman and CEO of Gold Eagle Co., succeeds Jon Owens, who served as president for three years. During his tenure, Owens helped advance the foundation’s mission of providing emergency financial assistance to aftermarket employees and their families.

Blackman brings extensive industry leadership experience and a commitment to the people who work in the aftermarket. As AACF’s secretary and an executive committee member, he has helped guide the foundation’s work and priorities.

As president, Blackman will draw on his experience building relationships, leading industry organizations and developing a people-focused company culture. His leadership will help AACF strengthen partnerships, engage supporters and reach more families facing unexpected hardship.

“I am humbled and honored to serve as President of the AACF Board of Trustees. AACF represents what is so special about our automotive aftermarket community: people coming together to help one another when it matters most,” said Blackman.
Gold Eagle’s Longstanding Support of the Foundation
Blackman’s election continues Gold Eagle’s connection to AACF. A Champion Donor and supporter for more than 20 years, Gold Eagle has helped sustain the foundation’s assistance efforts.
That commitment includes former AACF President Bob Hirsch, whose dedication helped establish a lasting tradition of giving back within the company.

“I’m grateful to follow the exceptional leaders who have served before me,” Blackman added. “I look forward to working with our Board to continue supporting aftermarket employees and their families in their time of need.”

Gold Eagle is a 94-year-old, family-owned American manufacturer of premium engine additives, specialty cleaners and protectants. At the company, Blackman emphasizes empowerment, continuous improvement, candid communication and trust.

His industry service includes previous terms as chairman of MEMA and the Automotive Aftermarket Suppliers Association’s board of governors. He also serves as a lifetime trustee of the University of the Aftermarket.

As AACF prepares for the transition, the foundation thanked Owens for his time, care and commitment. His service reflects the industry’s commitment to helping aftermarket employees and their families.

“Jon has given his time, energy, and heart to AACF, and we’re grateful for the leadership he has provided,” said John Kairys, AACF executive director. “Marc brings a thoughtful approach, deep industry relationships, and a clear commitment to our mission. We look forward to working together to build on that progress and help more families when they need us most.”

articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: The Aftermarket Warehouse Distributors Association (AWDA), a community of the Auto Care Association, presented the 2026 Art Fisher Award for Excellence in Education, to Corey Bartlett, CEO of Auto Parts Headquarters (APH) based in St. Cloud, Minnesota. The award was presented on November 1st by AWDA Vice Chair Young Suhr at AWDA’s 2026 Annual Conference in Las Vegas.

AWDA’s Art Fisher Award for Excellence in Education is presented annually to an aftermarket company or individual that demonstrates outstanding commitment to education and training, either within their organization or throughout the industry. Given in memory of former AWDA Chairman Art Fisher, the award grants scholarships in the name of the award winner to two students enrolled in the automotive aftermarket management program at Northwood University. AWDA Vice Chair Young Suhr presented the award.

He completed the University of the Aftermarket’s Leadership 2010 program and earned Automotive Aftermarket Professional and Master Automotive Aftermarket Professional designations in 2002 and 2009.

“Corey has shown incredible initiative in supporting training and continuing education,” said John R. Washbish, president and CEO, Aftermarket Auto Parts Alliance, Inc. “Through his leadership roles and example, he has consistently improved the education and standards of his staff, the Alliance, and the industry as a whole.”

articles.title: Bo Fisher Receives 2026 AWDA Lifetime Achievement Award
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: The Aftermarket Warehouse Distributors Association (AWDA), a community of the Auto Care Association, presented its 2026 Lifetime Achievement Award in honor of Martin Fromm to Bo Fisher, Chairman and CEO of Fisher Auto Parts. The award was presented by AWDA Chairperson Fletcher Lord III on November 1 at AWDA’s 2026 Annual Conference in Las Vegas.

AWDA’s Lifetime Achievement Award recognizes individuals who have, over the course of many years, distinguished themselves through their unselfish commitment to, and high level of performance within, the motor vehicle aftermarket industry. The award is named in honor of former AWDA President Martin Fromm.

As chairman and CEO of Fisher Auto Parts, Fisher has built upon a remarkable family legacy while leading one of the industry’s most respected independent distribution organizations. Under his leadership, the company expanded to approximately 500 company-owned locations and many more independent locations across 18 states, achieving tenfold growth over two decades while remaining debt-free.

Fisher has championed collaboration among independent distributors and built an organization grounded in relationships, customer service, integrity and commitment to the professional automotive service industry. His dedication to education continues the vision of his father, Art Fisher, through the Art Fisher Memorial Scholarship program, annual scholarships and the KOI/Fisher Training Cavalcade. His contributions earned him the Mort Schwartz Excellence in Education Award.

Throughout his career, Fisher has demonstrated humility, loyalty, generosity and a willingness to share knowledge and opportunity. His legacy extends beyond the company he has grown to the industry he has strengthened, the people he has inspired and the opportunities he has created.

articles.title: When dinosaurs are sold to the highest bidder, we all lose
articles.author: Kristi Curry Rogers

paras.en: Dinosaurs are more than extraordinary specimens with massive price tags. They are irreplaceable snapshots of our planet's history and our own human journey. When scientifically important fossils are reduced to luxury commodities, we are robbed of the evidence that makes them valuable in the first place.

On Oct. 27, a 19.6-foot-long (6 meters) skeleton of Nanotyrannus lancensis known as "Jodi" was sold at Sotheby's in New York for $47,255,000, far exceeding its $6 million to $9 million estimate. The buyer and seller were not identified. It was the latest in a string of multimillion-dollar dinosaur auctions, following the $50.1 million sale of a T. rex (Gus) in July and the $44.6 million sale of a Stegosaurus (Apex) in 2024.
Fossils like Jodi, Apex, and Gus belong in public collections, where they can contribute to science and remain accessible for future generations. Not in the hands of private collectors.

There are three main reasons why. First: Fossils are evidence, not objects. A dinosaur's bones can reveal how it grew, moved, fed, and lived. They preserve traces of injury and disease, help reconstruct ancient ecosystems, and offer clues about the "rules of life" governing our world that scientists are still learning to interpret.

Jodi illustrates exactly why access to physical evidence matters. For nearly half a century, paleontologists debated whether Nanotyrannus was a distinct dinosaur or simply a juvenile T. rex. A lack of well-preserved fossils available for study only fueled the uncertainty. And then a remarkable specimen, once in private hands, moved into the public trust.

The fossil was uncovered in Montana in 2006 alongside a Triceratops. Dubbed the "Dueling Dinosaurs," it took until 2022, and an appeal in the state's Supreme Court, for the remains to be acquired by the Museum of Natural Sciences so they could be fully studied. This research provided a powerful new perspective, arguing that Nanotyrannus lancensis was a distinct dinosaur and, moreover, that a second species of Nanotyrannus once roamed the American West.

This hypothesis has big implications for the health of ecosystems before one of Earth's most severe extinction events — but it currently rests on the scant few Nanotyrannus specimens housed in public collections. Specimens like Jodi could uphold or dethrone it. Without access, we, and Jodi’s true identity, will remain in the dark.

It is hard to overstate the irony of Jodi's sale: a specimen recently listed as a juvenile T. rex now captures the world's imagination, and commands double the price tag, as a "Nanotyrannus." Yet if a similar fate had befallen the Dueling Dinosaurs and they had remained in private hands, we would not have known for certain that Nanotyrannus ever existed.

Scientific progress depends on researchers being able to compare specimens, test hypotheses, and revisit earlier conclusions. When access relies on a private owner's permission, repeatability is not assured, and science cannot proceed. A specimen might be available today but inaccessible tomorrow. This is why access to the evidence must endure.
This brings us to the second problem with privately owned dinosaurs. Digital scans cannot replace the original fossil.

Three-dimensional scans and digital models are powerful tools. We use them to measure bones, compare anatomy, share information, and educate the public. But digital models capture only the most superficial aspects of a fossil's story.

To understand dinosaur growth, we examine microscopic structures inside fossilized bone through a technique called bone histology. We also analyze the chemistry of fossils to investigate diet, migration patterns, and metabolism. Such work requires physical samples, not just images of a bone's surface. We also need contextual data about the surrounding sediments, preservation mode, and ancient environment in order to explore questions about the ecosystems in which the animals once lived. Much of this information is lost in the rush to excavate and prepare fossils as quickly as possible for the auction block. It can never be reclaimed.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: We cannot predict what novel technologies future researchers will employ to make new discoveries from old bones, or even which questions they will ask. Technology will continue to advance, bringing analytical methods we cannot anticipate. A scan made today does not guarantee that researchers will have the physical evidence needed for tomorrow's discoveries. Digital access should complement preservation of original specimens, not justify losing it.

Finally, private ownership cannot guarantee lasting public access. Yes, some private collectors financially support research and education and donate specimens they purchase. Those contributions are valuable. But the issue is not whether an individual owner is generous; it is whether access is guaranteed over time.

A temporary loan is insufficient. A loaned specimen can be withdrawn, sold, or inherited by someone with different priorities, situations that are becoming increasingly common in the U.S. and abroad. By contrast, a fossil deposited in a responsible public research institution is documented, cared for, studied, and made available to future researchers and educators in perpetuity. The question is not whether people should be able to admire dinosaurs; it is whether the evidence that helps us understand them will remain available to everyone.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Nor should museums consider selling scientifically important fossils to cover operating shortfalls. Collections are not ordinary financial assets to liquidate when budgets tighten. Selling an irreplaceable specimen provides a one-time payment while sacrificing future scientific potential. Museums need sustainable funding for collections care, research, and education, not pressure to trade away the very resources they exist to preserve.

Jodi's sale is complete, but the fossil's long-term future remains uncertain. With the buyer's identity undisclosed, the public cannot know what arrangements, if any, will ensure continued access for researchers and educators. We hope the new owner will make Jodi available for scientific study and public education, through permanent placement in a public research institution. But hope is not a substitute for a guarantee.

There is a better way to support paleontology. Enthusiasts who want to share in the excitement of discovery can fund fieldwork and research, endow curatorial positions, strengthen museum collections, or donate important fossils to public institutions where we can all learn from them.

Dinosaurs inspire wonder because they connect us to a world vastly different from our own. But their importance extends far beyond their power to captivate us. They are part of our shared natural heritage and an irreplaceable record of Earth's history.

We should measure a dinosaur's worth not by the price it commands at auction, but by the knowledge it can help us build, and by whether we preserve that opportunity for generations to come. Earth's history belongs to all of us, not to the highest bidder.

She is also an Associate Research Professor at NC State University, President of the Jurassic Foundation, and Chair of the Ethics Committee for the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology. Her work champions transparency, inclusivity, and public access to science.

articles.title: Southern Taurid meteor shower could bring fireballs ‪this week —‬ when and where to look
articles.author: Jamie Carter

paras.en: One of autumn's best opportunities to see brilliant "fireballs" arrives overnight Wednesday and Thursday (Nov. 4-5) during the Southern Taurid meteor shower.

Although the Southern Taurids are a minor meteor shower that produces only a handful of "shooting stars" each hour, it occasionally features exceptionally bright meteors called fireballs, which can briefly light up the night sky. According to NASA, fireballs are meteors at least as bright as Venus.
The Southern Taurids are active for several weeks in fall and peak Oct. 14, but the American Meteor Society expects the "fireball swarm component" to peak around Nov. 4-5.

Meteors can streak across any part of the sky, but for this meteor shower, they appear to radiate from the constellation Taurus, which will rise in the eastern sky as night falls and climb higher as the night progresses. That makes the hours around midnight a good time to look for shooting stars. However, unlike major meteor showers such as the Perseids (which peak Aug. 12-13) and the Geminids (which peak Dec. 13-14), the Southern Taurids have a broad peak, so there's no need to be outside at an exact time.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The Southern Taurids are the first of two fireball-rich meteor showers to be visible this month. The Northern Taurids will peak overnight on Nov. 11-12, giving stargazers another chance to spot a fireball. Both meteor showers result from dust and debris left in the inner solar system by Comet 2P/Encke striking Earth's atmosphere.

Discovered in 1786, Encke is a massive comet, measuring 2.98 miles (4.8 kilometers) in diameter, according to NASA — around one-third the size of the object thought to have killed the nonavian dinosaurs. Encke orbits the sun every 3.3 years, one of the shortest known orbital periods of any comet in the solar system. Scientists theorize that Encke is one of many fragments of a giant comet that broke apart 20,000 to 30,000 years ago.

After the Southern and Northern Taurids, the next meteor shower will be the Leonids, which peak Nov. 17-18 and produce around 15 shooting stars per hour, and the Geminids, which peak Dec. 13-14 and can deliver up to 120 shooting stars per hour close to the peak.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

It's best to watch meteor showers with the naked eye, but a good backyard telescope will serve you well in the months to come. As the long nights of winter kick off in the Northern Hemisphere, skywatching opportunities abound — including four consecutive supermoons from Nov. 2026 to Feb. 2027.

Jamie Carter is a Cardiff, U.K.-based freelance science journalist and a regular contributor to Live Science. He is the author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners and co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and leads international stargazing and eclipse-chasing tours. His work appears regularly in Space.com, Forbes, New Scientist, BBC Sky at Night, Sky & Telescope, and other major science and astronomy publications. He is also the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com.

articles.title: This self-powered toothbrush makes electricity to kill cavity-causing bacteria
articles.author: Isha Ishtiaq

paras.en: A toothbrush that generates its own electricity with every stroke could offer a new way to fight the microbes behind cavities and gum disease.

Conventional toothbrushes rely on physical scrubbing to remove plaque from teeth and gums. But even after a thorough brush, some bacteria remain and begin rebuilding plaque. To solve that problem, researchers have developed a self-powered toothbrush that converts the friction of brushing into an electrical charge. That electricity is intended to zap the plaque-promoting bacteria and keep them from colonizing teeth.

"It's great to have new approaches that actually enhance the effect of mechanical cleaning," said Nicholas Jakubovics, an oral microbiologist at Newcastle University in the U.K. who was not involved in the study. "The idea that the toothbrush surface itself is actively doing something is really interesting."

The experimental brush has bristles made from polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), a plastic that generates electricity when bent; these types of energy-producing materials are called piezoelectric. As the bristles flex during brushing, they produce an electrical charge that then triggers chemical reactions in saliva and water. These reactions release reactive oxygen species (ROS), which are highly reactive molecules that can damage bacterial cells.

Even when the bristles are not being used to brush, they carry a faint surface charge that helps prevent bacteria from clinging to the brush head when the toothbrush isn't in use, the team reported Wednesday (Nov. 4) in the journal Science Advances.

In laboratory tests where the toothbrush was used on isolated germs, its electrified bristles killed more than half of the Streptococcus mutans bacteria present. These microbes contribute to tooth decay. By comparison, nylon bristles killed just 9% of the bacteria. They also reduced levels of Porphyromonas gingivalis, a bacterium linked to gum disease, by up to 78%, while nylon brushes reduced them by less than 8%.

When the researchers added an antioxidant — a compound that neutralizes ROS — the new toothbrush's antibacterial effect largely disappeared, highlighting that the ROS are likely the key to its effects.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team also found that the activity of certain genes in both S. mutans and P. gingivalis fell after exposure to the electrified bristles. These genes are involved in making ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters — molecular pumps that help shuttle essential nutrients across bacterial cell membranes. The researchers suspect that disrupting this machinery makes it harder for these microbes to survive and cling to teeth.

But Jakubovics was not convinced by that part of the team's explanation. "ABC transporters transport all sorts of different things," he said, adding that the findings did not clearly show how changes in these genes affected the bacteria.

The researchers also tested the new brush against plaque biofilms — hardy communities of bacteria that stick together and cling to tooth surfaces. For the experiment, they grew human dental plaque on cow tooth enamel and found that the brush removed more than 99% of the biofilm, outperforming a regular nylon brush.

Finally, the team moved to humans, putting the brush to the test in 115 adults with gum inflammation or tooth decay. These study participants were randomly assigned to use either the new toothbrushes or traditional nylon-bristled brushes twice a day for three months. (The study didn't note whether participants noticed a difference in sensation when using the electrified brushes.)

By the end of the trial, the participants who used the electrified bristles had less plaque, less gum inflammation and less bleeding than the participants who used ordinary brushes. Plaque samples also showed that the people who used electrified brushes had lower levels of bacteria associated with oral disease and higher levels of beneficial bacteria, which have previously been reported to suppress harmful oral bacteria and support oral health.

The researchers think that the disease-linked bacteria may have relatively fragile cell membranes, making them more vulnerable to damage from ROS than the beneficial bacteria. That's a theory that requires further study, though, so it's not completely clear how selective the brush is against plaque-causing bacteria.

In a test of the toothbrush's durability, the PVDF bristles retained their structure and electrical properties over three months of simulated use. Lab-grown mouse cells repeatedly exposed to brush material showed no signs of damage, and brushing on cow tooth enamel did not increase surface roughness. However, these tests cannot establish whether repeated use of these brushes is safe for humans.

"We would want to make sure that it is safe on the tissues for long-term use," Jakubovics said. He noted that, in lab tests, bacteria are grown directly on the bristles and exposed to their electricity for hours, "whereas in reality, in the mouth, your bristle is only in contact with the tooth or oral tissue for a very short time."

The trial with humans provides some insight into how the brush works in real life, but it was relatively small. Larger studies will be needed to find out whether the toothbrush offers a meaningful advantage over conventional brushes. For now, Jakubovics sees the recent study as just a proof of concept; more information and more convincing clinical data are still needed, he emphasized.

Isha Ishtiaq is a freelance health journalist based in Pakistan who covers health, medicine and biomedical research. Her work has appeared in Live Science, Science News, and Medscape, among other outlets. She holds a B.S. (Hons) in biotechnology from the University of Gujrat and an M.S. in biological sciences from the University of Sialkot, where her research focused on the use of deep learning models for disease detection.
