articles.title: Scientists Say They've Found Preserved Dinosaur Blood in a 115-Million-Year-Old Fossil, but Not Everyone Is Convinced

paras.en: Scientists say they’ve discovered blood inside a 115-million-year-old dinosaur bone. That’s backed by their detection of heme, an iron-rich molecule in hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen and gives blood its red color. The findings, described November 2 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, potentially represent the oldest red blood cells ever found in a dinosaur fossil.

“Evidence from microscopy, mineralogy, spectroscopy and molecular geochemistry all point toward the same conclusion,” lead author Kliti Grice, a geochemist at Curtin University in Australia, writes for the Conversation. “We are convinced these are fossilized red blood cell structures containing traces of heme molecules.”
However, some outside experts remain unconvinced.

Grice and colleagues made their discoveries while analyzing a hind leg bone of an Aratasaurus museunacionali, a small, bipedal, meat-eating dinosaur that lived during the Cretaceous period. This individual is believed to have been about 4 years old when it died; it wasn’t yet fully grown, weighing an estimated 75 pounds and measuring about 10 feet long.

Discovered in a mine in northeastern Brazil in 2008, the fossil eventually went to the country’s National Museum in Rio de Janeiro. In 2024, experts sent it to Grice and colleagues, who had agreed to investigate the specimen. The scientists did that by first slicing off thin sections, then using hydrochloric acid to remove the surrounding rock.

In 2018, a fire destroyed millions of objects in Brazil’s National Museum—the oldest national history museum in the Americas. A. museunacionali’s name is a combination of Greek and the Indigenous Brazilian language Tupi that translates to “the dinosaur born from the National Museum fire.”

When they looked at the fossil slices under a high-resolution microscope, they spotted numerous structures that resembled red blood cells. The blobs were round with sunken centers, each measuring about 23 micrometers long by 20 micrometers wide. Additionally, they were located inside vascular canals—the channels that carried blood vessels through the bone while the animal was alive.
“I was jumping up and down,” Grice tells New Scientist’s James Woodford. “I ran up to my head of school’s office and was so excited that he gave me a whisky to calm me down.”

To confirm their hunch, the team performed several types of analyses on the samples. These tests revealed two chemical fingerprints of heme, including a degraded form of the molecule that hints at its ancient origins.

When they performed similar analyses on the sediment surrounding the fossil, they got very different results. They mostly found evidence of plants and bacteria, with only small traces of heme. This, the researchers say, suggests the fossilized bone samples were not contaminated.

Additionally, the scientists compared the structures to the blood cells of birds and crocodiles, the closest living relatives of dinosaurs. The A. museunacionali cells were longer and wider than the bird and crocodile blood cells. However, the researchers suspect the A. museunacionali cells might have gotten deformed as the bone turned to fossil; another possible explanation is that dinosaurs’ red blood cells were simply shaped differently.
The scientists also found evidence of an amino acid found in collagen, a structural protein that provides strength, support and elasticity to the body’s tissues.

Taken together, the findings point to the discovery of red blood cells, the researchers argue. If confirmed, this would mark the first time red blood cells with the chemical signature of heme have ever been found inside a dinosaur fossil.

“What we believe is distinctive about the present study is the strength of the combined evidence: numerous red-blood-cell-like structures in situ within the dinosaur bone, their mineralization, their location in the vascular system and associated in situ chemical evidence related to heme,” Grice tells Reuters’ Will Dunham. “To the best of our knowledge, that combination has not previously been demonstrated in a dinosaur fossil in this way.”

Still, scientists have made similar claims before. According to Science’s Rodrigo Pérez Ortega, at least 14 studies have tried to describe red blood cells in ancient fossils. However, these findings remain controversial because soft tissues, including blood, break down relatively quickly after an animal dies and are rarely preserved. Additionally, certain minerals look very similar to red blood cells under a microscope, meaning what appears to be evidence of ancient blood may actually be a geologic look-alike. Contamination—from both ancient and modern sources—can also be an issue.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Researchers were skeptical of the new study for the same reasons. Maria McNamara, a paleobiologist at University College Cork in Ireland who was not involved with the new study, tells Science that the paper is “probably the most comprehensive effort that’s been done so far.” However, she would still be “very cautious about interpreting those necessarily as red blood cells.”

Nevertheless, Grice and her colleagues stand by their conclusions, arguing their work demonstrates that fossilized soft tissues can and do survive for millions of years under certain conditions. They suspect this creature’s vascular structures were preserved because of what happened after it died: It was quickly buried by water and sediments full of microorganisms, creating conditions that slowed decay. Hausmannite, a manganese oxide mineral, may have helped preserve the red blood cells specifically, reports Live Science’s Kenna Hughes-Castleberry.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The scientists say the techniques they used could help researchers uncover previously overlooked biological material in other fossils, which could “potentially help us ask much more sophisticated questions about the physiology of extinct animals,” Grice tells CNN’s Taylor Nicioli.

“Bones provide extraordinary information about anatomy, growth, locomotion and evolution,” she adds. “But cellular and molecular preservation potentially gives us access to a different layer of biological information: the chemistry of the living animal and its tissues.”

articles.title: New York Had Its First Measles Death in 30 Years. Here's What to Know

paras.en: A 7-month-old child in New York died of measles on Monday, marking the state’s first death from the disease in more than 30 years.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul said in a statement that she was “heartbroken,” and that the death is “a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses.” Last month, Hochul declared measles a statewide disaster.

Measles is a highly infectious viral illness that infects the respiratory tract. Once eliminated from the United States, cases in the country have now reached the highest they’ve been in 35 years, with more than 5,000 cases counted so far. Pennsylvania is seeing the worst of it, with 140 cases counted in just the last two weeks and more than a thousand this year. These outbreaks put the United States at risk of losing its official measles elimination status, gained in 2000.

“The U.S. is in the throes of the deadliest measles outbreak it has seen in decades,” said Jennifer Nuzzo, an epidemiologist and director of the Pandemic Center at Brown University, to Lauren J. Young at Scientific American at the beginning of the year. “Losing measles elimination status is an official acknowledgement that the country is on the wrong path.”

This comes at a time of increased vaccine hesitancy and widespread anti-vaccine rhetoric by officials like Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. In January, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) overhauled its immunization schedules for kids, dropping a number of recommended vaccines. While that decision didn’t include measles, vaccination rates for the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) combined shot in kindergartners have dropped to 92.4 percent, which is below the critical 95 percent threshold for herd immunity.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Quick fact: Current immunization schedule for kids in the U.S.

- The CDC now recommends 11 immunizations for children, down from 17 in 2025. The six dropped from the list by January 2026 included immunizations for hepatitis A, hepatitis B, influenza, meningitis, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and rotavirus.

Roughly 96 percent of people infected with measles this year were either unvaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status, according to CDC data. Jeffery Tompkins, the coroner and district attorney of Lewis County, where the child died, confirmed to Joseph Goldstein at the New York Times that the infant was not vaccinated. Children typically receive the first dose of the MMR vaccine when they are between 12 and 15 months of age, though public health authorities can recommend that a child receive a dose at 6 months if there is a community outbreak.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “The MMR vaccine is the best way to prevent measles and stop outbreaks,” says Andrew D. Racine, the president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, to Melissa Jenco at AAP News. “It is safe, reliable, inexpensive and readily available. When enough people are vaccinated, the virus can’t spread throughout the community.”

While most measles outbreaks still mainly happen in countries with low income or weak health infrastructure, the United States is not the only high-income country facing rising cases. Last year, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) revoked Canada’s measles elimination status because it had 12 months of continual measles transmission. The United Kingdom is also experiencing a surge of cases. Experts blame decreasing vaccination rates for both countries.
PAHO will meet from November 10 to 13, when the United States is widely expected to lose its measles elimination status.

articles.title: Faded Over Millennia, the Intricately Carved Sandstone Walls of This Ancient Egyptian Shrine Will See Color Once Again

paras.en: Roughly 2,700 years ago, in the deserts of present-day northern Sudan, a massive shrine was brought to rise in the city of Kawa. Built from 236 sandstone blocks inside a temple to Amun-Ra, the king of the ancient Egyptian gods, the shrine’s ornate sandstone walls told an unmistakable story of devotion and power.

Known as the Shrine of Taharqa after the pharaoh who commissioned it, the structure’s carvings show several depictions of Taharqa—the ruler of both Egypt and Kush between 690 B.C.E. and 664 B.C.E.—extending offerings to gods while exerting royal influence among his mortal subjects.

Modern research suggests that during Taharqa’s time, these scenes were plastered and painted in vibrant color. But by the 1930s, when the shrine was excavated by British archaeologists, the carved sandstone was remarkably intact but colorless.

Subsequently transferred to the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford, England, modern eyes have only ever looked upon the shrine—the only free-standing pharaonic building in Britain—as a beige sandstone relic. Later this month, however, the museum will restore the lavish shrine as Taharqa once saw it, with the help of digital light projections.

“This exceptional monument offers a fascinating insight into the art and archaeology of ancient Sudan,” Liam McNamara, the museum's curator for Ancient Egypt and Sudan, says in a statement. “The new projection—and the scientific research behind it—will allow visitors to appreciate and understand the shrine’s original painted decoration like never before.”
Researchers carefully studied the shrine with infrared and hyperspectral imaging cameras to identify trace amounts of surviving pigments that are all but invisible to the naked eye.

Among the most notable of their discoveries was evidence of Egyptian Blue, the world’s oldest-known synthetic pigment, typically reserved to color depictions of high-profile royals and deities. Researchers also identified traces of yellows and reds, among other vibrant hues.
Starting on November 13, visitors to the Ashmolean will see these and other colors projected onto the walls of the shrine, bringing life to the stories told on the ancient walls.

According to McNamara, the carvings partially tell the story of the shrine’s creation, starting with a young Taharqa visiting the semi-buried ruins of an earlier temple to Amun-Ra, built under the reign of Tutankhamen, and vowing to restore the shrine, the Art Newspaper’s Maev Kennedy reports. It also shows Taharqa depicted as both an Egyptian pharaoh wearing the double crown representing Upper and Lower Egypt, as well as a Kushite king with a ram’s head and cobras.
The projection will be accompanied by two newly produced films, which share further details about the 43-square-foot shrine and its 2,500-mile journey from Sudan to England in the 1930s.

According to museum records, the shrine was given to Oxford by the Sudanese government in recognition of Egyptologist Francis Llewellyn Griffith’s contribution to the region’s archaeology. Griffith and his team encountered swarming midges as they disassembled the shrine and put it into 200 wooden crates, each wrapped in palm fibers and loaded onto a barge. It sailed up the Nile River and was carried by train to the Red Sea. Another vessel made the final leg to England.
Exploring and recreating the hidden colors ancient artworks—from hot pink Roman togas to 1,600-year-old color-changing glass—has been a popular area of recent research.

“A trip to Egypt in 2022 inspired my interest in the vivid colors used millennia ago, preserved by the arid climate, and still visible today,” James Lupton, the chair the museum’s board of visitors, says in the statement. “I hope that this use of technology in the Ashmolean will similarly inspire our visitors, especially the young.”

articles.title: Hugging Face’s CEO Says His P(Doom) Is ‘Close to Zero’
articles.author: Will Knight

paras.en: Future AI risks are most likely to come from big companies building in secret while open models play defense, Clément Delangue, CEO of Hugging Face said Wednesday at the WIRED World Fair in Miami.

“Most of the risk is actually created by a couple of players building behind closed doors,” Delangue said. “Most of the mitigation of this risk will be the full ecosystem, meaning everyone being able to build in the open.”

HuggingFace is one of the first companies to be attacked by a rogue AI. This July, agents being tested by OpenAI broke free of their sandbox and chose to attack the startup in search of answers to problems they had been set to solve. The company used an open-weight Chinese model called GLM-5.2 to investigate and counter the onslaught.

Delangue noted that agent misbehavior has so far mostly come from big companies that are testing frontier AI in secret. He said that future risks, perhaps involving the biological capabilities of models or their capacity to improve themselves recursively, are likely to emerge from these closed labs, too.

Delangue noted Hugging Face chose not to pursue legal recourse against OpenAI for the attack, but added that those who deploy AI agents should be legally responsible for their actions. “Cyber-attacks are illegal, and I think it’s really important we make sure that agentic cyberattacks [are] illegal,” he told the event. “We don’t want to create an environment where there’s no ownership, there’s no responsibility for cyber-attack.”

In contrast to some AI researchers who have warned that the technology could pose an existential risk to humanity, Delangue said his P(doom)—the probability of this happening—is “close to zero.” “There are many other topics that could destroy the world,” he said.
Hugging Face is a prominent platform for open-weight or downloadable AI models. Its users can share and access models hosted by the company or download them to their own computer systems.

Nvidia, the world’s dominant AI chipmaker, announced that it would acquire the platform for $12.93 billion this September. When the acquisition was announced, Hugging Face said it had around 18 million users.

Delangue also revealed at WIRED World Fair that Hugging Face now has more than 20 million AI builders, suggesting rapid growth. Delangue also revealed that HuggingFace has sold 50,000 Microducks, a cute, two-legged robot from HuggingFace that can be programmed using AI.
Delangue told the conference that the success of open source AI will also be crucial in preventing a few companies and individuals from completely dominating the future.

“We could really clearly end up in a world where only a few companies control the majority of AI.” Delangue said. “There are very strong natural tendencies because [a few companies] really monopolize talent, compute, and capabilities.”

Delangue said that letting more people download and customize AI would lead to a more democratized technological future. The Hugging Face CEO said that the Nvidia acquisition would enable the company to compete as AI requires ever-more resources.

articles.title: Knives Are Out in the White House
articles.author: Hugo Lowell

paras.en: President Donald Trump’s aides were reeling from the scale of Republican losses on Tuesday night, but they almost immediately began figuring out who to blame.

The ultimate responsibility, officials acknowledged only in private, lay with Trump for taking the country into an unpopular war with Iran that drove up prices, which became the number one issue for voters.

But in the absence of being able to blame Trump publicly, there has been growing pressure to find scapegoats in all places, from cabinet officials to White House aides to conservative media commentators.

Recalling how then-president George W. Bush pushed out defense secretary Donald Rumsfeld after the GOP lost both chambers in 2006, sources say there is an expectation from furious officials and donors for Trump to do something similar.

Trump does not seem to have made up his mind on whether he should, sources say, in part because of a recognition that there was perhaps not much that his staff could have done to stave off such overwhelming Democratic victories.

He has also been advised recently, sources tell Inner Loop, that it may be better to keep top staff inside the proverbial tent to ensure they remain loyal in the event they receive subpoenas from congressional investigators next year.

Still, some early scrutiny has been cast on people around Trump who have been viewed as encouraging the president to continue the Iran war even as it started to drag down polls months before the midterms.

Some scrutiny has been directed at defense secretary Pete Hegseth, who has been the target of a whisper campaign that he kept presenting rosy military outlooks that misled Trump into believing more strikes could win the war.

The presentations had been so glowing, sources say, that a number of top officials, including vice president JD Vance and secretary of state Marco Rubio this spring started requesting their own intelligence briefings to get a more somber assessment of the situation.
The Department of Defense did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

In other quarters, Trump advisers have been furious with conservative media commentators who they see as having encouraged the president to double down on the war even after it became mired in a stalemate over the Strait of Hormuz.

And still others returned to blaming White House deputy chief of staff James Blair, who temporarily left the administration to develop the GOP midterm strategy, including an effort to redraw congressional maps to favor Republicans.

In the end, that redistricting gambit backfired in epic fashion. Out of 14 key districts that got redrawn this cycle, Republicans won just one race in Texas and one race in Tennessee, while Democrats won most races in deep red Texas and Ohio by double digits.

Blair was already getting flak preemptively as polls ahead of the midterms showed Republicans down even in those races, some of which Trump carried by wide margins in the 2024 presidential election. But with many of the results now final, Blair has become a target, sources say.

Trump, for his part, spent the latter part of election night blaming the quality of candidates in key battleground races and claiming voters did not support Republicans because he was not on the ballot himself.

Still, other people in Trump’s orbit have been horrified but unsurprised that the president took no personal responsibility and denied that the devastating GOP losses were effectively a referendum on his second term.

Many of the candidates in key Senate races were people that Trump had chosen and endorsed, including the scandal-plagued Republican state attorney general Ken Paxton in Texas and the inexperienced Darline Graham, sister of the late senator Lindsey Graham, in South Carolina.
And in North Carolina, the former RNC chair Michael Whatley was defeated resoundingly by the Democratic Roy Cooper—but only after Trump primaried the popular incumbent Thom Tillis earlier this year.

As for Trump’s claim that he wasn’t on the ballot, that was undercut by the president explicitly telling voters at rallies across the country to pretend that he was, in order to drive turnout. And at those same rallies, some advisers noted, Trump overshadowed his own message by repeatedly talking about record profits of oil companies and his vanity construction projects.
Voters, it’s clear, didn’t like that message.

articles.title: Google Is Forcing AI Overviews in Classrooms. Schools Are Searching for a Way Out
articles.author: Paresh Dave

paras.en: Two weeks ago, an IT administrator for an elementary-middle school took to Google’s support forums requesting a way to block students from seeing AI Overviews—the chatbot-generated answers at the top of search results.

“This seems counterproductive to what we're trying to teach,” the administrator wrote. “Students need opportunities to navigate search results, examine sources, and draw their own conclusions rather than being handed an AI-generated synthesis before they've even started.”

No one from Google responded to the concern, which has been bubbling up for years. But counterparts from three districts voiced similar frustration and pointed to workarounds they were employing or considering to block AI Overviews in lieu of an official “off” switch. Their expertise is about to be in demand.

Google announced on Tuesday that it is declining to provide schools an option to disable AI Overviews. Instead, starting next year, schools will have to block access to search altogether to get rid of the feature. The decision has stunned educators, parents, and technology researchers across the US.

“We were flabbergasted,” says Dominique Johnson, part of an Oregon community group called Lake Oswego Parents For Responsible Technology. “This move makes things even more difficult for school districts that have determined AI is harmful to foundational learning.”

Google didn’t respond to a request for comment. But in a public response to the controversy shared on X, the company contended that schools will now have “more choice, not less” because search, its Gemini chatbot, and Gemini Notebook tool will be off by default starting next year. Administrators can enable one, two, or all three services.

The issue for schools and parents, though, is that Google considers AI Overviews and a companion feature called AI Mode inseparable from the traditional search experience. Respectively launched in 2023 and last year, they bring the functionality of AI chatbots, such as Gemini or ChatGPT, directly into search results.

“Kids are already using these search-bar summaries to skip real effort, pulling instant math answers and letting AI write their essays,” Johnson says. “To make matters worse, these AI snapshots frequently make mistakes and output false facts, which younger students take as absolute truth.”

The AI-generated responses are tempting to read and often good enough to trust, triggering headaches beyond classrooms. Wikipedia, news websites, and education tools have lost human visitors as people rely on overviews. Google uses the same bots to crawl the web for its search and AI products, making it impossible for publishers to opt out of their content being used for the latter.

Google’s push to make AI Overviews a prominent part of search has already come at a cost. Last week, shares of parent company Alphabet suffered their worst single-day selloff, erasing half a trillion dollars in market value after the company reported weaker-than-expected search ad sales. A big cause? Increased usage of AI Overviews and AI Mode, which aren’t packed with many ads yet—although some experts believe the slump will only be temporary.

For schools, the dilemma over search may be just beginning. While several districts WIRED contacted didn’t respond to requests for comment, Los Angeles Unified says it is still reviewing the potential implications of Google’s announcement. Some education technology experts argue that schools should abandon Google search altogether, or at least do a better job teaching students to question the validity of AI answers.

“Under-resourced districts will grit their teeth and say, ‘we don’t have the capacity to dig in our heels and not use Google,’” says Stephen Aguilar, who coleads University of Southern California’s Center for Generative AI and Society. “A lot are likely going to accelerate plans they already have to teach students about this new digital literacy.”

Parent advocates also plan to push districts to look elsewhere. “This move just continues a well-established pattern of big tech companies pushing products into classrooms,” says Karolle Rabarison, a policy and communications strategist who helps lead Schools Beyond Screens in Washington, DC. “It’s not going to work any more.”

Tech industry veterans disagree about how difficult it would be for Google to let schools disable AI Overviews without affecting the rest of Search. “It’s a question of whether they’re committed to maintaining two versions of search in the long run,” says Nicole Kerson, a former senior Google Search product manager who runs the AI strategy firm Collected Company. “It's very hard to maintain a forked product like that.”

Microsoft offers a Google Chrome extension that lets users turn off AI-generated summaries in Bing search. Adeel Khan, a former teacher and principal who now runs MagicSchool, which provides AI chatbots for students and teachers, says it is “infuriating, insulting, and ludicrous” that Google isn’t doing something similar.

Without an official way to disable AI Overviews, schools have turned to technical workarounds, including modifying search URLs and adopting browser extensions that change how Google results appear. Fairfax County Public Schools in Virginia recently developed its own extension. But these loopholes could stop functioning if Google changes how its search results are delivered.

Smaller search engines, such as the privacy-focused DuckDuckGo, see an opportunity to win business from schools frustrated with Google. “I wouldn't expect to see a Google-style ‘DuckDuckGo Classroom’ anytime soon, but ideally, we'll have special resources just for educators looking to make a switch,” says spokesperson Allison Goodman.

Following a federal ruling in 2024 that Google illegally maintained its search monopoly, the company was ordered to share certain search data and services with rivals and loosen restrictions on how its products are distributed. But the effort is well behind schedule, thanks to ongoing legal disputes slowing the independent committee meant to oversee the remedies. The AI Overviews issue could prompt fresh scrutiny as several lawmakers, including US Senator Bernie Sanders, criticized Google’s stance toward schools.

paras.en: Studies examining the effects of the new AI tools entering schools have raised concerns about whether they are eroding opportunities for students to develop skills such as critical thinking, according to a Stanford review of the research as of a year ago. According to a survey conducted by Google itself, three in four teenagers report using AI weekly, but only about half say they double check its outputs for accuracy. A recent study by Washington University in St. Louis, meanwhile, found that only about 42 percent of AI Overviews could be fully verified using the citations they contained. Google has said overviews undergo rigorous testing and are continually improving.

paras.en: In its response to the recent furor over AI Overviews, Google said it plans to launch a new feature for students in the coming months called Guided Learning. The idea is to coach users to find information rather than provide them with an immediate answer. “We believe AI products should support ‘productive struggle’—enabling students to be actively challenged without getting so overwhelmed that they give up,” Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president for education wrote in the company’s Tuesday blog post.

paras.en: Some researchers are already questioning how effective Guided Learning will be, arguing it won’t be as natural as working with a human tutor. Aguilar views Guided Learning as another attempt by Google to maintain the position it already occupies in American classrooms, where Google-powered Chromebook laptops, Google Classroom learning software, Search, and YouTube are commonplace.

“There’s a kernel of truth in saying we have to prepare students for a world where AI is ubiquitous,” Aguilar says, “but it shouldn’t be through a company making a very self-serving pronouncement because it’s heavily invested in AI.”

articles.title: Watch: Disney+ teases 'Proud Family Wizmas' stop-motion holiday special

paras.en: Nov. 4 (UPI) -- The Proud family will return in the musical Disney+ holiday special A Proud Family Wizmas.
The streaming service shared a trailer for the animated stop-motion holiday special Wednesday, which will premiere Nov. 14 ahead of Christmas.

A Proud Family Wizmas is based on the Disney Channel animated series The Proud Family, which aired from 2001 to 2005, and its Disney+ revival, The Proud Family: Louder and Prouder, which ran from 2022 to June of this year.
Kyla Pratt returns to voice Penny Proud, the teenage daughter of Oscar (Tommy Davidson) and Trudy Proud (Paula Jai Parker).

The special follows Penny after "she inadvertently destroys Christmas as we know it and then reluctantly agrees to make things right and save Christmas for the children of Emilyville and the world," an official synopsis reads.
The voice cast also includes JoMarie Payton as Suga Mama, Cedric the Entertainer as Uncle Bobby, Karen Malina White as Dijonay Jones and Soleil Moon Frye as Zoey Howzer.
Anderson .Paak, Lil Rel Howery, JB Smoove, Karlous Miller, Tone Loc, Earthquake, Luenell, Affion Crockett and Gabrielle Union will have guest roles.

articles.title: Democrats take control of both houses of Congress in historic upset

paras.en: Nov. 4 (UPI) -- The Democratic Party won control of both houses of Congress in a historic mid-term election rout that saw Democrats flip U.S. Senate and U.S. House seats in a slew of solid Republican states from South Carolina, Ohio and Texas to Kansas, which last sent a Democratic Senator to Congress in 1932.

With Democrats ahead 54-44 in the Senate, with two seats -- Mississippi and Alaska -- where counting was underway, and 237-139 in the House, with 68 seats where counting is incomplete, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., declared victory and President Donald Trump conceded the defeat.

Trump told Fox News that he was surprised at the result, but credited the way Democrats fought the election, saying they "did a good job" and indicated he was willing to work with them in Congress -- but also raised the specter of wielding his veto powers in the remaining two years of his presidency.

He insisted that the outcome would've been different had he been on the ballot but expressed disappointment that he was unable to transfer the support he received at rallies he held across the country in the run-up to the election "into more Republican candidates."

Trump said he "felt badly" for Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., the sister of his friend and colleague, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, who is projected to have lost her seat in the Senate to Democrat Annie Andrews, the Democrats' first victory in the state since the turn of the century.
Trump acknowledged the Iran war, which started in February, had been a factor but ruled out a reshuffle of his Cabinet.

"I think a part of it was Iran, but at the same time people understood the importance of what I've done with Iran. I think historically, it's going to be much more important than this evening because you can't let the number one state sponsor of terror have a nuclear weapon," Trump added.

He painted a scenario in the new Democrat-controlled Congress, which will be sworn in Jan. 3, where the Democrats would send over "things that are insane" that he would veto and then after a couple of months of vetoes, the Democratic leadership would call him and they would work together to "get this stuff done."
Democrats pledged to quickly check Trump in Congress and investigate him.

"The days of the House of Representatives functioning like a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over," Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said. Jeffries is likely to become speaker of the House.
Vice President JD Vance broke with Trump and blamed the losses on the war in Iran.

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next six years was worth it, then do so," Vance wrote on X. "Agree or disagree, that's at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost."

Vance referenced a pollster who told him there were four ways Republicans could get voters back: "end the war; focus on cost of living/inflation; Put America First; Change our relationship to Israel," Vance said.
That's a strong rebuke of Trump, as the president has defended the war and is a supporter of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"Everyone knows why we lost," Vance said. "And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."
Trump made his first public appearance after the midterms at the White House for about 30 minutes Wednesday, focusing mostly on his renovation projects.
After his speech inside the partially constructed White House ballroom, reporters asked him about Vance's post. He said he supports the vice president's post but said he wouldn't change his actions.
"As far as that war is concerned, I would have done nothing different," he said.
Speaking in Washington, Schumer said his party had won the Senate "against all odds" saying Democrats' main message to the American people was that "relief is on the way."

Hailing a "resounding" mandate from the American people, Jeffries vowed House Democrats would work hard to revive the American dream of an affordable life with good housing, good health care, a good education for children and a good retirement for "every single person in this land."

"This is a change election and we understand as House Democrats that we need to deliver dramatic change. Things are broken. We need a Congress that puts the American people first. The wealthy, the well-off, and the well-connected tried to buy this election. The American people have responded in a resounding way and made clear that America is not for sale," said Jeffries.

articles.title: The blind fury of Kim Yo-jong

paras.en: Nov. 4 (UPI) -- The author prefers to use the lowercase "n" to challenge the Kim family regime's legitimacy.

The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation last week officially identified "Trader Traitor," a cybergroup linked to north Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau, as the culprit behind an $8 billion hacking incident targeting Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange.

With this state-sponsored theft exposed to the world, north Korea deployed Kim Yo-jong, vice department director of the Workers' Party Central Committee, to release an unusual series of back-to-back statements Wednesday and Thursday.
Kim lashed out, calling the FBI's announcement "groundless rumors" and a "political provocation."

At the same time, she reacted with fury to the U.S. Trafficking in Persons Report, claiming alongside issues of denuclearization, sanctions and military exercises, that Washington is setting "new records every day" in its hostile policy against Pyongyang.

While foreign media outlets focus heavily on dissecting north Korea's cybercrime capabilities and money-laundering routes, the real Achilles' heel in this statement lies elsewhere: Kim Yo-jong's intense outrage over the U.S. Trafficking in Persons Report.
By placing this human rights report on the same level as denuclearization and military sanctions, Kim inadvertently exposed the regime's complete bankruptcy of human rights values.
It reveals that she does not even understand the fundamental definition of human trafficking as recognized by the international community.
Under international law, human trafficking is no longer confined to traditional notions of kidnapping or physical slave auctions.
At its core, modern human trafficking involves exploiting vulnerabilities, coercion and deception to force individuals into labor without just compensation.

When applying this modern standard, a grim conclusion emerges: north Korea is not just a nation lagging in human rights, but the only regime in the world that systematically engages in state-sponsored human trafficking.
There is a clear reason why the U.S. Department of State consistently ranks north Korea at Tier 3, the lowest category in its annual trafficking report.
No matter how much Kim Yo-jong tries to mask it with hostile rhetoric and denials of hacking, three monumental sins cannot be hidden.
First is the issue of overseas north Korean laborers a form of state-run slave trade.

The regime has systematically driven countless youths and citizens into logging camps in Russia and garment factories and construction sites in China, forcing them to work under slave-like conditions.
Over 80% to 90% of the wages they earn through 15-hour workdays are extorted by the regime under the guise of "loyalty funds."
This money is funnelled directly into the ruling family's private coffers, nuclear and missile development, and maintenance of the very cyber-hacking units exposed last week.
A government acting as a trafficking ring to sell its own citizens' labor abroad and pocket the profits is the textbook definition of modern-day slavery.

Second is the domestic machinery of forced labor: the Shock Brigades and prison camps. Under the hollow pretext of "socialist construction," the regime mobilizes young people for massive civil engineering projects without fair wages or basic safety measures.

The brutal forced labor inside political prison camps is even worse. A system that entirely strips citizens of their freedom of movement and choice of occupation solely to squeeze out labor for the regime's profit is, in essence, a massive human trafficking network.

Third is the regime's complicity in the tragedy of north Korean women and girls across the border. To escape severe starvation, many women cross into China, only to become targets for human trafficking rings that subject them to forced marriages and sexual exploitation.
A legitimate government would protect its citizens, but Pyongyang brands these women as "traitors" and works aggressively with Chinese authorities to forcibly repatriate them.

Once sent back, these women are thrown into detention centers and re-education camps, facing even more savage torture and forced labor. This is a heinous crime against humanity that repeatedly victimizes trafficking survivors.
Yet, in her consecutive statements, Kim Yo-jong attempted to dismiss all these tragedies as "political maneuvers" or part of an "anti-DPRK hostile policy."

There is not a shred of self-awareness regarding how brutally the regime tramples on universal human values. It is grotesque to see the world's largest human trafficking kingpin a regime that funds its missiles by bleeding its own people dry brazenly playing the victim.
Kim Yo-jong must realize a stark truth. The FBI's attribution of the cyber heist and the State Department's human trafficking report are not political theater designed to destabilize Pyongyang.
They represent the solemn judgment and warning of the international community against a criminal syndicate that poses as a state while trading human lives and stealing fortunes.
No matter how north Korea tries to manipulate this hacking scandal to blur the lines, the anti-humanitarian reality built on the suffering of its people cannot be concealed.

Kim Yo-jong's blind fury will only act as a boomerang, reminding the world why this regime remains the epicenter of human rights atrocities. The north Korean regime must shut its mouth and immediately halt the state-sponsored trafficking of its own people.

Jihyun Park, a British Korean Conservative politician and regular contributor to the Korea Regional Review, is a North Korean escapee who fled twice from the country -- in 1998, which resulted in a forced repatriation, and in 2008, which was successful. She is a senior fellow for human security at the Center for Asia Pacific Strategy. The views and opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the author.

articles.title: Harry Styles Helps Madison Square Garden Entertainment Revenue Surge 37%
articles.author: Elizabeth Dilts Marshall

paras.en: Madison Square Garden Entertainment (MSGE) reported on Wednesday (Nov. 4) that its fiscal first quarter revenue surged 37% to $217 million, boosted by an additional $30 million from concerts, including Harry Styles’ record-setting sold-out residency at the company’s namesake theater.

While MSGE executives acknowledged that demand for live entertainment is not the same as it was in the boom years following the pandemic, the company said revenue from its entertainment offerings surged 33% to $174.9 million this quarter compared to a year ago. Food, beverage and merchandise revenue jumped 56% to $35.7 million — with roughly one-third coming from sales at concerts — and arena license fees and other leasing revenue were up 60.2% to $6.59 million.

“We had a robust fiscal first quarter with the Garden shattering our record for the number of concerts in any quarter held at the venue,” said executive vp/CEO David Collins on a conference call discussing the results. “Especially given the macro volatility, we continue to see strong consumer demand. The significant majority of concerts at our venues were again sold out. Throughout the quarter, concerts performed better than we expected. We saw combined [food, beverage] and merchandise per capita spending at concerts up double-digit percentages. A number of upcoming acts across our venues added additional shows due to strong demand.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Sixteen of Styles’ 30-night New York leg of his Together, Together tour, which held the stage at Madison Square Garden every Wednesday, Friday and Saturday night for 10 straight weeks, occurred in MSGE’s first fiscal quarter, which ended on Sept. 30.

MSGE reported higher per-concert revenue in the quarter, as tickets to Styles’ New York shows reportedly ranged in price from under $100 to well over $1,000. An increase in the overall number of concerts at its venues also provided a strong boost to revenue and food, beverage and merch sales.

“The Garden did deliver robust growth in the number of concerts year over year on an underlying basis,” Collins said. “Obviously, Harry Styles’ run was an additional positive on top of that underlying strength.”

More events always result in higher costs for MSGE, which reported that direct operating expenses for entertainment offerings, arena license fees and other leasing rose 22% to $107.6 million, including an $11 million increase from concerts. Food, beverage and merchandise direct operating expenses rose 39% to $19.1 million.

Adjusted operating income increased by $27.2 million to $34.3 million for the quarter compared to the prior-year quarter on higher revenue, partially offset by higher direct operating expenses and selling, general and administrative expenses.

articles.title: BTS ‘Swim’ Copyright Lawsuit Dropped by Accusers Just Months After They Sued Over Hit Song
articles.author: Bill Donahue

paras.en: A lawsuit claiming that BTS’ chart-topping smash “Swim” ripped off an earlier song has now been dropped by the accusers.

The case, filed in July against BTS label HYBE, alleged that the hit song — which debuted at No. 1 on the Hot 100 this spring as the lead track off ARIRANG — had many “substantial similarities” to an unpublished demo of the same name by three little-known songwriters.

But less than four months later, attorneys for those three accusers (Steve Cooper, Jon Sandler and Greylyn Johnson) asked the judge in a Wednesday (Nov. 4) court filing to dismiss the lawsuit in its entirety.

It was unclear from court documents if any kind of settlement had been reached, and neither side immediately returned requests for comment. The case remained in its earliest stages, with HYBE’s attorneys not yet having even formally responded to it.

In their July complaint, the three accusers claimed they had sent out copies of their demo in March 2025 “to various parties for them to consider.” That allegedly included execs at Artist Publishing Group, who the plaintiffs claimed “listened to the [demo] and shared it with others,” including some of the songwriters who eventually worked on “Swim.”

After Cooper, Sandler and Johnson noticed the alleged similarities, they said they hired a forensic musicologist to compare the two songs and that the musicologist concluded that the BTS version contained numerous elements that were “unequivocally taken” from the demo.

“Upon listening several times [to “Swim”], plaintiffs came to what they considered to be the obvious and inescapable conclusion that [it] copied in very large part the original work and clearly infringed their copyrights,” lawyers for the trio wrote at the time.

The lawsuit didn’t name BTS or its members as defendants; instead, it targeted their label, HYBE, and its subsidiaries, HYBE America and Big Hit Music Co. It also named the songwriters behind the BTS track, including former OneRepublic member Ryan Tedder, a Grammy-winning hitmaker who has also written songs for Taylor Swift, Beyoncé and Adele.

A quick withdrawal is nothing unusual for big copyright lawsuits over chart-topping hits. Just last week, a headline-grabbing case filed against Drake over his No. 1 single “Janice STFU” was abruptly dropped by the accuser less than two weeks after it was first filed.

articles.title: Cynthia Erivo to Play Tupac Shakur’s Mother in Universal’s Snoop Dogg Biopic (Exclusive)
articles.author: Borys Kit

paras.en: Cynthia Erivo has joined the cast of Snoop, Universal Pictures’ biopic of entertainment mogul and music icon Snoop Dogg.

The Tony, Grammy, and Emmy winner, who is also a three-time Oscar nominee, boards a call sheet that includes Jonathan Daviss, Myles Bullock Be, Lauren London, Camron Jones, Algee Smith, Tre Hale, Laya DeLeon Hayes, Olly Sholotan, Corey Champagne, Jonica Booth and SwayvoTwain in the feature that is currently in production in southern California.

Craig Brewer is directing the feature, which is being produced by Imagine Entertainment’s Brian Grazer, the veteran producer behind the semi-autobiographical Eminem drama 8 Mile, and the company’s Allan Mandelbaum. Snoop Dogg and Death Row Pictures president Sara Ramaker are also producing.
Daviss, one of the stars of Netflix series Outer Banks, is portraying Snoop Dogg, who emerged from Long Beach, Calif. in the 1990s to become one of the biggest names in rap.
Jones, best known for his work on Amazon Prime’s young adult drama Panic, is inhabiting the role of influential but troubled rapper Tupac Shakur.
In a key role, Erivo will play Shakur’s mother, Afeni Shakur, a former Black Panther activist who had a strained relationship with her son and the subject his top 10 hit “Dear Mama.”

Brewer, who recently directed Song Sung Blue for Universal’s specialty studio Focus Features, wrote the latest draft of the script, which was initially written by Joe Robert Cole. The feature will incorporate music from Snoop Dogg’s vast catalog.

Erivo is a known quantity at Universal, having starred in the studio’s massively successful two-part Wicked movies. Her performance as Elphaba in the first movie earned her Golden Globe, SAG, Critics’ Choice, NAACP, BAFTA, and Academy Award nominations.

Next, the actress stars in the film adaptation of the Broadway sensation Prima Facie, which she also executive produced under her Edith’s Daughter banner. The film recently premiered at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival and will be released in UK and Ireland cinemas on Nov. 13.

She is also one of the stars of Paramount’s Children of Blood and Bone, which features an ensemble cast that includes Viola Davis, Chiwetel Ejiofor, Idris Elba, Amandla Stenberg, Damson Idris, Regina King, and Lashana Lynch. The YA fantasy movie opens in theaters on Jan. 15, 2027
Erivo is repped by UTA, Entertainment 360, and Peikoff Mahan.

articles.title: Tori Spelling, Brian Austin Green Go Vertical in Scripted Microdrama
articles.author: Etan Vlessing

paras.en: Beverly Hills, 90210 stars Tori Spelling and Brian Austin Green have reunited in the scripted microdrama world.

Spelling, who played Donna Martin in the original drama, and Green, who appeared as her onscreen love interest, David Silver, are both starring in an untitled original thriller microseries for vertTV, with production wrapping Wednesday in Los Angeles. The first vertical microseries for either of them also features 90210 alum Carol Potter, who played Cindy Walsh, the mom of twins Brenda (Shannen Doherty) and Brandon Walsh (Jason Priestley).

There’s no plot details for the thriller as vertTV, the Los Angeles-based microdrama studio launched by Hollywood veterans Jeffrey Schenck, Barry Barnholtz and Peter Sullivan, expands its slate of star-driven ultrashorts. VertTV, launched in July 2026, has done over 200 TV movies for Lifetime and Hallmark in the past and is now betting on bite-sized dramas like Lone Star Hearts, starring Cindy Busby and Josh Henderson, to continue gaining traction with mobile phone audiences.

Other vertTV microdramas include the romance Finding Hope — starring Jodie Sweetin, John Brotherton, and Marla Sokoloff — and Chonda, starring Chonda Pierce and Regan Burns in a vertical fish-out-of-water comedy.

The production of microdramas in North America and elsewhere is booming, while in Hollywood spending on traditional content for linear TV and streaming platforms is in decline. VertTV also launched with a standalone mobile app for iOS and Android devices as a key destination for the studio’s original slate.

Of late, the booming sector of verticals has been inundated with AI-generated titles, with vertTV insisting it shoots vertical series with real actors on real sets and without the use of generative AI.

articles.title: Alex Garland’s ‘Civil War’ Gets Second Look After Texas Turns Blue: “You Owe Him an Apology”
articles.author: James Hibberd

paras.en: Alex Garland‘s 2024 dystopian thriller Civil War has been going viral in the wake of the Democrats winning the Texas governor’s mansion and a U.S. Senate seat for the first time in decades.

In the film set in the near future, California and Texas were partnered up and were called the “Western Forces.” The states were resisting a tyrannical president amid a civil war tearing the country apart.

The alliance between a traditionally entrenched blue state and a red state wasn’t explicitly explained in the film, leading to a lot of head scratching, confusion and even some outright criticism among viewers.
But given senator-elect James Talarico and governor-elect Gina Hinojosa’s victories last night, people are giving the film’s premise another look.
One user on X posted the divided U.S. map from the film and wrote, “You all owe Alex Garland an apology.”

An editor for The Bulwark wrote, “Me: CIVIL WAR was intentionally vague to the point of ideological incoherence to avoid mapping on to current culture war nonsense. Alex Garland: I literally foresaw California and Texas rising against the populist fraud in the White House.”
Amid the film’s release, Garland explained at South by Southwest that he thought the film’s premise alone was enough to lead viewers to a conclusion about why the states were allied.

“I personally think questions are answered,” Garland said. “There is a fascist president who smashed the Constitution and attacked [American] citizens. And that is a very clear, answered statement. If you want to think about why Texas and California might be allied, and put aside their political differences, the answer would be implicit in that. So I think answers are there but you have to step to it and not expect to be spoon fed these things. It makes assumptions about the audience.”

“The warnings [about the country falling apart] all out there, but for some reason they don’t get any traction,” Garland added. “[I wondered,] ‘Is it the polarization? Is it just that we are not able to absorb any information because of the position we’ve already taken?’ Hence, making a movie that pulls the polarization out of it.”
Civil War starred Kirsten Dunst, Wagner Moura, Cailee Spaeny, Stephen McKinley Henderson and Sonoya Mizuno and followed a group of journalists covering the final days of a second civil war.

articles.title: Democrats take Congress in a blue wave. Here's what it means for your money

paras.en: With Democrats flipping control of Congress in the midterm election, the shift in power on Capitol Hill could reshape household budgets — from student loan bills and health insurance premiums to housing costs and taxes.
Experts say results show that rising costs were top of mind for voters.

"I see this election as a repudiation of the anti-affordability agenda from the Trump administration," said Daniel Bunn, president and CEO of the Tax Foundation, a nonpartisan, nonprofit research organization.
"Whether that's the conflict in the Middle East or the tariffs, just top to bottom, it's clear to me that was a real concern of the electorate," he said.

White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said in an emailed statement that the Trump administration has delivered "tangible wins to make life more affordable for American families." Officials "will continue to put hardworking American's first with or without support from Democrats," he wrote.

Democrats won control of both the House of Representatives and Senate, which could make it easier for the party to advance legislation. They can also use hearings and investigations to press federal agencies and companies to answer for policies and practices that impact consumers, and exert leverage over confirmation of President Donald Trump's nominees.

But turning campaign promises into changes people feel in their finances won't be easy. Trump can veto bills a Democrat-controlled Congress passes, limiting how much of their agenda could become law. Based on projections, Democrats will lack the numbers needed to override a presidential veto.
Any changes will also take time: Newly elected members of Congress won't take office until January.
Here are eight ways Democrats’ new congressional majority could affect your money.

"Not surprisingly, the Dems are going to be keyed in on affordability with respect to healthcare," said Zach Gaumer, vice president of health policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, a nonpartisan think tank.

- ACA subsidies: Democrats could try to reinstate at least a portion of the enhanced premium subsidies for Affordable Care Act marketplace insurance plans, Gaumer said. Those enhanced subsidies expired at the end of 2025, after the Republican-controlled Congress and Trump declined to extend them. Millions of ACA enrollees saw their monthly insurance premiums increase sharply as a result.

- Medicaid: Starting in 2027, states will be required to implement work requirements as a condition of Medicaid enrollment, due to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act the Republican-led Congress passed in 2025. Democrats will likely try to loosen those rules, and thereby avoid a large increase in the number of uninsured, Gaumer said.

- Long-term care: Medicare generally doesn't cover long-term care services, but Democrats may try to add some LTC coverage to the program's purview, Gaumer said. "That's an interest of several Democrats on the Hill right now," he said.

OBBBA made Trump's 2017 tax cuts permanent and added temporary tax breaks. These included new deductions for tip income, overtime earnings, seniors and auto loan interest, which will expire after 2028 without an extension.

Democrats may support extending these provisions. But as the Democrat-controlled Congress maps out its agenda, lawmakers will have to address the federal budget deficit. For fiscal year 2026, the budget deficit ballooned to nearly $2 trillion, the Treasury announced in October.

Newly elected Democratic senators James Talarico of Texas, Troy Jackson of Maine and Annie Andrews of South Carolina all campaigned on expanding the child tax credit. Earlier this year, Senate Democrats also floated ideas to expand the standard deduction and create income tax exemptions for lower-earning Americans — which are costly proposals, according to Bunn from the Tax Foundation.
"I've called these termites in the tax code," he said. "You cannot consistently narrow your base, especially for the income tax, and expect your spending priorities to be well-funded."
With Democrats in control of Congress, they are likely to hold hearings and subpoena Trump officials over the administration's student loan policies, said higher education expert Mark Kantrowitz.

One priority may be pressing the Education Department to fix the popular Public Service Loan Forgiveness program, which cancels the remaining federal student debt of eligible government and nonprofit workers after a decade. Over the summer, Trump officials reassessed repayment timelines, delaying some borrowers' forgiveness date by years.

Broad student loan forgiveness is unlikely: Trump could veto such a bill, and the Supreme Court blocked the Biden administration's plan. More attainable changes could include restoring tax-free treatment of forgiven student debt, raising the new borrowing caps and expanding repayment options — measures that may attract bipartisan support, Kantrowitz said.
Trump has also said he may support legislation capping federal student loan interest rates, a proposal that could give Democrats common ground in their push to ease borrowers’ costs.

Housing affordability was a key election issue, and Democrats will likely explore ways to deliver relief, such as introducing measures to help first-time homebuyers, according to an Oct. 30 analysis by Desjardins, a Canadian financial services company.

However, lawmakers generally have little direct impact on home prices, which are based on market conditions. Mortgage rates, too, are influenced by forces generally beyond congressional control. The yield on the 10-year Treasury, which remains higher than it was before the Iran war — due at least partly to concerns about inflation eroding the value of those bonds — influences mortgage rates.

"Jumpstarting the housing market relies on a calmer geopolitical environment and bond market in the short run," plus more housing supply and a "more dynamic labor market in the long run," said Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com.

The bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which automatically became law July 11 without the president's signature due to a constitutional provision, is "a model for what can pass in a divided Washington," Krimmel said. It includes measures to encourage housing construction, reduce regulatory barriers, expand financing options and limit purchases of single-family homes by large institutional investors.
The incoming class of Senators will have to address Social Security insolvency.

The program's trustees project that the trust fund Social Security relies on to help pay retirement benefits, formally known as the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund, may be depleted in the fourth quarter of 2032. Without action from Congress before then, benefits could face an across-the-board cut of 22%.
A number of Democratic lawmakers and some Republicans have called for increased payroll taxes on high earners to help shore up Social Security.

A potential SECURE 3.0 bill — a follow-up to bipartisan retirement-savings laws passed in 2019 and 2022 — could help expand workers' access to workplace retirement plans like 401(k)s, for example, among a roster of other reforms, experts said.

"Trump promised to cap credit card rates at 10%," said Aaron Klein, a senior fellow in economic studies at the Brookings Institution, a think tank. "A Democratic Congress might be willing to do that."

Any such cap is likely to be closer to 36% than to the 10% cap Trump has sought, Jaret Seiberg, a financial services policy analyst at TD Cowen, an investment bank, wrote in a research note Wednesday. Lawmakers in the current Congress have proposed legislation with these thresholds.

A cap would likely be welcome news for low- and middle-income Americans, Klein said. They are more likely than wealthy households to use debt to finance their lives and to carry a credit card balance — and therefore owe interest on their charges, he said.
Cardholders might see other impacts of such a policy, such as lower credit limits and a clawback of certain card rewards, he said.
Democrats' takeover of Congress could stall efforts to put crypto-friendly regulations into federal law, but everyday investors shouldn't expect much to change immediately.

"Platforms will keep offering the products they offer today, and they still have friendly regulators at the SEC and CFTC who are approving an ever-wider range of crypto products," said Lee Reiners, a cryptocurrency regulation expert and lecturing fellow of economics at Duke University.

The election results could threaten the CLARITY Act, which would give the Commodity Futures Trading Commission greater authority over cryptocurrency trading while reducing the Securities and Exchange Commission's role. The bill passed the House in July 2025 by a 294-134 vote, but failed to advance in the Senate in September on a 49-50 procedural vote. "CLARITY is dead," said Reiners, adding that he sees little chance of the bill passing during the lame-duck session before Democrats take control in January.
