articles.title: Fake alerts warn of nuclear danger as Ukraine and Russia report emergency app hacks
articles.author: Yuliya Talmazan

paras.en: Nuclear danger, radiation threat and street combat: Ukrainians received a wave of messages Sunday night that raised alarm with a series of grave — and baseless — warnings.

Authorities said the country’s emergency alert application had been targeted in a cyberattack, and hours later Russia said its own alert system had also been hacked. The dueling accusations came just as a rare humanitarian ceasefire between the two sides ended, raising fears of intensified fighting rather than a move toward broader peace.

Residents in Ukraine have become used to the unsettling alerts that buzz their phones with news of incoming Russian missiles and drones — a service millions rely on to seek shelter before the attacks hit their cities. But the warnings Sunday night immediately stood out.
The messages, which began around 10:45 p.m. Kyiv time (3:45 p.m. ET), warned residents not to go outside because of radiation hazard, chemical threat and street fights.
Another message professed, in Russian, that all of Ukraine was under nuclear alert. “Don’t worry,” it added. “Oreshnik is in action,” referring to Russia’s nuclear-capable hypersonic missile.

That message referenced a Telegram channel called Hitcorecorp. Major pro-Kremlin Telegram channel Mash said it spoke with the group and that it took responsibility for the hack. NBC News could not verify who the group is and whether it was responsible for the alerts.

Shortly after the alerts went out late Sunday, Ukraine’s air force said the country’s Air Alert app had most likely been “compromised by the enemy,” confirming there was no “radiation threat” and urging calm.

In separate statements, the app’s creators said “unauthorized third parties interfered with the operation of the app,” forcing them to temporarily suspend its operations. They later called the incident a “cyberattack,” saying it was gradually restoring the service. “The team is carrying out additional measures to protect the app in order to prevent similar situations in the future,” one of the statements said.

Ukrainian media reported that users across the country received the alert, and authorities in the western Lviv region reported that some of the public warning sirens and loudspeaker systems broadcast a “radiation hazard” signal.
“I was outside with my dog when the first alert came,” said Olena Yermakova, 32, a researcher in Kyiv.
She picked up her dog and ran inside, she said, before checking the news to see what was happening.

Because the message was in Russian, “I thought it was a hack by the Russians,” she said. “But the seconds before that were absolutely terrifying. I started running through a checklist in my head of what to do during a nuclear threat and whether I had all the supplies at home, and my hands started shaking.”

Still, many other Ukrainians did not appear unduly alarmed or panicked by the alerts. In fact, many shared memes online, poking fun at what they saw as a blatant fake and the fact the warning was issued in Russian. “No one was particularly surprised,” a user wrote on X. “They might as well have thrown in a dinosaur attack, too.”
The State Emergency Service of Ukraine said Monday the national alert system was operating normally, and an NBC News producer in Kyiv did not experience any further issues with the Air Alert app.

Meanwhile, Russia’s emergencies ministry also said early Monday that its mobile application suffered a “massive cyberattack,” resulting in what it said was “dissemination of fake information to the public.” The public alert system was restored and was operating normally, it said shortly after. It emphasized that the app was only “an additional, supplementary information service.”

Screenshots shared by Russian media and some regional authorities suggested the alert, issued in Russian, warned of “nuclear warheads” launched at Russia. As with the Ukrainian alert, the wording was casual and did not appear official.
Russian authorities did not say who was to blame for the alleged cyberattack, only saying “malicious actors” were behind it.
It was not immediately clear whether the two incidents were linked.
It came just hours after a temporary ceasefire between Kyiv and Moscow came to an end in the occupied southern Ukrainian region of Kherson.

The truce, brokered with involvement from first lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV, held without violations from either side for six days, allowing the evacuation of hundreds of residents from the front-line town of Oleshky, which had been on the brink of a humanitarian catastrophe.
The truce amounted to the biggest de-escalation between Kyiv and Moscow since the war started in early 2022.

“On behalf of America, I commend Russia and Ukraine for their leadership and cooperation surrounding the Oleshky ceasefire,” Melania Trump said in a post on X on Sunday. “I hope Oleshky serves as a foundation for lasting peace between both nations.”

Ukraine’s omsbudsman for human rights, Dmytro Lubinets, said he was exploring opportunities for “further humanitarian initiatives” with his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, adding that it was “important to maintain this mechanism of cooperation.”
Before the truce took hold, the United Nations estimated that 2,000 civilians remained in Oleshky, many experiencing hunger and unable to leave safely because of heavily mined roads.

Neither side has disclosed the exact number of people evacuated, but the first lady said Sunday it was nearly 800. The evacuees could go into territory controlled by either Ukraine or Russia, or remain in the town, officials on both sides said.

Lantratova, the Russian human rights commissioner, said Monday that she had expected more people to evacuate from Oleshky, saying “quite a few empty buses” left the area. Many people chose to stay because they couldn’t leave elderly or sick loved ones, she said, or simply refused to leave their homes no matter what.
She said for those remaining, humanitarian aid deliveries would take place at least monthly, with the “coordination and mediation” of Melania Trump.

Ukraine’s armed forces accused Russia on Monday of using the truce to rotate its units and fortify positions in the area. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that Kyiv also could have used the ceasefire to regroup, calling it a “completely common practice in such situations.”

articles.title: Supermarkets across Europe hit by new fridge cyberattacks
articles.author: Reuters

paras.en: Supermarkets across Europe were hit Monday by a new wave of apparent cyberattacks affecting fridges and freezers.
The incidents caused temperature spikes and spoiled food at stores in Sweden, the Netherlands, Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg and Estonia.

They follow a cyberattack in France last month, in which, police said, hackers seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets, raising temperatures as high as 122 degrees Fahrenheit and causing fires and food losses.
Authorities have not indicated who could have been behind the incidents. There were no claims of responsibility.
The continent is confronting broader security fears stemming from Russia’s war in Ukraine.
The new cyberattack highlights how digital threats can increasingly affect people’s everyday lives, the European Commission said Monday.

The Ahold Delhaize supermarket chain in the Netherlands told NBC News on Monday that it was aware of an “IT incident” affecting the refrigeration systems in a number of its stores. “Our teams are working hard to fully assess the situation,” it said in an email.

Stephan Moelans, the CEO of the Belgian refrigeration company Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize’s systems, told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyberattack, in which the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode.

A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, said five shops’ fridge systems were attacked. The Carrefour supermarket chain in the country said a “cyberattack targeting refrigeration installations only had an extremely limited impact,” affecting 15 of its more than 700 stores.
The Swedish furniture giant Ikea said its store in Mons, Belgium, was also affected.
The “cyber incident” hit the shop’s refrigeration and freezer units, according to a statement sent via email. The company said it was investigating exactly what had happened.
The store in Mons is open to customers, and none of Ikea’s other stores in Belgium have been affected, it said.

Swedish grocery retailer chain ICA also told NBC News that its systems were not affected but that it had been informed of “an incident at a small number of stores that use an external supplier and have their connectivity outside ICA’s central network.”
The incident has affected the stores’ refrigeration and freezer systems, the company said in an email. “ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the incident,” it said.

The ICA Kvantum branch in Sjöbo in southern Sweden wrote on Facebook that its fridges and freezers had been hacked and set to 122 degrees Fahrenheit. It said it was working to discard the affected items.
The privately held grocery retail group Coop told the Swedish daily Aftonbladet that similar incidents had affected six of its stores.
In Ireland, the food wholesaler Musgrave said a cyber incident had affected refrigeration systems in 13 of its SuperValu stores, forcing it to remove some chilled and frozen products from sale.

“Our monitoring systems alerted us to the issue and we took immediate action,” it said in a statement. “Our investigation is ongoing.” The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In Estonia, a company that makes the affected technology said one of its clients had been hit by a cyberattack in which attackers accessed a computer controlling refrigeration and also turned up the temperature to 122 degrees Fahrenheit, public broadcaster ERR reported.

From refrigerators and heating systems to security cameras and alarm networks, an expanding range of devices can now be monitored and controlled remotely, creating new opportunities for cybercriminals.

Sweden’s national cybersecurity center — which said it could not speculate on who was behind the attacks — is working on several incidents affecting grocery stores across the country, the head of the center, John Billow, said Monday.
“We have in recent weeks ... identified that we have quite a lot of exposed operational technology devices in Sweden that we have been clear about the necessity to update or patch,” he said.

articles.title: U.S. Marine dies in Japan during training, military says
articles.author: Adela Suliman

paras.en: A United States Marine has died in Japan, following a “training incident,” the military said in a statement Wednesday.

The unnamed Marine was undertaking training at Camp Schwab in Okinawa, Japan’s southernmost prefecture, the statement said. The area is home to a large U.S. military presence and bases that serve as a regional hub in the Indo-Pacific.

The Marine who was with the 3rd Marine Division died Tuesday and will not be named until 24 hours after the individual’s family has been notified, the 3rd Marine Division said in a statement Wednesday.
“It is with heavy hearts that 3rd Marine Division announces the death of a Marine following a training incident at Camp Schwab, Okinawa, Japan, on Nov. 3, 2026,” the statement said.
“The circumstances surrounding the incident remain under investigation,” it added. “We express our deepest condolences to the family and loved ones of our Marine.”

Okinawa was under U.S. occupation following World War II until it was handed back to Japan in 1972. Today, the U.S. population on the island is nearly 80,000, with nearly 30,000 being active duty troops from all four branches of the armed forces, though the Marines make up the bulk of the forces.

Separately, Secretary of State Marco Rubio last month pledged to cooperate with Japanese authorities investigating allegations that a U.S. Marine murdered a woman in Okinawa. The case sparked widespread protests and led to a U.S. military curfew and mandatory training in standards and discipline.
Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, commander of the III Marine Expeditionary Force, said at the time that serving on the Japanese island “comes with responsibility.”

articles.title: Live: Education ministers consider screen time and generative AI limits in schools
articles.author: Joshua Boscaini

paras.en: Federal politics live: Education ministers consider screen time and generative AI limits in schools
Education ministers have agreed to consider imposing screen time limits and restrictions on kids using generative AI at schools across the country.
Follow all the updates in our live blog.
Education ministers agree to look at school screen time limits
Screen-time limits and limits on kids using generative AI will be considered at schools across the country as part of a push to improve education outcomes.
The move follows international testing which, earlier this year, revealed Australian students' reading and maths have been going backwards over the past 20 years.
The same tests, by the Programme for International Student Assessment, found Australian school kids spend more time using devices than kids in other OECD countries.
At a meeting of the nation's education ministers earlier this week, they agreed to set, or at least consider, screen-time limits.
Under the plan a digital detox taskforce will be established to lead the charge on cutting down on the use of devices in schools.
"We're announcing the next stage of reforms to help our kids learn and to support our teachers," Federal Education Minister Jason Clare says.
The education ministers also agreed to change the maths curriculum for primary school students and improve the way kids learn about antisemitism.
"Schools don't just teach numeracy, literacy and critical thinking skills. They also build character," Clare says.

articles.title: Opetaia moves to heavyweight to fight former world champ Wilder

paras.en: Jai Opetaia will move up to the heavyweight division to face former world champion Deontay Wilder.
The fight will be on the undercard of the all-British heavyweight showdown between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua.
The fight will be in Cardiff and on Netflix on Friday, December 11, local time.
Jai Opetaia has been handed the fight of his life as he gambles on moving up to heavyweight to take on thunder-hitting former world champion Deontay Wilder.

Australia's unbeaten cruiserweight maestro, a contender for the sport's best pound-for-pound fighter, will move into uncharted waters by tackling the explosive American veteran on the undercard of the blockbuster Tyson Fury-Anthony Joshua show at Principality Stadium on December 11 in Cardiff.

Wilder is now 41 and perhaps not the destructive force of old, but taking on one of the biggest hitters the sport has witnessed still represents a daring gamble for Opetaia, 10 years his junior, as the world-beating Gold Coast-based southpaw and The Ring Magazine champion protects his perfect 31-fight record.
It is the first major fight above the 200-pound division for Opetaia, with his promoter Dana White admitting: "It's a very dangerous fight for him considering where he sits in his division right now.
"But he's a fighter; he'll fight anybody, even at heavyweight with a guy who hits as hard as Wilder does."
It looks poised to be a one-off, with Opetaia likely returning to cruiserweight afterwards to chase a showdown with American David Benavidez, the division's other major unbeaten force.

Last time out in Nevada in September, Opetaia stopped Noel Mikaelian in the ninth round and called out ringside observer Benavidez, whose heritage has earned him the nickname the "Mexican Monster", with the request: "Respectfully, let's get it on.
"That's the fight Jai really wants, so we've got to figure that one out," White said.
"He wants to stay active, he wants to fight, and he doesn't care if it's at heavyweight or wherever. He's ready to go."

Wilder, though, is by far the biggest name Opetaia will have faced, a champion who held the WBC belt for five years between 2015 and 2020 and who had an epic trilogy of fights with Briton Fury, coming off worse twice after an extraordinary draw in their first bout.

But he has lost four of his last seven contests and, in his last outing, had to battle to earn a scruffy points win over British contender Derek Chisora in London in April, leaving his career record at 45 wins, four losses and a draw.

The all-British bill-topper between Fury and Joshua is being sold as the biggest night of boxing ever witnessed in the UK, with tickets in Cardiff going within an hour of going on sale and the bill being screened globally on Netflix.

articles.title: Woman taken into foster care as a child now helping others
articles.author: Piper Duffy

paras.en: When Rose Taylor reflects on how different her life could have been if she had not met the teacher who became her foster carer, she is overcome with emotion.
"I genuinely wonder if I would still be alive at 43."
The Newcastle-based woman spent her formative teenage years in foster care placements and refuges, and was homeless before she experienced stable living.
Now, decades later, Ms Taylor works at the coalface of that same system, which is experiencing a national shortage of carers.
She said her story demonstrated how important it was for more people to step up.
When she was 12, Ms Taylor left for school one day unaware she would not return home.
Strangers, who she later learned were foster care case managers, took her out of class without warning and told her she was not safe living with her parents.
"I was absolutely terrified," Ms Taylor said of being placed into emergency care.
By the time she was almost 16, she had shifted between five foster care placements, two refuges and a semi-independent living program.
Left feeling unwanted and hopeless, the teenager felt she was better off alone living on the streets, and stopped telling the child welfare authorities her whereabouts.
"If I couldn't have my family, I wanted nobody," Ms Taylor said.
"I lived with this false facade that I was hardened, and I didn't care.
"But I can tell you I never cried more or felt more scared than the time I was living on the streets of Parramatta and Liverpool in Sydney as a 15-year-old."
Despite being homeless, Ms Taylor found "solace in school" and turned up each day.
When other students went home to their parents, she would find a place to roll out her sleeping bag and hang her uniform over a park bench for the night.
Ms Taylor had been living on the streets for weeks when someone took notice.
"I had a teacher who saw through [the facade] and could see I was trying to tell the world something," she said.

"When I would blow-up and storm out of a classroom, this teacher would turn up in the playground or wherever I was, sit with me and say, 'What's happening? Are you okay?' Which are questions no-one had asked."
Eventually the teacher found another colleague to care for Ms Taylor full time, and together they took her under their protective wing.
"It's not like they walked into my life and I was magically better … [but] while I was working things out they just approached me with care, curiosity and gentleness," she said.
After more than a year of stability with both teachers as her caring guardians, Ms Taylor started to see a brighter future and finished her schooling.
"I had a hard time [at 15] seeing beyond a week, let alone doing the HSC and seeing what the future looks like … that was enormous," she said.
Data from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare shows as of June 30, 2021, there were about 9,000 foster care households across the country.
However, by June 2025, that number had dropped to about 5,900.
Life Without Barriers, which connects young adults and children with a safe environment, said about 45,000 children across Australia needed care.
The not-for-profit's youth and family services boss in New South Wales, Deanne Carroll, said cost-of-living pressures had contributed to a national carer shortage.
"I think since COVID we've seen a lot of societal changes … which has meant becoming a foster carer has become out of reach for some people,"
"There's a whole range of impacts, but generally it seems to correlate with cost-of-living increases, which has impacted directly on our need for carers."
Ms Taylor, now 43 and with a family of her own, is using her upbringing to enlighten people about how they can make a difference in a child's life.
For the past decade, she has worked as an operations manager at Life Without Barriers in Newcastle, helping recruit people who could be well-suited for foster caring.
"We've got a national foster carer shortage, which is really why I've decided to speak up," Ms Taylor said.
"At the end of the day [these children] are our future adults, our future leaders, and we can all play a role [in helping]."

articles.title: Jimmy Kimmel roasts Trump in late night monologue amid 'blue tsunami' midterms
articles.author: Alexandra Mae Jones

paras.en: Jimmy Kimmel roasts Trump in late night monologue amid 'blue tsunami' midterms
Trump has repeatedly called for Kimmel to be fired by ABC
Late night host Jimmy Kimmel had some choice words for U.S. President Donald Trump last night as a “blue tsunami” stormed the country during the U.S. midterm elections.

Kimmel, host of ABC’s Jimmy Kimmel Live!, dragged the president through the verbal mud in his monologue Tuesday night, in a clip that has since racked up more than 8 million views as of Wednesday afternoon.
“Trump was reportedly angry and cursing as the results came in,” he said. “Word from inside the White House is he’s already run out of dipping sauce containers to throw at the television set.”
He added, “the blue wave made landfall, and now the Red Wedding begins,” referencing a famous massacre in the HBO show Game of Thrones.

No major late-night shows aired live during the election results, but Kimmel’s show was taped later in the night than usual, around 7 p.m. in Los Angeles, so that Kimmel could react to the early results.

“After all the talk about Nicki Minaj’s ass, John Husted’s ass, the only ass on Trump’s mind tonight is the one that just got handed to him,” Kimmel said, referencing Trump’s perplexing comments in recent weeks fixating on the gluteal physique of colleagues.
Jimmy Kimmel poses with the award for outstanding host for a game show for Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? during the Emmys in 2026, in Los Angeles. (Chris Pizzello/The Associated Press)
“Democrats have officially taken the House, thanks to President Trump. Blob Vila flipped another house.”
The night saw Democrats retake the House and the Senate, winning several key races and flipping seats long held by Republicans.

Although the full results aren’t in yet, the Democrats have already gained seven seats in the Senate, 25 seats in the House, and five seats among governors, according to The Associated Press, making for a historic midterms for the U.S.
Leading up to the midterms, Trump frequently urged his supporters to “pretend I am on the ballot” in a bid to rally his base.
- Updated Trump strategy unchanged after Democrats' midterm landslide, says Canada-U.S. trade minister
- Until the midterms, only 3 Black governors were ever elected in U.S. Tuesday saw 5 wins
- Analysis What the Republican midterm defeat means for Trump, the U.S. and Canada
He struck a different tone on the phone to Fox News as the results came in, claiming that the sitting president always loses the midterms, and taking no responsibility for the Republican defeat.
“I shouldn’t feel guilty, because virtually … no matter how good the president is, you lose. I don’t know why. Nobody’s explained that,” he said.

He has blamed losses on lackluster candidates, even though Trump himself had endorsed or selected many candidates who suffered historic losses in areas long thought to be safe Republican seats. Trump hand-picked Darline Graham to replace her late brother Lindsey Graham as Senator in South Carolina, but she lost to Democrat Annie Andrews in an upset. Trump also endorsed Ken Paxton for Senator in Texas, only for James Talarico to make history as the first Democrat elected to the Senate in Texas in nearly 40 years.

paras.en: “I have to believe he saw some of this coming, because this morning he was bragging about his approval rating in another country,” Kimmel said in his monologue, before playing a clip of Trump on Fox News talking about how he has a 99 per cent approval rating in Israel and joking that he’d move to Israel to become prime minister “if people ever get tired of me in the U.S.”
“That might be the best idea he’s ever had,” Kimmel said.

He slammed Trump for focusing on transgender people, “reflecting pools, racism against whites, Tylenol and Canada,” instead of priorities that align with “what Americans are worried about,” such as war, healthcare, climate change and inflation.

The Republicans’ historic losses come after an estimated $183 million US was poured into anti-trans attack ads attempting to criticize Democrats for supporting transgender people, according to The Associated Press.

articles.title: Kellogg's Rice Krispies changed its U.K. recipe, muffling its iconic snap, crackle and pop
articles.author: Natalie Stechyson

paras.en: Kellogg's Rice Krispies changed its U.K. recipe, muffling its iconic snap, crackle and pop
The cereal will continue to be made with real rice in Canada, Kellogg's confirms
This the way the world ends: not with a pop but a whimper.

Some consumers in the U.K. are in an uproar after cereal-maker Kellogg's recently changed its recipe there for Rice Krispies, replacing the whole rice grains in the family-favourite breakfast with rice flour.

This change is due to "changing weather conditions" affecting the quality and availability of rice, a spokesperson for Kellogg's in the U.K. told CBC News in a statement on Tuesday. The swap does not affect Kellogg's cereals in Canada or the U.S., another spokesperson for U.S.-based WK Kellogg Co. confirmed to CBC News.

"Our Rice Krispies cereals in the U.S. and Canada (e.g., Kellogg’s Rice Krispies, Kellogg’s Cocoa Krispies, Kellogg’s Frosted Krispies) are made with real rice and will continue to be," the spokesperson said in an emailed statement.
"There are no changes to their ingredients or recipes and consumers can continue to expect the same delicious Rice Krispies taste they know and love."

However, in the U.K., both Rice Krispies and Coco Pops now contain wheat gluten, making it unsafe for those with celiac disease or a wheat allergy. The change is reflected on the company's U.K. website, where the ingredients now include rice flour and wheat gluten, and its listed allergens include wheat and barley.
The Canadian website still shows rice as the cereal's main ingredient, and doesn't declare any allergens.
Boxes of Kellogg's breakfast cereal are seen at a supermarket in Springfield, Pa., on July 11, 2025. (Matt Slocum/The Associated Press)
As many have noted, the recipe change also eliminated the iconic sound the cereal used to make when you add milk — a cornerstone of the brand's marketing for nearly a century.

"They've lost their snap, crackle and pop!" Susanna Reid, a co-host on Good Morning Britain, exclaimed after co-host Ed Balls poured milk over a bowl of the reformulated cereal on air Wednesday morning.
She held a microphone to the bowl. There was only silence.
"There's no snap, crackle or pop in these. My toddler won't eat them and she usually eats them every day," a person posted on TikTok.
"You can immediately tell the difference. They're soggy, pale, they don't have the snapping sound when you put milk in. It's really gross," someone else commented.
Kellogg's Rice Krispies were first released in 1928, advertised as a "delicious cereal made from choice rice, cooked, puffed and toasted," according to the company website.

The words "snap, crackle and pop" first appeared in a print ad a year later, and have been printed on the cereal's packaging since 1932. The gnomes by the same name appeared in 1933 and made their television debut in 1955.
The cereal has been in the U.K. since 1928, Kellogg's pointed out in a 2018 press release, adding that it was marketed as "the talking cereal" due to "the sound it made when milk was poured onto it."
The rice grain fills with air when it's cooked, the company explained then, and when you add milk this forces the air to escape, creating the snap, crackle and pop.

- How the Canada-U.S. trade war might change your shopping habits

The U.K. Kellogg's spokesperson says it recently swapped out the rice because it "helps us maintain consistent quality at a time when changing weather conditions are affecting the quality and availability of some of the rice and grains used in our cereals."
"We appreciate that even small changes to a much-loved product can feel noticeable and that’s why we have approached this with a lot of care and consideration," the statement continued.

The global rice crop is declining due to various weather issues in major producer countries, like reduced rain in India, El Nino-related disruption in Indonesia and drought in Italy, Europe's largest supplier.
The USDA predicts 2026 global rice production will fall 4.6 per cent compared to last year, reports industry news site Farm Progress.

articles.title: Questions arise over emergency treatment given to Spanish soccer player in fatal collision
articles.author: Joseph Wilson

paras.en: Questions arise over emergency treatment given to Spanish soccer player in fatal collision
Talk of how quickly CPR was performed and whether medics used defibrillator
While Spain mourns the death of a soccer player who suffered a cardiac arrest after an on-field collision, the emergency medical treatment he received is falling under scrutiny.
Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel died Tuesday, a day after absorbing a heavy hit by the opposing team's goalkeeper during a match in Spain's second division and being rushed to hospital.

Spain's National Police opened an investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter, a standard procedure for a non-natural death. Investigators are expected to assess whether Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono's challenge went beyond the normal course of play.

But the incident also raised questions about the on-field treatment the 30-year-old player received after collapsing on the pitch Monday, including how quickly CPR was performed and whether medics used a defibrillator.
Elvira Gonzalez, president of Spain's Association of Nurses, Emergency Medics and Caregivers, told The Associated Press on Wednesday her organization was seeking more information.
"We can't say if they acted correctly or incorrectly, but we can demand that all the emergency procedures follow international standards of correct practice," Gonzalez said.

Team medical staff was at his side 20 seconds after De Miguel collapsed after being crunched in mid-air by Owono while disputing a high ball late in the game. Emergency workers quickly followed, running a stretcher to the scene in less than a minute.
It is unclear what medical attention De Miguel received during the five minutes he was prone on the pitch before being rushed off on a stretcher and placed in an ambulance waiting just off the field.
Some Spanish media reported he received CPR in the ambulance and recovered a pulse, while others say he received CPR on the field. It has not been established whether a defibrillator was used.
The Tenerife soccer club did not answer repeated calls and an email request asking for more information about the emergency treatment De Miguel received.
"There is contradictory information," Gonzalez said. "The first thing we need to know is where and when he supposedly recovered a pulse."
She said CPR must be performed from "minute 1" and that using a defibrillator is crucial.
"The first minutes are critical. You can only move a person once a pulse is restored," she said.

On-field treatment proved lifesaving for other athletes who collapsed on the field of play including Danish soccer player Christian Eriksen, whose heart stopped during a European Championship game in 2021. In the NFL, Damar Hamlin of the Buffalo Bills was treated with CPR and defibrillator on the field after he suffered cardiac arrest in 2023. Both survived.

Some local media say the police probe is also looking into the immediate medical treatment De Miguel received at Tenerife's stadium. The National Police in Madrid and in Tenerife would not comment on that to AP.
Tenerife's largest shareholder, Rayco Garcia acknowledged there is still much to be clarified.

"There are those who say that the impact caused his death, and that later they were able to stabilize him artificially even though it was very difficult to bring him back," Garcia told Spanish radio station Cadena Ser on Tuesday. "I prefer to wait for the autopsy and then we can take steps and talk about what needs talking about."
He said the medical team followed protocol and "were fast to get on the field."
- South African midfielder Jayden Adams, 25, dies weeks after playing in World Cup

But, Garcia added, "I would like to know through the investigation if there is something we don't know so that this doesn't happen again. If there is something that was in our hands to do that could have prevented this tragedy."
When asked why the ambulance didn't enter the field to help evacuate De Miguel, Garcia said the club's medical service didn't order it to approach.

The Spanish soccer federation regulations say that the home team must have at least one doctor on site, and that the home club must have an ambulance equipped with life support, including a defibrillator, at the ready.
La Liga did not respond to a request for comment on emergency protocols.
De Miguel's death stunned the soccer community in Spain and beyond. Teams across Europe paid tribute to De Miguel before Champions League games on Tuesday.
Fans left flowers in a makeshift shrine outside Tenerife's stadium.
Owono issued a statement through his club on Wednesday, offering his condolences to De Miguel's family.

"These are the most difficult days of my life," the goalkeeper said. "I feel an immense pain over the loss of Jesus. I think of him, his family, and everyone who loved him. I know there will be many matters to address, and I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect."
De Miguel is survived by his wife and 1-year-old daughter who were at Monday's game. His parents quickly flew to Tenerife, which is part of the Canary Islands archipelago.
The team will travel to the mainland to attend a funeral for De Miguel that Garcia says tentatively will be Thursday in the central province of Toledo.

articles.title: Africa's shifting role in the global drug trade

paras.en: For years, Africa was primarily known as a transit point for international drug trafficking networks.
But recent drug seizures and laboratory discoveries show that illicit drugs are no longer only passing through African countries — they are increasingly being manufactured there.

Recent discoveries of methamphetamine laboratories in countries such as Nigeria, South Africa, Kenya and Mozambique have fueled concerns that Africa is becoming a significant production hub for synthetic drugs.

According to the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), synthetic drug production increasingly involves transnational criminal networks and clandestine laboratories capable of supplying both local and international markets.

The debate gained new urgency this year after Nigeria's National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) dismantled what the agency described as the largest clandestine methamphetamine laboratory ever uncovered in the country.

The operation in Nigeria's southwestern Ogun State led to the arrest of 10 suspects, including three Mexican nationals whom the NDLEA said had been brought into the country to help manufacture methamphetamine.

NDLEA's chairman, Mohamed Buba Marwa, said officers seized more than 2.4 metric tons of methamphetamine, precursor chemicals and other materials with an estimated international market value of about $363 million (€312 million).
The scale of the operation attracted widespread attention in Nigeria.

"It is no longer something you only see in movies," said DW correspondent Olisa Chukwumah. "The discovery raised serious questions about the level of local consumption if production is now happening in Nigeria."

Chukwumah said Nigerian authorities have uncovered meth laboratories before, but the size and sophistication of recent operations suggest that drug manufacturing networks are becoming more deeply established.
Dokun Adedeji, co-founder of the Compassionate Care Recovery Initiative, said Nigeria's drug landscape has evolved significantly over the past decade.
"We used to think we were only a transit nation," he explained. "Then we became a consumer nation. Now we are discovering that we are also a production nation."
He noted that authorities have uncovered dozens of smaller laboratories over the years, with meth production sites identified in multiple states.
According to the UNODC, increasing local drug consumption and the expansion of illicit drug markets have coincided with the growth of synthetic-drug production in West Africa.
Adedeji described the impact of drug laboratories as "devastating and destructive."

He said substance abuse is contributing to school dropouts, family breakdowns, mental health challenges and rising criminal activity. Many families struggle to seek help because of stigma and fear of public judgment.
"We see families suffering every day," he said. "Many people are unable to speak openly about addiction because of concerns about reputation and discrimination."
The UNODC says young people are increasingly affected by drug-use disorders, with 34% of people receiving treatment for such disorders in Africa under the age of 25.

In addition to traditional drugs such as cannabis, users are increasingly turning to synthetic substances, including methamphetamine, often known on the streets as "ice." There is also growing misuse of prescription medications and reports of experimentation with dangerous inhalants and other toxic substances.
Nigeria's National Drug Law Enforcement Agency has intensified enforcement efforts in recent years, leading to a series of high-profile drug seizures and arrests.
NGOs have increasingly stepped in to fill the gap through awareness campaigns, particularly on university campuses where drug use is becoming more visible.
Chukwumah said there is still no coordinated, top-down policy approach and that much of the awareness work is being carried out by civil society groups.

Adedeji argued that policies based solely on punishment often drive users underground, making it harder for authorities and healthcare providers to identify and support people struggling with addiction.
UNODC and civil society groups advocate a broader response that extends beyond law enforcement.

Among the proposals being discussed are stronger national policies on substance abuse, expanded rehabilitation services, workplace drug prevention programs and increased regional cooperation across West Africa.
This article has been adapted from an episode of DW's AfricaLink podcast.

articles.title: Kosovo: Outrage as authorities accused of not helping femicide victim

paras.en: Arlinda Zekaj repeatedly asked the Kosovo police for protection. They said she was exaggerating.

On October 25, the 49-year-old once again reported her husband to the police. This time, he was arrested. But Zekaj also asked the police for additional protection — this time against her husband's family. But to no avail.

The police drove Arlinda Zekaj home. Her killer was waiting. At 8:58 p.m., Zekaj got out of the squad car. A short time later, the police received an emergency call. When officers arrived at Zekaj's house at 9:10 p.m., they found only her body.
The 49-year-old had been brutally murdered in her bedroom with an axe. By that time, the alleged perpetrator — her brother-in-law, Albert Sylaj — had fled.

The murder, which took place in the village of Vitomirica, near the city of Peja in western Kosovo, has sparked numerous public protests and demonstrations involving thousands of people across the country.
It was the eighth femicide in Kosovo in 2026 — and apparently the most brutal.

More so than almost any other femicide in the country in recent years, Zekaj's death demonstrated that one of the things that made her killing possible was the fact that police and prosecutors ignored the victim's pleas for help .
One of the first protests took place on October 26, when a group of feminists emptied buckets of red paint on steps outside the seat of Kosovo's government in the capital, Pristina.
"The state killed Arlinda," read a banner that the activists hung at the entrance to the building.

In the days that followed and on November 1, public anger brought thousands of people to streets across Kosovo. Many carried photographs of murdered women. One slogan appeared again and again: "The government has blood on its hands."
The protesters are demanding that charges be brought against the police officers and prosecutors responsible for handling Zekaj's case.

They are also calling for the resignation of Interior Minister Xhelal Svecla and Justice Minister Donika Gervalla, whom Kosovo Prime Minister Albin Kurti appointed national coordinator for protection against domestic violence in March.
Both Svecla and Gervalla have rejected calls to step down.
For his part, however, Kurti acknowledged that certain Kosovo state institutions had "failed."
In many ways, this was a murder foretold.

As far back as the summer, Arlinda Zekaj had reported her husband to the police for making threats against her. A court in Peja subsequently issued a protection order, granted her temporary custody of their son and gave her the right to remain in the family home.

The protection order allowed her husband to continue living in the same house, provided he did not come within two meters (about 6.5 feet) of her. Outside the home, he was required to keep a distance of at least 20 meters.
Zekaj had decided against moving to a women's shelter because she wanted to continue living in her own home with her son.
Even after the protection order was issued, she repeatedly made complaints to the police, among other things about threats from her brother-in-law Albert Sylaj.

Three days before the killing, on October 22, Zekaj reported that members of her husband's family, including Sylaj, were in her home against her wishes. According to her account, he threatened her with the words: "Leave or I'll kill you."
Nevertheless, Sylaj was questioned only as a witness in the case against Zekaj's husband.
Police arrested him near Peja on October 27. He is now under investigation for murder.
'A collapse of the state and society in relation to women'
Since 2010, 55 women in Kosovo have been killed by partners or family members, often after years of documented abuse and ignored complaints.
In recent years, successive Kosovo governments have adopted a number of laws and regulations aimed at better combating violence against women.
These measures include the possibility of life sentences for perpetrators in femicide cases.

Activists argue, however, that the authorities responsible for enforcing these measures — including police, social services, prosecutors and courts — have failed to implement them consistently and in a coordinated manner.

Writing in an article for the news portal Nacionale, lawyer Njomeza Zejnullahu said that "After every murder, we hear the same word: failure. 'The institutions have failed.' I disagree. Failure is when something happens once, when a system that normally works breaks down at one point. When the cases keep repeating themselves, when the victims are almost always women and each of them had previously knocked on the door of an institution, it is no longer a failure. It is a collapse of the state and society in relation to women in general."

paras.en: In the aftermath of Arlinda Zekaj's killing, several senior police officers from Peja and the surrounding area have been suspended. A prosecutor who had handled Zekaj's complaints has also been suspended.
For the protesters in Kosovo, however, this is not nearly enough.

"All those involved within the chain of responsibility must not only be removed from office but also criminally prosecuted for failing to fulfil their official duties," said Liridona Sijarina, a political scientist and feminist activist with Kosovo's Kolektivi Feminist (Feminist Collective).
"That includes not only police officers, prosecutors and judges, but also Mayor of Peja Gazmend Muhaxheri and, ultimately, government ministers," she told DW.

Sijarina went on to say that feminist activists are also calling on the Interior Ministry to create a dedicated unit that would treat women's safety as a matter of national security and focus specifically on preventing femicides.

She also said that the government should make its draft legislation on affordable social housing a top political priority and ensure that women who have experienced domestic violence are eligible for social housing.

"In our view," said Sijarina, "the behavior of the institutions so far has deepened women's distrust of the state and, as a result, allowed violence against them to escalate. The government now has the opportunity to show whether it truly takes women's lives seriously by clearly responding to our demands."
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: 36 years later: Hungary opens Communist-era secret service files

paras.en: On November 4, 1956, tens of thousands of Soviet soldiers and tanks swept into Hungary, brutally suppressing the country's anti-Communist uprising. Decades of dictatorship followed, relying on Hungary's brutal secret police to keep the system in place.
Events on Nov. 4 this year represent something of a reckoning with this dark chapter of Hungarian history.

Prime Minister Peter Magyar's government is ordering the full release of the country's secret police "agent files," which contain the names of Hungarian state security informants, some of whom cooperated out of their own volition even as others passed on information unwittingly.

Magyar and his Tisza party had previously promised to make the "agent files" public if elected. Their release is an historic event, as it comes after over three decades of heated debate over how to handle such sensitive files. The decision to publish is also sure to spark further debate on Communist-era guilt and responsibility.

Hungarians have been calling for the release of the files for years. After the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 and the end of Soviet rule, civil rights activists and smaller Hungarian political parties said the files should be released. Demands for their publication were expressed repeatedly over following decades.

Yet Hungary's first post-Communist prime minister Jozsef Antall, a conservative, rejected the idea as did Viktor Orban's long-ruling Fidesz party. The latter blocked efforts to open the files, voting more than 30 times against such plans since 2010, according to Hungarian news platform Telex.

A partial release of state security files did occur in the 1990s, when the Hungarian parliament passed the so-called "agents law" in 1994. This required members of the government, members of parliament and certain public servants to undergo background checks to determine whether they had ever worked for the former state security services.
From 1997, Hungarian citizens have been able to view their own files and in 2003, permissions were expanded. But they have never been able to find out the names of informants.

The law relevant to the files contained provisions that were open to broad interpretation, which allowed government agencies such as the Ministry of Interior to prevent the transfer of files from the secret police to the Historical Archives of the Hungarian State Security, or ABTL, if they believed it would compromise national security.

Such a selective release of files not only prevented Hungarian society from learning the truth about its state security service, it also made it possible for files to be exploited in political power struggles, for example, by leaking compromising information about politicians to the public.
One such case involved former Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Medgyessy, who was exposed by the Fidesz-affiliated daily Magyar Nemzet in 2002 for having worked as a Communist-era secret agent.
Magyar's government is putting an end to this. From Nov. 4, databases containing all the names of, and key information about, informants will be made available online.

Additional databases will be released as well. They include one of the most extensive databases on individuals recruited to work for the Hungarian state security agency. Confidentiality provisions set out in the old "agent law" have also been scaled back, meaning significantly more files will likely be accessible in the future.

The upcoming release of data on up to 60,000 out of an estimated 150,000 secret police informants could have major political consequences. Even so, ABTL director Bendeguz Gergo Cseh recently cautioned that, "you can't believe everything the state security agencies and their files claim." Many documents were incomplete and not fully reliable and many files had been destroyed, he said.

Others are also skeptical about the release. Historian Janos M. Rainer, an expert on Hungary's dictatorship, told Telex that the publication would have made sense right after the fall of the regime. Releasing the files after all these years is more of a symbolic gesture, he argued.

Meanwhile historian Krisztian Ungvary, who has researched the state security files extensively, welcomes the upcoming publication. It will allow historians to pursue new research and society to engage in fresh debates, Ungvary told DW. He believes Hungary will benefit from such reflection, as "societal lies inevitably lead to a strained relationship with politics and the price we paid for that was 16 years of Fidesz rule."
For Magyar, making this information public carries great significance. The idea of coming to terms with the past, especially the years of the Orban regime, is one of his favorite topics.

When the Hungarian parliament amended the law about the files in mid-September, Magyar wrote on Facebook that, "after a 36-year delay, the Hungarian parliament today decided, at the initiative of Tisza, to make the 'agent files' public. Fidesz did not support the motion. I wonder why?"
It was an allusion to the fact that many prominent figures in Fidesz' ranks and in Orban's inner circle were members of the Hungarian Communist party or secret police.
The most well-known of the latter is likely Jozsef Horvath, a former full-time employee of the department of Hungarian state security that was responsible for suppressing the domestic opposition.

Under Orban, Horvath worked as an intelligence officer and security advisor, and in 2024, he became the research director of Orban's Sovereignty Protection Office. This was an agency that exposed supposed enemies of the Orban regime, branding them " foreign agents ."
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: The biggest winners and losers of the 2026 US midterms

paras.en: Democrats had a big night in Tuesday’s United States midterm elections, winning control of both chambers of Congress and pulling off some surprising victories in longtime Republican strongholds.

From turning Texas blue to electing the country’s first Muslim senator, there were plenty of historic wins. But the night also brought some major setbacks for US President Donald Trump and his allies, including one who spent hundreds of millions of dollars backing losing candidates.
Here’s a look at some of the election’s biggest winners and losers.

Annie Andrews: In one of the most surprising wins of the night, Democrat Annie Andrews flipped a Republican-held Senate seat in a deeply conservative South Carolina, beating out the Trump-backed candidate Darline Graham.

A paediatrician who campaigned on healthcare and affordability, Andrews became the first Democrat elected to the Senate from the state since 1998, and its first elected female senator. The victory was a major breakthrough for Democrats and helped them take control of the Senate.
Abdul El-Sayed: Progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan, becoming the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.

The former public health official overcame attacks on his faith and a bitter primary battle against establishment-backed Democrat Haley Stevens, who went on to endorse Rogers. “You chose hate and Michigan chose hope,” El-Sayed told Rogers in his victory speech.

Chuck Schumer: After facing criticism from fellow Democrats for not pushing back hard enough against Trump, as well as anger from progressives over his support for arms sales to Israel, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer is now poised to reclaim his position as majority leader.

Schumer helped recruit candidates including Sherrod Brown and Roy Cooper, who flipped Republican-held Senate seats. He celebrated the victory on Tuesday, saying, “We have five words for the American people: ‘Relief is on the way’.”

James Talarico: After years of Democrats trying to turn Texas blue, James Talarico finally pulled off a major upset by winning a US Senate seat in a state Trump had carried by double digits just two years ago.

The 37-year-old former middle-school teacher, state legislator and Presbyterian seminarian gained national attention for using his Christian faith to challenge the religious right. But his campaign against Republican Ken Paxton also focused on the cost of living and corruption, including the influence of wealthy donors like Elon Musk, who supported Paxton.

Vivek Ramaswamy: Biotech billionaire and Trump ally Vivek Ramaswamy lost Ohio’s governor’s race to Democrat Amy Acton in light of a controversial attack ad in which Acton’s estranged mother accused her of lying about her difficult childhood.

What the ad left out was that her mother lost custody after Acton’s stepfather was indicted for raping her as a child. The widely condemned ad dominated the final month of Ramaswamy’s campaign, with his team eventually pulling it after spending about $1m to keep it running.

Haley Stevens: Michigan Democratic Congresswoman Haley Stevens ended up on the losing side for the second time, after first losing the Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, and then endorsing his Republican opponent Mike Rogers just two days before the election.

Stevens broke with El-Sayed over his criticism of Israel and an ad linking US military aid to rising grocery prices, which he disavowed. El-Sayed won anyway, while Stevens was left facing a backlash from Democrats and a wave of resignations from her own team.

Elon Musk: The world’s richest man spent more than $400m backing Republicans, only to see them lose both chambers of Congress. Among the candidates he supported was Ken Paxton, who lost the Texas Senate race to Democrat James Talarico.

Musk now faces possible congressional investigations into his leadership of Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and his companies’ federal contracts, with Democrats gaining the power to subpoena documents and even call him to testify under oath.

Donald Trump: Though Trump wasn’t on the ballot, the midterms are a major blow to the final two years of his presidency, with Democrats winning control of both chambers of Congress. Republican candidates backed by Trump lost Senate races in longtime strongholds like Texas and South Carolina.

The results mean Trump will spend the remainder of his time in office facing a Democratic-controlled Congress with the power to block his legislative agenda, investigate his administration, and hold his officials accountable for alleged malfeasance.

articles.title: US midterms 2026: What key races remain undecided?

paras.en: A Democratic romp in the midterms has rocked the US political landscape, but several closely contested races remain too close to call.

- Alaska Senate: Republican Senator Dan Sullivan is seeking to retain his seat against Democratic challenger Mary Peltola, who has a 626-vote lead. If neither candidate gets more than 50 percent of the vote, then it will go to ranked-choice voting under Alaska law.

- Alaska governor: Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is facing off against Republican Bernadette Wilson. Kreiss-Tomkins’s share of the vote is 49.2 percent with an estimated 74 percent of ballots counted.
- Kansas governor: Democrat Cindy Holscher has a lead of less than a percentage point over Republican Ty Masterson. Holscher’s lead is 5,557, with an estimated 98 percent of the votes counted.
- Mississippi Senate: Democratic candidate Scott Colom leads Republican incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by 43 votes with an estimated 96 percent of votes counted.

- Los Angeles mayor: Incumbent Mayor Karen Bass is locked in a tight contest with Nithya Raman, who is backed by the Democratic Socialists of America. Bass has 48.9 percent of the vote, compared with Raman’s 51.1 percent, with an estimated one-third of the ballots uncounted.

articles.title: WHO approves trials for two new Ebola vaccines

paras.en: Incredible celebrations as last patient leaves a DRC Ebola centre

The World Health Organization (WHO) has approved clinical trials for two new Ebola vaccines, as doctors fight to control the largest outbreak in the history of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).
On Monday, WHO expert groups recommended adding two vaccine trials designed to fight the Bundibugyo strain, which has killed more than 5,300 people, most in the DRC, since May.
Public health agencies have struggled to contain the Bundibugyo virus, which has a fatality rate of 50 percent due to the lack of a vaccine or treatments designed specifically for the strain.
WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said a trial that began last month used the Ervebo vaccine, which was approved for the Zaire strain of the Ebola virus but is not designed for Bundibugyo.
Tedros said the new vaccines undergoing trials are designed specifically for the Bundibugyo virus. Results from the vaccine trial are expected in early 2027, the WHO reported.

The DRC’s National Institute for Biomedical Research is leading the trial, backed by the WHO and other partners, said Tedros. The vaccine was developed by the University of Oxford with the Serum Institute of India and Moderna.

“Vaccines are powerful tools, but they are not substitutes for the proven measures that can save lives now: early care, contact tracing, isolation, safe and dignified burials and trusted engagement with communities,” he added.
The African Centres for Disease Control and Prevention said 10,444 cases of the Bundibugyo virus have been confirmed, making it the fastest-growing outbreak in DRC’s history.
In Kenya, nine cases have been reported, including two deaths. One case has been confirmed in Nigeria, according to the WHO.
Tedros urged that travel restrictions imposed by some countries be lifted, warning that they could discourage transparent reporting.
“Such restrictions punish countries for doing the right thing, create disincentives for transparency, and harm the response,” said Tedros.
The WHO said it is supporting all countries neighbouring DRC to prepare for cases to spread across borders.
Meanwhile, a British healthcare worker infected with Ebola is being evacuated from the DRC to the United Kingdom for specialist treatment, a UK government spokesperson said.
In a statement, the government said the patient is in a stable condition and is expected to arrive in the UK by Thursday, then be transferred to a high-consequence infectious disease unit.
The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low, the statement said.

articles.title: Democrats seize full control of Congress. And, which candidates made history last night
articles.author: Brittney Melton

paras.en: Democrats seize full control of Congress. And, which candidates made history last night

Democrats have gained full control of Congress for the first time since 2023, flipping both the House and Senate with significant wins in deep red states. Abdul El-Sayed defeated Mike Rogers in Michigan, and Troy Jackson defeated Susan Collins in Maine, winning their states' closely watched Senate seats. In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, ending more than 30 years of Republican control, while Democratic state Rep. James Talarico won the U.S. Senate race. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton became the first Democratic senator elected in nearly a century. A record number of candidates endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America were elected to the House, growing the organization's presence on Capitol Hill. Nine states also made history with their gubernatorial picks. Take a look at how key demographics voted.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Here are 6 midterm takeaways from NPR's senior political correspondent Domenico Montanaro:
All the signs were pointing in Democrats' direction heading into election night. But nothing indicated quite this level of a romp.

- President Trump wanted this election to be about him. It was and that hurt Republicans: Trump was historically unpopular. People were frustrated with the economy and the war, and it hurt the GOP. It turns out when you wage the kind of war that you said you wouldn't get into — that drags on, raises gas prices and piles on people who were already feeling the pinch, don't be surprised when you pay the price.

- Republicans tried to insulate themselves with redistricting, but it didn't work: Trump strongly encouraged conservative-led states to redistrict — but it backfired. There was always the possibility that weakening safe districts could make them more competitive and that happened. It's a true cautionary tale of the "dummymander."

- Latinos are a true swing group in America now: Trump only lost Latinos by 5 points in 2024. In this election, they sided with Democrats by 27 points. The economy and deportation tactics were big reasons why. In a real indictment of the Trump deportation policies, the voter poll found 59% overall said they disapproved of ICE.

- Is Texas — and other red states — in play for Democrats or was this election a giant asterisk? Democrats won in a lot of red states. The party has needed to show it can win in red and rural areas. They did that this time. But will that last, or is it a Trump-sized asterisk?

- The results of this year's elections don't mean the country is enamored with the Democratic Party: The party is still unpopular and fissures within their coalition will be laid bare over the next several months in the 2028 presidential primaries. They'll have to be careful politically with how they approach leadership with the opportunity they've been handed.

- The polls got the direction right. If anything, they underestimated Democratic support: For a decade, polls have underestimated Republican support. In these elections, that was not the case. It's important to understand that it's hard to poll when the country has been going through as significant a political realignment as it has been in the Trump era.

President Trump lashed out early on as results showed Democrats ahead in many key races, but later congratulated the Democrats and said more than once that he would respect the outcome of the elections.

- 🎧 The president positioned himself as the central figure in the midterm elections, relying on his personality and appeal to supporters to counter low approval ratings and economic concerns. NPR's Franco Ordoñez tells Up First that this strategy made it more difficult for vulnerable candidates to distance themselves from him. Ordoñez says he expects there to be a confrontational relationship between Trump and the Democrats, especially as they prepare to investigate him and his family.

After the Democratic victory in the House, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries is poised to become the first Black lawmaker to be elected Speaker. Last night, Jeffries said, "We understand as House Democrats that we need to deliver dramatic change." With a Democratic majority, they'll have the chance to exert more influence in the legislative branch.

- 🎧 The large Democratic margins in the House and Senate will serve as a check on the White House, NPR's Barbara Sprunt says. A Democratic Senate majority will provide massive roadblocks for the president's confirmation of the future cabinet and judicial nominees. In the House, Sprunt says to expect numerous investigations. Jeffries plans to hold those involved in corruption accountable, and the House will have subpoena power to compel witnesses to testify. Democrats have a list of targets in mind already, but Sprunt says the party is cautious about pursuing a third impeachment of Trump, because it doesn't support their argument that they have more to offer than just being anti-Trump party.

paras.en: About 1 in 20 Americans experience seasonal affective disorder (SAD), and it typically lasts for nearly 40% of the year. If you're dealing with SAD, you might feel sluggish, depressed and lose interest in activities you once enjoyed. You might also find yourself oversleeping, overeating and gaining weight. As winter approaches, NPR's Life Kit offers advice on recognizing these feelings and finding ways to boost your mood and energy.
- 💙 Women are more vulnerable to SAD, and the condition is more common in the Northern Hemisphere.
- 💙 Some people need more light. Experts often recommend SAD lamps, which are significantly brighter than typical indoor lighting.
- 💙 Stop eating three hours before bedtime to help your body rest. Eating within a consistent 10- to 12-hour window signals your body about the time of day, no matter what else is happening.
- 💙 Exercising during the day helps your body recognize its daily rhythm, keeping you alert when needed and allowing for rest in the evening.
- 💙 Try to reduce stress by decorating a room with bright colors, seeing a therapist to discuss your feelings, or trying meditation for relaxation.

Typhoon Halong severely impacted small Native villages in Western Alaska last fall, destroying infrastructure and displacing more than a thousand people. A year later, many remain displaced. In Kipnuk — a village of under 200 homes — dozens of houses were swept off their foundations. The community is now mostly scattered across Alaska, and some have relocated far from their ancestral lands. Climate change increases the vulnerability of towns like Kipnuk to future storms. While most residents wish to rebuild the village in a safer location, current FEMA funding only allows for restoring what was damaged. See these photos of the town now, as its people continue to pick up the pieces.

- Ancient Egyptian mummies were once marketed as medicine. Archaeologists are using chemistry to better understand how they were made.
- New World screwworm cases have increased to 99 since June, as the outbreak accelerates across Texas, New Mexico and Arizona.

articles.title: The world is reacting to the Democrats' sweeping midterm elections victory
articles.author: Kate Bartlett

paras.en: The world is reacting to the Democrats' sweeping midterm elections victory

One color dominates international headlines about the U.S. midterm election results. French newspaper Libération called the Democrats' win "une vague bleue," or blue wave, Britain's Daily Mail dubbed it a "historic blue tsunami," and The Times of India's headline ran "midterm blues for Trump."

Countries at war were also watching closely, with Ukrainian newspaper The Kyiv Independent's online headline hopeful: "Democrats seize control of Congress in blow to Trump, potential boost for Ukraine."

Russia had a different take. Rossiyskaya Gazeta, the state-run daily newspaper, suggested the results would in fact be a blow to Ukraine, which has firm support from the European Union. "Brussels, brace yourself. After the Republicans' defeat, Trump's wrath will fall on Europe," read the headline.

Iran's Tehran Times said "Call it Operation Midterms Hammer" — a play on the U.S. military's Operation Midnight Hammer strikes against Iran in June 2025. Since the United States and Israel renewed their war against Iran this February, the fallout has pushed up the price of oil and other goods, becoming a major election campaign issue. The article ran a cartoon of a man slamming a mini-Trump with a hammer in a game of whack-a-mole.
In Israel, which just held its own parliamentary elections last week, headlines focused on what the Democrats' victory means for the U.S. support of the Jewish state and its war in Gaza.

The Times of Israel ran a headline focusing on Democrat Abdul El-Sayed's triumph in the U.S. Senate race in Michigan, saying "Anti-Israel El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate race, pledges no money for 'apartheid, genocide.'" A headline in Israel's Haaretz read: "Abdul El-Sayed Shows Opposition to Israel Is No Barrier to Winning Battleground States."
Newspapers in U.S. neighbors Canada and Mexico, meanwhile, noted the results were a rebuke and setback for Trump.
Some foreign politicians celebrate, others keep silent

International leaders tend to shy away from commenting directly on the results of U.S. midterm elections, as opposed to presidential races when they routinely congratulate the winner. However, this time several have made public statements.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that with Trump accepting the midterms results, the focus can turn to ending wars and bringing down prices.

"The world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that's the cost of living," Burnham told reporters Wednesday. "I can't get people's cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, the conflict in Ukraine started by Russia, these are the things we have to focus on now."
"I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all - and that's the cost of living."
Reacting to the Democrats' victory over Trump's Republicans in the Senate, PM Andy Burnham says now is an opportunity to focus on other matters. pic.twitter.com/xkGl4eogSY
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who has an acrimonious relationship with Trump, was forthright in his response.

"Yesterday, American society voted against policies that only impoverish. Against hate. Against machismo. Against climate denialism and against the privileges of the elites," Sánchez wrote on social media.

In South Africa, where diplomatic relations with the U.S. are at an all-time low after Trump falsely accused the government of persecuting its white minority, President Cyril Ramaphosa said "The people of America have spoken."

Ramaphosa made the comments as he cast his own ballot in South Africa's municipal elections Wednesday, adding: "I do think that this is going to introduce a new era in world relations. … We're hoping that on a bilateral basis there will be a coming together of minds."

A senior Russia diplomat suggested the Democratic Party's return to power in both houses of Congress bode ill for U.S.-Russian relations. "The approach of the activist wing of the Democratic Party towards Russia is extremely negative. There's nothing new in that," said Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov in an interview with the state RIA-Novosti news service. Ryabkov also signaled there would be no grand shifts in Russian foreign policy as a result.

In Germany, Defense Minister Boris Pistorius congratulated Democrats on an "historic victory," adding that Berlin's commitment to cooperating with the administration in Washington remains unchanged. He stressed that Berlin will be reaching out to both Democrats and Republicans.

Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere said the results are a "powerful political signal about a change of course among American voters." Speaking to Reuters, Stoere said "voices are now emerging in American politics that are closer to us than the president and the administration have stood for, for example on climate and environment, and in foreign policy and development aid policy."

A spokeswoman for China's Foreign Ministry told a daily press conference that the midterm elections "are an internal affair of the United States." She added that "China is willing to continue working with the U.S. to … strengthen communication, properly manage differences, expand cooperation, and build a constructive, strategically stable China-U.S. relationship based on the principles of respect, fairness, and reciprocity."

Japan's top government spokesman, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara, told a news conference that Japan's alliance with the U.S. remains essential for global peace and stability, regardless of the outcome of midterm elections.

The alliance "remains the cornerstone of Japan's foreign and security policy" and is crucial to "maximizing its national interests" amid an increasingly volatile and uncertain global situation," he added.

Iran's Parliament Speaker and top negotiator Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf commented on X: "Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message. If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare."

For Israel, the U.S. midterm results fall during a time of political uncertainty, amid coalition-building talks after Trump's ally, incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, lost his parliamentary majority in Oct. 27 Israeli elections. "In some ways Netanyahu lost two elections in the last week," said Israel-American analyst Mairav Zonstein.

Netanyahu's rivals seized on the midterm results. One Israeli opposition leader, Yair Golan, said the U.S. results reveal "just how toxic Netanyahu is among both Democrats and Republicans." Another, Yair Lapid, said the U.S. results "eliminate any possibility of a unity government led by Netanyahu."

Laura Cain in London, Charles Maynes in Moscow, Esme Nicholson in Berlin, Lauren Frayer in Tel Aviv, Hadeel Al-Shalchi in Istanbul, Aya Batrawy in Dubai and Anthony Kuhn in Seoul contributed reporting.

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed welcomes Trump's plan to cut Israel aid, calls for end to arms sales
articles.author: Steve Inskeep

paras.en: Abdul El-Sayed welcomes Trump's plan to cut Israel aid, calls for end to arms sales
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed made history in Michigan, defeating Republican Mike Rogers to become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate as his party reclaimed control of Congress.

The 42-year-old former public health official campaigned on lowering costs, Medicare for All and getting corporate money out of politics. Rogers, backed by President Trump, repeatedly attacked El-Sayed over his Muslim faith and opposition to U.S. military aid to Israel.

But Israel and the war in Gaza became a defining fault line in the race. Haley Stevens, whom El-Sayed defeated in the Democratic primary, endorsed Rogers just days before the election amid a bitter dispute over Israel.
After a campaign marked by heated disagreements over Israel, El-Sayed now finds himself on the same side of an issue as Trump.
The president announced plans to end roughly $4 billion in annual military aid to Israel by the end of the year, though he offered no details on how the cuts would work.
Speaking to Morning Edition after his victory, El-Sayed welcomed the proposal.
"I think the president is actually right on this policy," he said. "I'd also like to see us stop selling weaponry that gets used to do the worst things, including genocide and apartheid, to Israel."
The U.S. provides Israel with $3.8 billion in annual military aid under an agreement that runs through 2028.
His argument goes beyond Israel. El-Sayed also questioned U.S. military support for Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Pakistan, saying American tax dollars should be spent at home.
Winning Michigan's Senate seat, however, doesn't mean every division within his party has disappeared.

During a visit to Michigan before the election, NPR's Michel Martin heard concerns about El-Sayed from some Jewish and Black voters. Asked whether he still had work to do to win their support, El-Sayed said the election results challenged that narrative.
"There's always more work to do. There's always more to build. There's always more conversations to have," he said.
Listen to the full interview live by clicking on the blue button above.
The digital version was edited by Treye Green.

articles.title: NYC's Mamdani says Abdul El-Sayed's Senate victory in Michigan 'means so much to so many'

paras.en: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Wednesday that Abdul El-Sayed's Senate election victory in Michigan "is one that means so much to so many."
El-Sayed, who will become the first Muslim U.S. senator in history, toppled former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers in what was one of the most-watched contests of the election.

"I haven't spoken to him yet. I'm sure he is quite busy. I've had the privilege of speaking to him in the past, and I have to say that his election is one that means so much to so many," Mamdani said Wednesday.

"And to see to see that victory in the face that all that he had to reckon with over the course of that campaign, whether in terms of the extraordinary amount of money spent to oppose him or the racism and slander that he was met with on a daily basis, it is incredibly exciting to see as he said last night, that the good guys won," Mamdani added.
Mamdani added that "what last night showed us is that Americans are tired of being told that their needs are unrealistic by politicians who have been bought by the wealthiest people in the country.

"This country has elected a new generation of leadership, a generation with a mandate to lower the cost of living, to build, not bomb, to never betray the working people who entrusted them with power," he added. "And I hear often that the politics that we're fighting for here in New York City are not possible outside of city limits. And what last night showed us is that working people are the majority, whether we are speaking of Austin or Ann Arbor or Astoria, and it is time to put those same people first in our politics and last night shows us that it's possible to do so all across the country."
