articles.title: Breaking Free a Seized Wheel Bearing Hub
articles.author: BCA Bearings by NTN

paras.en: A wheel bearing hub unit that is seized into a suspension knuckle can turn a routine repair into a struggle. The hub may be retained by bolts, but corrosion between the hub and knuckle can hold it in place after every fastener is removed. Understanding what formed that bond helps you choose an effective removal method and avoid damaging the knuckle, axle, or nearby components.
When a steel hub seizes in a knuckle bore, oxygen and moisture have reacted with metal at the interface. For iron in the steel, a simplified rust-forming reaction is:

The iron hydroxide then changes into hydrated iron oxides—the reddish-brown corrosion commonly called rust. These corrosion products take up more space than the original metal. As they build up in the narrow clearance between the hub and knuckle, they can wedge the two parts together. But, the oxides are very reactive and brittle.

The joint may also involve dissimilar metals. Many hubs are made of steel, while some knuckles are aluminum. In the presence of moisture, these metals can form a galvanic cell that accelerates corrosion. De-icers and road salt can make the problem worse in areas that receive snow. When a steel hub is mounted in an aluminum knuckle, galvanic corrosion can occur alongside rust on the steel hub, so it may not be accurate to describe the entire bond as iron oxide. BCA Bearings identifies galvanic corrosion at steel hub and aluminum knuckle interfaces as a common cause of hubs becoming difficult to separate.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The goal of removal is to break the mechanical bond created by corrosion products. Vibration, impact or movement can crack them. Heat can create stress at the interface, while penetrants may reduce friction and help the parts move once a gap opens. Dedicated rust removers can react chemically with corrosion, but they may also attack the base metal or nearby finishes.

During the vehicle inspection, look for other corrosion damage. Dust shields and parking brake components inside the rotor hat can be perforated by rust and corrosion. Spotting this damage during the inspection can help you avoid delays while waiting for replacement parts.
What heat and chemicals can—and can’t—do

Heat does not reverse the rust reaction. It does not turn iron oxide back into iron. Instead, heating and cooling create differential expansion and contraction between the hub, knuckle, and corrosion layer. That movement can stress and crack brittle deposits. If the outer part of the joint expands more than the inner part, the temporary increase in clearance can help the components move.

Where you apply heat matters. The knuckle surrounds the hub, so heating the knuckle near the bore can expand the bore; however, uncontrolled torch heat can damage or distort the knuckle and nearby ball joints, seals, sensors, brake parts, or suspension components. BCA recommends against torch heating the knuckle and suggests an induction heater for localized heat at the wheel end.

If you plan to use heat, follow the vehicle and tool manufacturers’ instructions, and apply it only where you can control its effects. Be aware of wiring for the wheel speed sensor and brake pad wear sensor, as well as suspension bushings that could be damaged by heat. You are not trying to melt the hub unit. The goal is to use controlled heating and expansion to help break the corrosion bond.

Penetrants work differently. Most penetrating oils do not chemically dissolve iron oxide. They can seep into small clearances, lubricate contact surfaces and reduce friction as the hub begins to move. A light tap or controlled vibration may help the fluid reach the interface. Give it time to soak, and reapply as needed.

Rust removers, often acid-based, are designed to react with or dissolve corrosion. They may be useful on accessible parts after removal, but they are not automatically safe to use on an assembled hub and knuckle. Check product compatibility with aluminum, coatings, seals and nearby components. Keep penetrants and other flammable products away from open flames and hot surfaces, and follow label directions before applying heat.

When selecting a penetrant, make sure it is a penetrant and not a lubricant. Penetrants are formulated to wick into areas between the hub unit and knuckle. Also, penetrants do not catch fire or damage rubber and plastic materials like ball joint boots. If any penetrant contaminates the brake pads or rotor, clean it off immediately with a solvent.
Most of all, take your time and read the directions with these products. Also, use in a well-ventilated area because some of the ingredients can cause health problems.

Always begin with the vehicle safely supported and the service procedure for that application in hand. In recent years there have been a lot of tools introduced to remove hub units faster. They can range from a simple bar the attaches to the flange that you can strike with a sledge hammer, to application specific tools that use hydraulics to force the hub unit out of the bore. But, all of these tool do the same thing, they help to breakdown oxides between the hub and knuckle.

An air hammer can help, but technique matters more than simply increasing force or buying a larger air hammer. The key is to use a suitable blunt attachment on the hub’s mounting flange or ears to make the hub rotate slightly in the knuckle. Avoid driving the tool between the hub and knuckle as a wedge; that can gouge the bore or break the casting. BCA recommends using the air hammer to rotate the hub flange relative to the knuckle, while keeping the tool off the knuckle. Once the hub moves, continue around the flange and pull it out squarely.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: A hub puller, hub shocker, or forcing-screw tool applies controlled extraction force. Use the correct adapters for the vehicle and make sure the tool is centered and aligned for a straight pull. Increase force gradually, checking for movement and repositioning only as the tool instructions allow..

Another tip is to look at the service information for the procedures and recommended tools. Some OEMs might include an flat part of the knuckle that can be used by a puller or forcing screw to remove the hub unit.

After removal, clean corrosion from the bore and mounting face without removing base metal. Inspect for cracks, gouging, or deformation, then install the replacement hub according to the vehicle procedure and specified torque.

You can add a light coating of moly anti-seize to the bore of the knuckle to decrease the chances of future corrosion. Avoid getting any anti-seize on the bolt holes of the knuckle. Any lubricant can change the torque value of a fastener.
The most important step to removing a stuck hub unit is to review the service information and TSB. Often, the service procedure will be amended to include information on procedures and special tools.

If you’re unable to free the hub unit from the knuckle, don’t take it personally. One of the most important skills gained through experience is knowing when to stop trying to remove a hub unit with heat, brute force or chemicals. In some cases, recommending replacement of the knuckle along with the hub unit is more productive and makes for a better repair.

Aftermarket replacement knuckles are available, and some lines cover applications where hub units can be especially difficult to remove. Experience also helps you recognize which applications are most likely to cause frustration.
Wheel End Service: Do You Have These Tools?

Over the past decade, tool companies have introduced new wheel end service tool and have improved existing tools. These next generation tools can be used on their own or together to make your next hub unit job easier.

Hub Strikers: A hub striker is a solid metal bar that bolts to the hub flange and provides a striking point outside the wheel well. This helps reduce the risk of hitting the fender while using a sledgehammer. Hub strikers can work well on some Gen 2 and Gen 3 hub units that use orbital forming to retain the flange and set bearing preload. Depending on the application, they can make removal much faster.

Lug Nuts and Washers: Another tool you can use to hammer on the hub unit is an old brake rotor with the same lug pattern. Secure the rotor to the flange with lug nuts and washers. The rotor provides a solid surface to strike with your hammer.

Forcing Screws: A forcing screw uses a threaded rod or fastener to apply force between the hub flange and the knuckle, pushing the hub outward. Some applications allow a suitable bolt to be used as a forcing screw, but it must have adequate thread engagement and bear against a solid part of the knuckle. Purpose-built tool sets use a plate that attaches to the hub, often at the wheel studs, and a forcing screw to push the hub out. Use the correct setup for the vehicle and keep the force aligned with the hub.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Slide Hammer: A slide hammer can attach to the hub flange and apply repeated outward force as the hammer is moved along its shaft. It can be effective when the knuckle does not provide a suitable surface for a forcing screw. Use an appropriate hub adapter and keep the hammer’s path clear of the body and nearby components.

Air Hammer: An air hammer can help break the corrosion bond by vibrating or rotating the hub flange relative to the knuckle. Use a suitable attachment and work around the flange without striking or gouging the knuckle. Tool size alone does not determine effectiveness; consider the hammer’s stroke, operating rate, air supply, and how well you can control it. More force is not always better. BCA recommends using the air hammer to rotate the hub flange rather than wedging the tool between the hub and knuckle.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Hydraulic Press: On some vehicles, you may need to remove the knuckle to free the hub. Success depends on using the correct fixtures and adapters to support the knuckle securely and keep the press load aligned. Special press plates are available for some applications. Protect the knuckle, dust shield, and machined surfaces from damage, and follow the tool manufacturer’s instructions.

Heat: Heat can help loosen the joint through differential expansion and contraction; it does not reverse the corrosion reaction. Options include a propane or MAP-Pro torch and an induction heater. A torch can supply sufficient heat, but it is difficult to control and can damage CV-joint, tie-rod, and ball-joint boots, along with other nearby parts. An induction heater uses an electromagnetic field to heat metal, and many units include a flexible coil that can be positioned around the hub or knuckle. Use only a heating method and location appropriate for the application. BCA cautions against torch-heating the knuckle and recommends localized induction heating for wheel-end work.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Chemicals: Penetrants are formulated to flow into tight clearances and reduce friction at the hub-to-knuckle interface. Some use solvents or other additives, but most penetrating oils do not dissolve rust. Apply the product as directed and allow time for it to soak in. Tapping or gently working the hub can help the penetrant reach the joint. Rust removers are different: many react chemically with corrosion, but they may also attack the base metal, coatings, or nearby finishes. Check product compatibility before use.

articles.title: AWDA Names Richard and Lisa Beirne 2026 Outstanding Leader
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: The Aftermarket Warehouse Distributors Association (AWDA), a community of the Auto Care Association, celebrated the recipients of its 2026 AWDA Industry Awards during the AWDA General Session on Nov. 1 in Las Vegas, Nevada. The annual awards take place during the AWDA Annual Business Conference and recognize individuals who exemplify leadership, innovation, education and service to the automotive aftermarket.
AWDA presented its 2026 Outstanding Leadership Award in honor of Jack Creamer to Richard and Lisa Beirne of Auto Parts Headquarters.

Formerly known as the “Leader of the Year,” the award honors an aftermarket professional who has contributed to the industry in a unique and significant way. It is named for former AWDA President Jack Creamer. The award was presented by 2025 recipient Don Bickle, former AWDA Treasurer.

Richard’s aftermarket career spans nearly six decades, beginning in 1968 as a delivery driver. With Lisa’s steadfast partnership, he led United Auto Supply as president and CEO, guided its successful partnership with Automotive Parts Headquarters (APH), and built a reputation for valuing employees, customers and supplier partners. Today, he serves as a senior advisor for APH, while he and Lisa continue supporting APH and Auto Value expansion efforts throughout the Midwest.

Richard’s decades of AWDA service include roles as board member, treasurer, chairman, treasurer emeritus and lifetime board member. He also helped lead AWDA’s merger with the Automotive Aftermarket Industry Association. Richard and Lisa have participated in Auto Care Association Leadership Meetings, Capitol Hill advocacy and Right to Repair initiatives, while consistently supporting the Auto Care Political Action Committee.

The Beirnes’ investment in the next generation is equally significant. Richard serves on the University of the Aftermarket Foundation Board of Trustees and has supported its scholarship and contributions work. Richard and Lisa became Lifetime Trustees in 2019 and, in 2025, were the first individuals named Gold Lifetime Trustees, recognizing cumulative contributions exceeding $250,000.

articles.title: Webb and Hubble discover new details in one of our galaxy's spookiest objects
articles.author: Brandon Specktor

paras.en: In space, nobody can hear you scream — or meow, for that matter. This was as true for Félicette — the stray Parisian tuxedo cat who safely completed the world's first (and only) suborbital feline flight, in 1963 — as it is for the gargantuan Cat's Head Nebula, which is featured in stunning new images from the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes.

Rising from the cloudy Carina Nebula some 7,500 light-years from Earth, the Cat's Head Nebula is a column of star-sculpted gas and dust that vaguely resembles a feline sitting with its back to us, coyly turning its head to show off a single red eye. That eye is a young star that's embedded deep within the dust and possibly transforming it before our eyes.

Nebulas like these occur when the radiation from active young stars lights up and erodes the material around them. They are beautiful and easy to find; if this cosmic cat gets bored staring at us, it can just waltz over to the other side of the Carina Nebula and crawl into a similar globule of gas that looks exactly like a box with an open lid. (Cats will be cats, after all.)

In honor of Halloween, the European Space Agency (ESA) shared three competing views of the Cat's Head Nebula — one from the Hubble Space Telescope, which captures optical light, and two from the infrared instruments aboard the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The three views, shown below, reveal different features of the nebula in different wavelengths of light, getting progressively spookier as more color drains out of the scene.Take a look at all three images — and cast your vote for the spookiest in the poll at the end.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Observing the nebula in the same visible wavelength range that you could see through a strong backyard telescope, Hubble highlights the dark pillar of dust that has survived the ultraviolet assault of nearby stars. The wispy edges at the right of the column show where starlight is evaporating the gas around it, slowly whittling it away to nothing.

The glow of blue, yellow, orange and red light around the dust pillar mark where starlight is interacting with different gas molecules, including oxygen, hydrogen and sulfur, according to ESA. The process is similar to how different molecules in Earth's atmosphere produce different-colored auroras when excited by solar radiation — just on a much grander scale.

Switching to light human eyes cannot see, JWST's Near-Infrared Camera cuts through the wispier outer layers of dust to show the densest material at the column's center. Countless additional stars and galaxies appear in the field of view as their infrared glow penetrates the surrounding material.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Here we see a more complex, turbulent column, showing how stellar radiation is carving up the inside of the cat's head as well as its edges. JWST's view also illuminates a disembodied, hand-like structure to the left of the cat, reaching out as if to pet its cosmic companion.

The final view, taken with JWST's Mid-Infrared Instrument, cuts to the ghostly core of the nebula, showing little more than smoky, bluish light. According to ESA, these are the emissions of molecules called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons — typically colorless molecules of carbon and hydrogen related to combustion.

While most starlight disappears in this view, a strange new bright spot emerges to the right of the cat's head. This orange speck is a true mystery, according to ESA, and its relationship to the rest of the nebula is unknown.

Brandon is the space / physics editor at Live Science. With more than 20 years of editorial experience, his writing has appeared in The Washington Post, Reader's Digest, CBS.com, the Richard Dawkins Foundation website and other outlets. He holds a bachelor's degree in creative writing from the University of Arizona, with minors in journalism and media arts. His interests include black holes, asteroids and comets, and the search for extraterrestrial life.

articles.title: 5,300-year-old kidney stone the size of a grape found in Bronze Age man's burial near Black Sea
articles.author: Kristina Killgrove

paras.en: A Bronze Age man buried in a monumental tomb near the Black Sea may have died from complications of a urinary tract infection (UTI) more than five millennia ago, according to a new study. Archaeologists identified a grape-size object consistent with a kidney or bladder stone in the man's burial.
"He lived with a chronic urogenital infection," study lead author Natalia Berezina, an anthropologist at Lomonosov Moscow State University in Russia, told Live Science in an email.
"It was not a brief episode," she said. "His last years were probably marked by considerable and more or less constant pain."

Berezina and colleagues investigated a small, stone-like object found in an Early Bronze Age burial in the Stavropol Upland region of southwestern Russia. They published their findings Sept. 30 in the journal Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences.

The burial was part of a kurgan cemetery, an ancient steppe funeral tradition that involved constructing a large mound of dirt over a grave. Archaeologists discovered a catacomb when they excavated the mound, and inside was the skeleton of a man who was in his 40s when he died around 5,300 years ago. The researchers found a flint arrowhead near the man's pelvis.

But during a laboratory analysis after the skeleton was excavated, researchers noticed an odd stone-like object in the collection of hand bones. The brownish object was round with several protrusions and measured about 0.8 inches (2.1 centimeters) in diameter, or roughly the size of a grape. A small crack in the object showed a crystal-like structure inside.

To learn more, the researchers used several analytical methods to determine what the tiny object was made of. First, X-ray fluorescence analysis revealed that the main components of the object were calcium and phosphorus. Then, they used X-ray powder diffraction analysis to identify the crystal structures.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In addition to common minerals, the researchers discovered the presence of whitlockite, a rare calcium salt that is known to occur in kidney, bladder and prostate stones. These "stones," collectively called calculi, are hard masses of minerals, such as calcium-containing salts. They differ in terms of the organ they form within, the exact mechanism of how they form, and their chemical makeup, although kidney and bladder stones tend to contain very similar compounds.
Whitlockite is strongly associated with bacterial infections in the human body, which suggests that the Bronze Age man had a chronic infection that resulted in the stone, the scientists concluded.

"On the balance of the available evidence, we regard a renal [kidney] stone secondary to chronic upper urinary tract infection as the most probable origin," the researchers wrote. That is, the man dealt with chronic or recurrent UTIs, which led to the formation of the stone and likely caused him considerable discomfort. UTIs can contribute to the formation of kidney stones by altering the acidity of urine and making minerals more likely to accumulate.
The researchers aren't sure why the man had urinary tract issues or whether it contributed to his death.

Notably, kidney stones can sometimes travel to the bladder, so it's unclear exactly where the stone was in the man's body when he died. If the stone had obstructed the man's ureter — one of the two long tubes that connect the kidneys to the bladder — it may have caused kidney swelling, a secondary infection or sepsis. These conditions were frequently fatal prior to the invention of antibiotics.
Other possibilities for what caused the stone include a bacterial infection of the man's prostate gland or even a sexually transmitted infection.

The man was likely on the move frequently within this Early Bronze Age steppe society, and other injuries to his skeleton suggested he had a physically demanding life, the researchers wrote. His bones showed that he was well muscled but was also dealing with degenerative joint disease in his spine, shoulders, hips, hands and feet. He had a series of healed fractures in his right shoulder, ribs and forearm.

"These were people who worked with cattle and heavy wagons on the open steppe," Berezina said, "and the injuries that follow from that are the injuries we find." In a previous study at a nearby cemetery, Berezina and colleagues found the skeleton of a man who was injured when a wagon ran over him, several years before his death. "Against that background, four healed fractures in our man look unremarkable," she said.

But the urinary tract stone would have made the man's life difficult, the researchers noted. "This individual suffered from a painful and debilitating chronic urogenital infection, a condition that would have significantly impacted his quality of life," they wrote.

Berezina, N. Ya., Statkus, M. A., Kalmykov, A. A., Abdrashitova, I. V., Kolesnik, I. V., Platonov, V. B., Shashurin, D. A., Garmay, A. V., Korobkova, V. V., Ryleeva, V. S., & Gresky, J. (2026). Urolithiasis in the Early Bronze Age of the North Caucasus: A paleopathological case study and insights into ancient lifeways. Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences, 18(10), 209. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12520-026-02574-7

articles.title: Would you risk your health to visit Mars?
articles.author: Kenna Hughes-Castleberry

paras.en: A crewed mission to Mars could be one of humanity's greatest achievements, but getting there may come with serious health risks. Beyond the challenges of surviving in space for months at a time, astronauts would face prolonged exposure to cosmic radiation — high-energy particles in space that can penetrate the human body and potentially damage vital organs.
- Chinese lander reveals giant 'cavity' of radiation between Earth and the moon — and it could change how lunar exploration is done
- 'Everything we know about space travel is going to change within a decade': The fusion breakthrough that could unlock a path to the stars
- Scientists finally know why astronauts struggle to poop in space — and reveal a hidden risk of long-haul spaceflight

A new study suggested that cosmic radiation could pose a particular threat to heart health. Researchers found evidence that rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what human astronauts might encounter during a mission to Mars and back developed more scar tissue around the small vessels in their hearts compared with rats that weren't exposed to space radiation.
Although the findings haven't been confirmed in humans yet, they add to the growing concerns about the long-term health effects of sending astronauts on long-duration space missions.

NASA and other space agencies are working on ways to eventually send humans to Mars and beyond. Given these latest findings, would you travel to Mars? Vote in the poll below, and let us know your thoughts in the comments.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry is the Content Manager at Live Science. Formerly, she was the Content Manager at Space.com and before that the Science Communicator at JILA, a physics research institute. Kenna is also a book author, with her upcoming book 'Octopus X' scheduled for release in spring of 2027. Her beats include physics, health, environmental science, technology, AI, animal intelligence, corvids, and cephalopods.

articles.title: After Observing the Sky for 22 Years, a Beloved NASA Space Telescope Is Expected to Meet a Fiery Death This Week

paras.en: NASA’s groundbreaking Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, which stared at the cosmos for more than two decades, is expected to crash down to Earth this week. The U.S. Space Force estimates the beloved space telescope will re-enter the planet’s atmosphere around November 4, where most of it should burn up.

“We’ve known this day would come since before Swift was launched. At least in low-Earth orbit, what goes up must come down. And that end is catastrophic,” says John Nousek, an astronomer at Pennsylvania State University who led the control team, to Marcia Dunn at the Associated Press

Swift’s fiery death comes after an attempted Hail Mary earlier this year. The aging telescope recently had been falling from its orbit faster than predicted because of unusually strong solar activity in late 2024. That increased atmospheric drag on the observatory, pulling it down.

In response, NASA contracted Arizona-based company Katalyst Space Technologies to build a spacecraft that would use robotic arms to lift Swift back into higher orbit. It launched on July 3, but the first-of-its-kind mission failed when the rescue craft had issues with its orientation control system, among other problems.

Scientists are now mourning the loss of Swift. It launched in November 2004 for what was supposed to be a two-year mission to study gamma-ray bursts. They’re the most powerful explosions in the universe and often associated with the collapse of massive stars or the birth of black holes.

Instead, the observatory spent 22 years observing more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts, 1,400 supernova explosions, stars being shredded by black holes, asteroids, comets and countless other cosmic phenomena and objects. Its data was quickly accessible to researchers, and by the end of its career, it had contributed to roughly 7,000 scientific papers. Some of the telescope’s biggest discoveries happened in 2017, when it detected signs of a merger between two dense stellar leftovers, called neutron stars, and helped trace a ghostly, high-energy neutrino particle to its origin.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Swift was considered a first-responder telescope. It provided alerts about interesting phenomena, which other instruments, like the Hubble Space Telescope and James Webb Space Telescope, followed up on for more thorough investigations, per the AP. NASA shut Swift down in late October because it was too unsteady.

Without Swift, “we’re going to miss out,” says Judith Racusin, an astrophysicist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center, to Meghan Bartels at Science News. “Not just on the common events we have thousands of, but the really rare, unusual ones, which are often the ones we learn the most from.”

While most of the 3,200-pound observatory will go up in flames during its re-entry into Earth’s atmosphere, some of its internal workings could survive the fall, says Darren McKnight, a senior technical fellow at the satellite-tracking company LeoLabs, to Leonard David at Space.com. Those leftovers will likely fall into the ocean, but parts of Africa, Australia, India, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America are within their re-entry zone, reports the AP.

Experts can also gain new insights about re-entering spacecraft by observing Swift’s descent, which could help the design of safer satellites in the future. “We also need to understand what the melted stuff does to the chemistry of the upper atmosphere, because there’s an emerging concern that we may be screwing the climate and the ozone layer with all of these re-entries,” says Jonathan McDowell, an astrophysicist who recently retired from the Center for Astrophysics, Harvard & Smithsonian, to Ellyn Lapointe at Gizmodo.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: While Swift will soon meet its fiery end, that doesn’t mean it will stop contributing to research.

“There’s a massive amount of Swift science data in the archive for people to mine and make new scientific discoveries,” says Caryl Gronwall, an astronomer at Penn State and a member of the Swift science team, to Nature’s Jenna Ahart. “We’re super proud of the legacy that Swift leaves behind.”

articles.title: Archaeologists in Scotland Discovered the Skeleton of a Roman-Era Man Who Was Decapitated Nearly 2,000 Years Ago. Now, You Can See What He Might Have Looked Like During His Lifetime

paras.en: In 2010, archaeologists conducting excavations ahead of construction in Musselburgh, Scotland, stumbled upon the remains of four Roman-era men. Their heads had been separated from their bodies, apparently after death.

Experts don’t know exactly why these individuals were decapitated postmortem, but they have a few theories: Perhaps the ritual was a holdover from an early Celtic cult that attributed power to severed heads. Alternatively, the beheadings might have served as a punishment or a precaution to ensure the dead didn’t come back to life.

The rationale for the decapitations might be unclear, but that hasn’t stopped archaeologists from piecing together what happened to these ancient Britons during their lifetimes. Thanks to a cutting-edge collaboration led by National Museums Scotland (NMS), the public can now envision what one of the men looked like when he died in his early 50s, between 140 and 165 C.E. A digital reconstruction of his face will soon go on view alongside his skull in “Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire,” a forthcoming exhibition at NMS’ flagship Edinburgh location.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: - Soldiers led by the Roman general Agricola invaded what is now Scotland in 79 C.E., winning a major victory at the Battle of Mons Graupius in 83 or 84.

- The Romans soon retreated, only returning to the region during the reign of Antoninus Pius. Around 142, his forces built the Antonine Wall, which replaced Hadrian’s Wall as the northernmost border of the Roman Empire.
- Inveresk was active during this period but was abandoned around 160 along with the Antonine Wall.

The man “lived a hard and physically active life,” according to a statement, “and his appearance would have betrayed his age through lines around his brown eyes and the graying of his dark hair.” Although he lived near the Roman fort of Inveresk, he probably wasn’t a soldier, as he had a condition that would have prevented him from easily wielding a sword in his right hand. John H. Reid, an archaeologist at the Trimontium Trust who wasn’t involved in the research, tells Live Science’s Tom Metcalfe that the individual might have worked a “desk job,” perhaps serving as a clerk or in another noncombat role. Alternatively, he may have simply used his left hand to hold a weapon.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “I have worked with the finds from Roman Inveresk for years, but this facial reconstruction finally gives me a sense of what one of its inhabitants looked like,” Fraser Hunter, a curator at NMS, says in the statement. “Archaeology tells us about people who had hopes and fears just like us, and it is a privilege to present a vision of this resident of Inveresk using contemporary scientific techniques. We cannot know how exactly he looked, but we think his family and friends would have spotted the likeness.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: To approximate the man’s appearance, forensic artist Chris Rynn drew on an osteoarchaeological assessment conducted by NMS, isotopic analyses led by experts at Durham University, and ancient DNA extracted by the University of York and Harvard Medical School. As Rynn writes in an Instagram post, “Hair, eyes and skin color [are] all determined by DNA, but a range of possible hairstyles are depicted, which all fit the DNA analysis.” These looks include a thinning widow’s peak and a bushy beard flecked with streaks of gray, as well as a fuller head of curly dark hair.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The individual’s skeleton shows that he suffered several serious injuries, including a broken nose and a rib fracture, both of which had healed by the time of his death. He had a bone growth around the elbow joint of his right arm, likely the result of septic arthritis. Wear patterns on his teeth indicate that he made up for this mobility loss by picking up objects with his mouth.

The new facial reconstruction builds on previous research about the mysterious Briton. A 2020 study published in the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports looked at his strontium isotopes, which reflect where someone grew up. The authors found that he probably spent his childhood in southern Britain, hundreds of miles away from the region where he died.

Of the four decapitated individuals unearthed in Musselburgh, two seemingly came from England. The third grew up in Scotland, while the last traced their origins to somewhere in the Mediterranean. “These results suggest that decapitation burials were afforded to migrants to the Lothian area but [are] not indicative of a common origin, implying that something more complex than a shared geographic childhood origin united these individuals,” the researchers wrote.

According to a separate 2020 paper published in Scottish Archaeological Internet Reports, the subject of the facial reconstruction was buried on his back, with his feet and shoulders raised above his torso. His head was placed on the right side of his body, facing inward. Cuts on the bones indicate that the head was severed toward the base of the neck. Researchers didn’t recover any funerary goods from the man’s grave, but his remains were among the most well-preserved skeletons found at the site.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: To date, archaeologists have uncovered more than 500 Roman-era decapitation burials across the United Kingdom. Some of these individuals were beheaded postmortem, while others were killed by having their heads chopped off. Experts have proposed numerous explanations for this phenomenon, including “execution, trophy-taking, desecration, human sacrifice, war, cult practice, releasing the soul, laying the unquiet dead and banishing witches,” per a 2021 study published in Britannia. But the issue is contentious, and scholars have yet to reach a firm consensus.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Whatever the reasoning for the beheadings, the Musselburgh burials are unique. They represent the “earliest known examples of Roman inhumation and decapitation in Britain, and their apparent ethnic diversity coupled with a shared burial rite reflects the cosmopolitan nature of the Roman army,” according to the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports.

In the NMS statement, Jess Thompson, the museum group’s curator of osteoarchaeology, notes that the skeletons “are exceptional and incredibly rare survivals from Roman Scotland.” She adds: “Taking an interdisciplinary approach to the analysis of human remains allows us to understand the physical attributes of these individuals as well as their life stories. We can investigate where these men had traveled from to reach the frontier, what they were doing there and what became of them.”
“Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire” will be on view at the National Museum of Scotland in Edinburgh from November 14, 2026, to April 18, 2027.

articles.title: See the World's Tallest Day of the Dead Skeleton, Made From Steel, Fiberglass, Papier-Mâché and 70,000 Marigolds

paras.en: A massive female skeleton dressed in a long purple gown took center stage during Mexico City’s recent Día de los Muertos (Day of the Dead) celebrations—and set a new world record in the process.

The towering figure known as La Catrina stood in the city’s main square, the Zócalo, as friends and families gathered to honor and remember their deceased loved ones during the annual holiday on November 1 and 2.

Standing a little more than 109 feet tall—roughly the height of an 11-story building—the colorful installation broke the previous record of 92 feet set in Puerto Vallarta, Mexico, in 2023, according to Guiness World Records.

More than 140 people with the Xibalbá art workshop, led by director Carlos Camilo Báez, helped bring the project to life, using steel, fiberglass and papier-mâché to create La Catrina and her 88-foot-long dress. The statue is surrounded by a large memorial altar, or ofrenda, featuring an estimated 70,000 marigold plants grown in the city’s Xochimilco borough, Andrew Paul reports for Popular Science.

The temporary installation was originally scheduled to stand through November 2. However, Mexico City’s mayor, Clara Brugada, revealed on social media that the statue will remain on view through November 11.

Observed primarily in Mexico and other parts of Latin America, Día de los Muertos is a festive, joyous occasion that celebrates the enduring connection between the living and the dead. Families create elaborate altars decorated with photographs, candles, marigolds, favorite foods and other meaningful items that are meant to help guide the spirits of their departed loved ones home. They also clean their loved ones’ graves and decorate their headstones, gathering in cemeteries to remember and commemorate the people they have lost.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The holiday, which was inscribed to UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity list in 2008, blends Indigenous traditions with Catholic influences introduced by the Spanish conquest. Día de los Muertos draws on the beliefs of several ancient Mesoamerican civilizations, including the Aztecs, Toltecs, Olmecs and Maya. These cultures viewed life and death as interconnected parts of a continuous cycle, rather than separate beginnings and endings. They believed the dead could periodically return to visit the living and reconnect with the earthly world.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: La Catrina has become synonymous with the holiday. The figure was developed by José Guadalupe Posada, a Mexican cartoonist and graphic artist who lived from 1852 to 1913. La Catrina was just one of the many calaveras, or satirical skulls and skeletons, that Posada created during his lifetime. Originally known as Calavera Garbancera, La Catrina first appeared in 1912 on single-sheet broadsides that were sold to the poor and working classes throughout Mexico City for a penny.

The figure was Posada’s satirical depiction of the city’s garbanceras, indigenous women who sold garbanzo beans at street markets, Mathew Sandoval, a cultural historian at Arizona State University, wrote for the Conversation in 2023. The artist was poking fun at the way they adopted European customs—powdering their faces and wearing French clothes—in a bid to pass as upper-class.
La Catrina didn’t become an icon right away. She didn’t catch on until decades later, when other artists, including painter Diego Rivera, rediscovered Posada’s work.

Posada probably “never expected his female calavera to become so famous,” wrote Sandoval. “He merely wanted to use traditional Day of the Dead humor to make fun of the flamboyantly dressed garbanceras he saw hanging around Mexico City’s central plaza.”

articles.title: Democrats projected to win control of U.S. House

paras.en: Nov. 3 (UPI) -- Democrats were projected Tuesday to win control of the U.S. House of Representatives in a race largely seen as a referendum of President Donald Trump's second term.
Though counting continued Tuesday evening -- and was expected to carry over into Wednesday -- both NBC News and Decision Desk HQ projected that Democrats would flip the House.
"Victory for America!" Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the expected new speaker of the House said on social media in celebration.
The Democratic Cause of the U.S. House of Representatives was also quick with comment.

All 435 seats in the lower chamber were up for election Tuesday, with high expectations of a Blue Wave to wash the Democrats back to its helm, after the GOP held a narrow majority of the House during the last Congress. Almost evenly split, the House sat 218 Republicans, 214 Democrats, one independent -- Rep. Kevin Kiley, I-Calif., who caucuses with Republicans -- and two vacancies.
Both NBC News and Decision Desk HQ are project the Democrats to win 248 seats. They estimate that the Republicans will win 187.

The two vacancies are in Florida's 20th District, left by Democrat Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick, and Texas' 23rd District, vacated by Republican Tony Gonzales. Both seats have been vacant since April when they resigned under scrutiny.

Several states have redrawn their congressional districts over the past year because President Donald Trump asked them to in the hopes of making the districts more favorable for Republican candidates. Texas redistricted, adding five more districts likely to pick up Republicans, and California redistricted making five more districts favorable to Democrats. Virginia tried to follow California to add new Democratic strongholds, but the state supreme court rejected the plan.

Missouri redrew its districts, but the U.S. Supreme Court has rejected its new map multiple times. Louisiana and Tennessee also passed new maps, each removing a majority-Black district. Voters and politicians in some states, including Indiana and Georgia, rejected measures to redistrict.
But redistricting doesn't guarantee wins. Voters still get to decide, as they will Tuesday.

There are three races in Virginia that are being closely watched Tuesday. In Virginia's 1st District, incumbent Rep. Rob Wittman, R, is projected to lose his to challenger Shannon Taylor in a flip for the Democrats. In the 2nd, Rep. Jennifer Kiggans, R, is projected to lose to challenger Elaine Luria, D. And in the 5th, Rep. John McGuire, R, faces Tom Perriello, D. Virginia's polls close at 7 p.m. EST.

In Iowa, the three races to watch are in the 1st, 2nd and 3rd Districts. All four of Iowa's House seats are held by Republicans, but they face tough races, as Iowa is mostly farm country. The price of diesel fuel has made the harvest more expensive this year, leaving Republicans to defend Trump's war in Iran. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, R, is facing Democrat Christina Bohannan; Rep. Joe Mitchell, R, faces Democrat Lindsay James; and Rep. Zach Nunn, R, is projected to lose to challenger Sarah Trone Garriott in a flip for the Democrats. Iowa's polls close at 9 p.m. EST.

articles.title: Georgia elects nation's first Black female governor

paras.en: Nov. 3 (UPI) -- Democrats were poised Tuesday to flip at least four Republican-held governorships as voters in 36 states cast ballots for their states' top executive offices.

Republicans entered Election Day controlling 26 governorships nationwide, compared with 24 held by Democrats. Each party was defending 18 seats. Based on Tuesday's preliminary results, Democrats are poised to control a majority of the governorships, though several races remain pending.
According to preliminary results in Georgia, with all localities reporting, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms received 54.26% of the vote to Republican businessman Rick Jackson's 45.74%.
With the win, Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, will become Georgia's first woman governor and the first Black woman governor anywhere in the United States.
"Thank you, Georgia. I am honored to be your 84th governor," Bottoms said in her victory speech.
"And no matter who you voted for tonight, I will be a governor for all of Georgia."
Jackson, a self-proclaimed conservative outsider, conceded defeat Tuesday night.
"Every person, every story I heard on this journey, touched my heart and will always be carried with me," he said on social media.
Bottoms and Jackson were competing for a governorship held by Republican Brian Kemp, who was term-limited from running again.

In conservative Texas, where Republican Gov. Greg Abbott was seeking a fourth term, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, a Texas state House representative and daughter of former Texas Democratic Party Chair Gilberto Hinojosa, was poised to be the state's first Democratic governor since 1995.
According to preliminary results, Hinojosa received 52% of the vote to Abbott's 46.65%, with 31% of polling locations reporting.
In conceding defeat, Abbott acknowledged that while there were still votes to be counted that "mathematically we're not going to win this election."

"I let Gina know that I will assist her and her team in a period of transition," he told supporters. "But also, I want everybody to know, the thing I'm most proud about is that you all helped me to be your governor for 12 years. Thank you very much."

In Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton, a former state health director, was poised to become the state's first woman elected governor. Nancy Hollister briefly served as governor for 11 days in 1999 after succeeding George Voinovich.
Acton ran against Republican Vivek Ramaswamy in a race to replace term-limited Republican Gov. Mike DeWine.
Preliminary results showed that with nearly 90% of Election Day precincts reporting, Acton received nearly 51% of the vote compared to Ramaswamy's 45.67%.
Acton, in claiming victory, said in a statement that Ohio had chosen "unity and decency over division and hate."
"Ohio is ready for a governor who will fight to lower costs, take on corruption and build a state where everyone gets a fair shot," she said.
"This isn't about party; it's about building a better future for our state."
In conceding defeat, Ramaswamy called Tuesday "a tough and challenging night for republicans across the country and for us here in Ohio."
He told supporters that he had called Acton and left her a message to wish her well in leading the state.

"It was a tough race," he said. "It was bitter at times in both directions, but the time tomorrow is to hopefully have her leadership bring this state together and I have hope and confidence that she will do what is required to bring Ohio together, to bring our voters and our citizens together to lead Ohio to the best place possible."
In Iowa, Democrat Rob Sand, the state's auditor, claimed victory Tuesday night over Republican Zach Lahn, as the two competed to replace Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds, who did not seek re-election.

He thanked Republicans and independents who voted for him for their courage, saying "we do live in a broken two two-choice political system where it requires real listening to learn that the candidate that is in the other party doesn't see you as the enemy."
"We have to have bigger hearts and minds than just our party and everyone who did that across party lines with a republican endorsement showed that, and we thank you for it."
Lahn, a Republican businessman, conceded defeat, while vowing to continue to fight for Iowa.

"America is at a crossroads right now," he told supporters. "It's undeniable. I think now more than ever the talk that we put forward about culture matters more than maybe anything. If we're not here to defend the culture, especially with what we saw tonight, then I'll tell you our kids and grandkids will not inherit the promise that we want them to inherit."
According to preliminary results, with 91 of 99 counties reporting, Sand had received 55.6% of the vote to Lahn's 44.2%.
Other key gubernatorial races include Alaska, Arizona, Kansas, Michigan, Nevada, and Wisconsin.
The results will help determine the balance of power in state governments during the final two years of President Donald Trump's term and ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
In New Mexico, Democrat Deb Haaland, former U.S. interior secretary, is running against Republican Gregg Hull.
Haaland, who previously served in Congress, could become the first Native American woman to govern a U.S. state.
Several other races could shift control of governor's offices between the parties.
Nevada Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo is seeking re-election against Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford in a race considered competitive.
In Wisconsin, Democrat David Crowley faces Republican Tom Tiffany for the seat being vacated by Democratic Gov. Tony Evers.
Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek, a Democrat, faces Republican Christine Drazan in a rematch of their 2022 election.

Alaskan voters are also choosing a successor to Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy in a race featuring Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and Republican candidates Dave Bronson, Treg Taylor and Bernadette Wilson.

Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, which allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference. The counting process could extend beyond Election Day if no candidate receives a majority of first-choice votes.
Polls begin closing at 6 p.m. EST in Indiana and Kentucky, followed by Georgia at 7 p.m. and several other states throughout the evening.

articles.title: North Korea fires missiles as Kim Yo Jong rejects U.S. dialogue

paras.en: SEOUL, Nov. 4 (UPI) -- North Korea launched several missiles toward the sea separating Korea and Japan on Wednesday morning, South Korea's military said, as Pyongyang continued a series of weapons tests and rejected dialogue with Washington under current U.S. policy.

The launches were detected from the Sondok area on the North's east coast, the Joint Chiefs of Staff said in a text message to reporters. South Korean and U.S. authorities were conducting a detailed analysis to determine the missiles' specifications.
The allies monitored preparations and detected and tracked the missiles immediately after launch, the JCS said.

"Maintaining a robust combined defense posture, the South Korean military is keeping a close watch on various activities by North Korea and remains fully prepared and capable of responding overwhelmingly to any provocation," it added.
The Hawaii-based U.S. Pacific Command said it was aware of the launches and was consulting closely with allies and partners.
"Based on current assessments, this event does not pose an immediate threat to U.S. personnel or territory, or to our allies," the command said in a statement.
The launches came as Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, dismissed prospects for talks with Washington unless it abandoned what she called its hostile policy.

In a statement carried Wednesday by the state-run Korean Central News Agency, Kim described U.S. findings linking Pyongyang to a record $6.3 billion theft from cryptocurrency exchange Binance as an "extension of Washington's invariable hostile policy toward the DPRK."
The Democratic People's Republic of Korea is North Korea's official name.
"It is our clear stand that we have no need to sit face to face with such unreliable and hostile persons who refuse to abandon their policy of confrontation while talking about dialogue," Kim said.
"The choice for peace includes dialogue of course, but this is not surely equated with national interests for us," she added.
Kim also criticized U.S.-South Korean military exercises, sanctions and Washington's calls for North Korea's denuclearization.

Her remarks followed a statement Tuesday calling the cryptocurrency theft accusation a "grave political provocation." International experts say Pyongyang uses cryptocurrency theft and fraudulent overseas information technology work to generate revenue for its nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programs.
U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly expressed interest in meeting Kim Jong Un and said in August that he expected to meet the North Korean leader this year.

North Korea has conducted a string of weapons tests in recent days, firing around a dozen short-range ballistic missiles from the Wonsan area last Thursday and testing a cluster warhead for tactical ballistic missiles Saturday.
On Tuesday, the North said it had tested what it called a "dispersal warhead" for a strategic cruise missile the previous day.

articles.title: Barbie’s Diwali Doll Is Back in Stock for the Festival of Lights: Here’s Where to Find It Online
articles.author: Latifah Muhammad

paras.en: All products and services featured are independently chosen by editors. However, Billboard may receive a commission on orders placed through its retail links, and the retailer may receive certain auditable data for accounting purposes.

Barbie released its first-ever Diwali doll in 2024 in collaboration with Indian fashion designer Anita Dongre, and the limited-edition collectible quickly sold out in stores and online. But, we’ve spotted the official Diwali Barbie back in stock for this year’s Diwali dates.
The Barbie Diwali doll commemorates the annual celebration popular in Indian culture and known worldwide as the “Festival of Lights” (the word Diwali means “row of lights” in Hindi).

Barbie’s Diwali doll is dressed in a festive, Moonlight Bloom set with a choli top, floral Koti vest and lehenga skirt adorned with dahlias, jasmine and Indian lotus symbolizing strength and beauty, according to a press release sent to Billboard. The doll accessorizes with golden bangles and shimmering earrings.

While the Barbie Diwali doll originally retailed for around $40, it has since become a collector’s item and Amazon and Walmart have raised the price accordingly. Still, it’s rare to find this collectible online — and Mattel hasn’t produced another Diwali doll since — so we recommend adding it to cart while it’s still in stock.

“In celebration of Diwali, Barbie and I are both encouraging fans around the world to celebrate the beautiful heritage of Indian fashion and culture,” Dongre said in a statement when the doll was first released. “My brand has always been driven by a mission to empower through fashion, and as the ultimate symbol of women empowerment, partnering with Barbie to create the Barbie Diwali doll couldn’t be a more perfect alignment of our values.”
Mattel says this Barbie “celebrates diversity and offers endless possibilities for storytelling and fashion exploration,” while being “designed to reflect the world kids see today.”

Diwali is one of the biggest Hindu celebrations, held in India and other countries around the globe including the U.S. This year’s Diwali celebration runs from Nov. 6 to 10, 2026, with the official Diwali day on Nov. 8.

paras.en: KATSEYE’s Michigan debut will have to wait, after the pop group postponed their show set for Tuesday night (Nov. 3) at Little Caesars Arena due to illness within its ranks.
“Unfortunately, Megan is unwell and unable to perform tonight, and we want to make sure she has time she needs to rest and recover,” explains a message, posted just hours before showtime.

“We know so many of you have travelled, made plans and been looking forward to tonight. We are incredibly disappointed that we won’t get to see you, and we’re truly sorry for the inconvenience,” reads the post on KATSEYE’S Instagram Stories.

In another, the venue urged EYEKONS to hang tight. “We’re sorry to share that the KATSEYE show scheduled for tonight at Little Caesars Arena has been postponed,” reads a statement on the venue’s socials.
A new date will be announced, for which Tuesday night’s tickets will be valid. An email with further information will be distributed shortly.

“We sincerely apologize for the disappointment and inconvenience, especially to those who traveled to be with us tonight,” the venue statement adds. “Thank you for your patience, understanding, and continued support.”

According to sources at the show, the group did a VIP soundcheck with Megan missing and reportedly resting-up for the show. Doors had opened and fans were seated when a message confirming the postponement was splashed on the big screens, roughly 40 minutes before the scheduled start.
The group is presenting its WILDWORLD TOUR, which has sold outruns across Europe, the United Kingdom and, currently, North America.

Assuming Megan Skiendiel makes a prompt recovery, the group is next booked for the United Center in Chicago, IL on Thursday (Nov. 5). KATSEYE’s 2026 North America shows are slated to conclude Nov. 28 with the second of two nights at Palacio de los Deportes in Mexico City, MX.
A two-month break will follow, after which the group will embark on a tour of Asia, Australia and New Zealand, kicking off Jan. 27, 2027 at Yokohama Arena, Japan.

Promoted by Live Nation, the sprawling arena trek is in support of WILD (HYBE x Geffen Records), which blasted to No. 1 on the Billboard 200 in August for the group’s first leader. WILD was the followup to 2025’s Beautiful Chaos, which peaked at No. 4 on the all-genres albums survey.

articles.title: CISAC Reports Record Global Creator Royalties, Warns of ‘Largest Test’ From AI
articles.author: Lars Brandle

paras.en: Global music publishing collections grew to nearly 14.6 billion euros ($15.89 billion) in 2025, up 11.9% from the prior year’s total of 12.6 billion euros ($13.62 billion), according to data published in CISAC’s latest Global Collections Report.
CISAC director general Gadi Oron noted that the growth demonstrates “both the resilience of collective management and the enduring demand for creative works around the world.”

However, more than half of the increase, or 6.6 percentage points was due to the first time inclusion of revenue from the Mechanical Licensing Collective (MLC), the U.S. collection agency, while only only about 5.3 percentage points came from organic growth. On the other hand, the 5.3% organic growth from publishing outpaced the 4.8% increase for 2025, as counted by IFPI, that the record label side of the music business experienced.
While the industry is still growing, a counterbalance worry is how the double-edged sword of artificial intelligence will impact the economic model.

“Our confederation now faces its largest test with artificial intelligence, new business models and changing patterns of consumption,” Oron writes in the forward to the CISAC annual report. “This technological change also means that the future can bring real opportunities for creators…The issue is no longer whether AI will transform our industries, but whether the systems that protect creators’ rights are evolving quickly enough to keep pace.”

Fortunately, CISAC and its member societies are at the center of the debate around new laws, and is “contributing to numerous consultations, policy debates and legislative processes around the world, so as to ensure that creators’ rights remain at the heart of AI policy making,” Oron wrote.

Adds CISAC president and ABBA co-founder Björn Ulvaeus, “Human creativity is not something to be replaced or bypassed. It is something to be valued, protected and celebrated. And I hope that if we get it right, artificial intelligence will not diminish human creativity but will help inspire its next chapter.”

Getting back to the numbers, digital is now the largest generator of publishing royalties comprising 45.6% of music publishing royalties. In 2025, digital royalties totaled 6.41 billion euros ($7.25 billion) or a 28% increase over the 5.01 billion euros ($5.42 billion) collected in 2024. But it is here where the additional of the MLC is having its biggest impact.

Otherwise, background music and concerts was second largest at 25.8% of music publishing revenue with a total of 3.624 billion euros ($4.1 billion), or a 7.2% increase over the prior year when that category total 3.38 billion euros ($3.66 billion).

All other categories of publishing royalties produced declines in 2025 when compared to 2024. For instance, television and radio brought in another 23.6% of total publishing revenue in 2025 with 3.315 billion euros ($3.75 billion), but that was down 3.1% from the prior year total of 3.42 billion euros ($3.67 billion.) Similarly, CDs and video produced 326 million euros ($358.6 million), or a 8.9% drop on the 358 million euros ($387.3 million) garnered in 2024; while private copying assessments brought in 252 million euros ($285 million), or a 6.7% decrease from the prior year’s total of 270 million euros ($292.1 million); sync also declined slightly to 58 million euros ($65.6 million) from 62 million euros (467 million); and all other licensing sources generated 70 million euros ($79.15 million) or a 24.1% decline from 92.25 million euros ($99.8 million).

paras.en: Looking at revenue by the continents, Western Europe brought in the most revenue, accounting for 45.2% of revenue with 6.353 billion euros ($7.2 billion emanating from these territories); with North America coming in second, comprising 31.6% of total revenue with 4.442 billion euros ($5.02 million). Asia-Pacific with 1.87 billion euros ($2.12 billion) was third largest at 13.3% of royalties; followed by Latin America at 5.6%, or 785 million euros ($887.6 million); Central and Eastern Europe with 529 million euros ($598 million), or 3.8%; and Africa with 77 million euros ($87.1 million), which was one half a percent.
