paras.en: Within the continents, looking at the five largest countries for music publishing royalties, the United States accounted for 4.073 billion ($4.61 billion); France 1.59 billion euros ($1.8 billion); the U.K with 1.283 billion euros ($1.45 billion); Germany at 1.05 billion euros ($1.185 billion) and Japan at 907 million euros ($1.025 billion).

In addition to music, the collection management organizations also collect royalties on literature, drama, visual arts and audiovisual and when those revenues are added in CISAC counted total revenue at 15.5 billion euros ($17.53 billion), or a 11.3% increase over the prior year’s 13.92 billion euros ($15.06 billion).

CISAC represents 225 collective management organizations located in 110 countries and territories. Looking ahead, Oron noted “As CISAC approaches its second century, our purpose remains to strengthen the international framework that recognizes creators’ rights, supports effective collective management and enables creativity to continue flourishing in an increasingly interconnected world.”

articles.title: Hasan Piker Threatens Further Legal Action Against Conservative Pundits He Claims Have Defamed Him
articles.author: Abid Rahman

paras.en: After filing a $72.5 million defamation lawsuit against CNN contributor Scott Jennings last week, the progressive political Twitch streamer Hasan Piker‘s legal team is promising more legal action against conservative pundits they feel have defamed their client.

In an interview with Vanity Fair, Piker’s attorney and defamation specialist Daniel Watkins said there is a “reckoning coming.” “There are other people and other entities that will likely receive outreach from my law firm in the coming days,” Watkins said.

The more aggressive legal posture from Piker’s camp stands in marked contrast to his previous tendency to let the more controversial, and often baseless, accusations against him slide. Since he became a national and international political figure — he has been namechecked by both Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu in 2026 — Piker has faced a torrent of claims against him, including animal abuse, racism and misogyny, and has become something of a lightning rod for Republican and centrist Democratic attacks.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: That all changed on Aug. 11, when Jennings, appearing on his Salem Media podcast, presented a spliced video montage alleging that Piker advocated for lynchings. Jennings used the completely out-of-context segment to urge Michigan voters to reject Senatorial candidate Abdul El-Sayed over his ties to the streamer.

Watkins issued a formal retraction demand to Salem Media’s chief legal counsel, Christopher Henderson, in late August. When that yielded no response, Piker filed suit, demanding $27.5 million in compensatory damages and $45 million in punitive damages.

“I have been very deliberately anti-litigation for a very long time,” Piker told Vanity Fair. “But something shifted that’s been bubbling up where… people like Scott Jennings, and there are others as well, started trafficking in outright lies, defamation, and slander.”

Watkins stressed the severe impact of the clips on Piker’s career, calling the targeted misattributions “disgusting and vile and dangerous” for a public figure built on advocacy for marginalized groups. For Piker, the legal action stems from personal fallout — including reputational damage and safety concerns after an individual stalked him at a public event.
“When is the last time you experienced eight consistent months of [mainstream media] having one primary villain?” Piker asked. “It’s not fun at all. It sucks.”

With midterms wrapping up, with big wins for Piker-backed candidates, the streamer and his legal team are already eyeing their next potential targets. Piker highlighted former RNC chair Ronna McDaniel, who repeated the lynching claim on C-SPAN, and Sen. Ted Cruz, who reshared Jennings’ montage on X. Piker publicly taunted the Texas senator online shortly after filing his suit against Jennings, posting: “Hey Ted you seen this?”

Speaking directly to people who have made false claims against him, Piker added, “If you felt as though you could outright fabricate quotes and make up totally ridiculous claims about me, you should probably work on your retractions immediately.”

articles.title: Ben Shapiro Says 2026 Midterms Were “A Wipeout for Republicans”: “The President Was Kind of on the Ballot”
articles.author: McKinley Franklin

paras.en: Ben Shapiro reacted to the early results of the 2026 midterms during an appearance on the All-In podcast Tuesday night, noting that he thinks early tallies indicated that “the president was kind of on the ballot.”

“This not an evening to remember,” he said on the podcast, which streamed from 8 p.m. ET to 10 p.m. ET on Tuesday night, before some of the major race results were called. “I think that, honestly, the president said going in that the election was going to be a referendum on him, act like he’s on the ballot, and I think that, you know, the president was kind of on the ballot.”

Shapiro argued “if this were just the case of a few outstandingly bad Republican candidates losing, like Paxton in Texas, for example, or if it were just a matter of an outstanding Democrat candidate winning somewhere, like Josh Turek in Iowa, … but the fact that South Carolina is going, you basically have an empty suit in South Carolina losing.”

Texas had history-making results, as the state elected James Talarico as defeated Ken Paxton, becoming the first Democrat elected as a senator in 38 years; Gina Hinojosa also beat Greg Abbott to become the first Democratic governor of Texas in 36 years.
As for South Carolina, Annie Andrews became the state’s first Democrat elected to the Senate in over 20 years. She also became the first woman from South Carolina to be elected to the Senate.

“Or the fact that Florida stayed red, but very, very, very closely. I mean, that’s my home state so I know that state very well, Angie Nixon is a full-scale nutcase, and Angie Nixon is going to lose that senatorial race by about two points,” he added. (Democrat Nixon was defeated by Republican Ashley Moody in Florida’s U.S. Senator race.)
“It’s a wipeout for Republicans,” Shapiro asserted. “There’s no way to sugarcoat that. And again, if you’re looking at it across the map, that bodes pretty ill for 2028.”

articles.title: Kimmel Bashes Trump After Democrats’ Midterms “Tsunami”: “The Only Ass on His Mind Is the One That Just Got Handed to Him”
articles.author: Hilary Lewis

paras.en: Jimmy Kimmel became the first late night host to take on the results of the 2026 midterm elections late Tuesday night.

While none of the major late night shows went live on election night, ABC’s Jimmy Kimmel Live! reportedly taped later than usual on Tuesday night to react to some of the early returns. Comedy Central’s The Daily Show was the only other major late night show to air a new episode Tuesday night, but that was taped before many of the polls closed. Stephen Colbert regularly took his Late Show live on election nights, but, of course, CBS canceled his show last year and it came to an end in May.

Kimmel’s late taping allowed the host to get in some early jokes on a night that saw the Democrats projected to win both the House and the Senate amid historic, surprise victories in Georgia, Texas, Ohio, South Carolina and Kansas.
And Kimmel had plenty of barbs ready for President Donald Trump, with whom he has long feuded.
Early in his monologue he homed in on Trump’s recent fixation with complimenting people’s rear ends.
“It seems to be after all the talk about Nicki Minaj’s ass, Jon Husted’s ass, the only ass on Trump’s mind tonight is the one that just got handed to him.”
Kimmel even revived the false 2024 rumor about Vice President J.D. Vance once having sex with a couch.
“The Democrats took so many seats, J.D. Vance can’t even find one to have sex with him,” Kimmel said.
Returning to Trump, Kimmel joked that he spent the day watching Fox News coverage of the results “trying to give himself an insurrection.”

“Word from the from inside the White House is he’s already run out of dipping sauce containers to throw at the television set,” Kimmel joked. “Man, oh man, would I hate to be the Door Dash driver who delivers Trump his Papa John’s tonight?”
Kimmel went on to recap where some key races stood at the time of his show taping and paid tribute to outgoing House Speaker Mike Johnson with a compilation of some of his funniest moments.

articles.title: Treasury yields fall as investors crowd into bonds for safety amid election stock sell-off

paras.en: Treasury yields moved lower on Wednesday as investors sought shelter from a sell-off in equity futures sparked by potential big victories from Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections.

The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield was last seen 1 basis point lower at 4.9291%. The 30-year bond yield slid 1 basis point to 5.3125%, and the shorter-term 2-year note yield pulled back 1 basis point to 4.5996%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.
Democrats are on course for a clean sweep, with the party winning at least the House and projected to win the Senate according to a CNBC Election Desk.
Democrats are projected to have flipped Senate seats from Republicans in Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas, the Associated Press projected.

Stock futures fell sharply as election results rolled in. Contracts tied to to the S&P 500 were seen 0.34%, and Nasdaq-100 futures slid 0.46%. AI-related shares, which have led the bull market, paced the overnight decline on fear Democrats would slow the data center buildout.

articles.title: Novo raises full-year outlook as Wegovy pill sales impress

paras.en: Novo posted quarterly earnings ahead of expectations early Wednesday as sales of its Wegovy pill blew past estimates.
The Danish weight-loss drug maker is looking to regain momentum following a tumultuous year in which it fell behind rival Eli Lilly.

The company updated its outlook to now see adjusted revenue and operating profit growth of between negative 2% and 2% at constant exchange rates. It previously saw full-year sales and operating profits, which it hiked in August, at negative 6% to flat for both metrics.

Sales in the third quarter came in at 79.2 billion Danish kroner ($11.9 billion), up 4% year-on-year and ahead of FactSet estimates of 73.6 billion kroner. Adjusted operating profit (EBIT) was 31.7 billion kroner, compared with the expected 28.6 billion kroner.
This is a breaking news story. Please refresh for updates.

articles.title: Stock futures fall as Democrats win big in midterms with traders betting they slow data center buildout: Live updates

paras.en: Stock futures dropped as traders speculated that Democrats were headed for majority control of Congress and some key gubernatorial wins in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections.

Futures tied to the S&P 500 traded 0.34% lower, while Nasdaq-100 futures shed 0.46%. Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average were down 89 points, or 0.15%. Futures were off their worst levels of the session.

The Democratic Party is projected to win both chambers of Congress, according to The Associated Press. The AP also projected that Texas Democratic governor candidate Gina Hinojosa is the winner over Republican incumbent Greg Abbott. Hinojosa has pledged a moratorium on data centers in the key tech hub.

Democrats securing a sizable majority in the House and Senate — the so-called blue wave scenario — would pressure the market and especially stocks related to the artificial intelligence buildout, according to some on Wall Street. Investors fear a big Democratic win could mean more restrictions on data centers nationwide. AI-linked stocks have already pulled back in recent weeks on concern about a slowing pace in data-center spending.
Big Tech shares Microsoft, Amazon and Nvidia were all trading lower in overnight trading on Robinhood.
Elon Musk's SpaceX was down 4.6% on Robinhood, while Tesla shares were down 4.1%. Data center play CoreWeave was down 3.2% in Robinhood overnight trading, while Alphabet was some 0.6% lower.

Equities "trended lower as it's looked more likely that Democrats are going to pick up the House and most likely the Senate," said Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise Financial, Tuesday evening as futures were pulling back.

He added: "If you get some governorships that are Democratic, what does that mean for the data center buildout, which has already seen a lot of skepticism over the last couple weeks in terms of the hyperscaler capex spending?"

AMD shares initially surged double digits in post-market action after the company, a key player in the AI trade, reported third-quarter earnings and revenue that blew past analyst expectations. The stock was last 5% higher on Robinhood as stock market futures traded lower.

On the overall market, investors believe a blue wave would also be a headwind as it likely rules out any more business-friendly policies like tax breaks and possibly increases scrutiny on industries like banking.

Renewable shares like solar stocks traded higher in the post-market on speculation a Democratic majority in Congress would halt policies by President Donald Trump taken against the industry. The Invesco Solar ETF was up 3% in Robinhood trading.

President Donald Trump may have helped ease pressure on the market a bit overnight by not challenging the midterm results in an interview with the Wall Street Journal. Trump told the WSJ, "I think we'll work with the Democrats, and we'll get along very well with them."

articles.title: The 2026 midterms are today—here’s what scientists say is at stake

paras.en: The 2026 midterm elections are finally here, and as the results roll in on Tuesday night and through this week, scientists will be watching closely. That’s because the results could influence the very foundations of U.S. science, from funding decisions to data center expansion to research agency budgets.

Those foundations have been rocked by the second Trump administration. Since 2025 the government has sought to redirect grant money toward artificial intelligence, technology, and nuclear energy and has reduced funding for climate, health and social science projects. The administration has repeatedly proposed mass cuts to NASA and National Science Foundation budgets and has laid off thousands of federal workers, including researchers. At the same time, universities have come under federal investigation, while the number of international students and early-career researchers has been limited by new visa rules. Amid all this, the administration has also sought to discredit vaccines, slash climate regulations and pull the U.S. back from global collaborations in science.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “This election's critical,” says Gretchen Goldman, president and CEO of the Union of Concerned Scientists. “It will determine a lot of what happens next, especially with this administration and their actions. This cycle is critical in terms of how the federal government is run and what kinds of checks and balances we’ll have in the next two years.”

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The results of Tuesday’s vote could determine both how money is allocated to science and how much of that is actually dispersed for research, she says.

Should either the House of Representatives or the Senate, or both, flip to Democratic control, Goldman anticipates there could also be a flood of investigations from subcommittees into what has happened to federal science under the Trump administration.

“There’s a tremendous need for oversight investigations, really taking a hard look at what this administration has been doing to federal science,” she says, for example, “from [the Committee on] Environment [and] Public Works on the Senate side.... I think the House [Committee on Science, Space, and Technology] will be an interesting one, to see what they can do. This is a key place where we can really provide more accountability on the administration’s defiance of Congress’s will to fund science.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Should Democrats win Congress outright, there would still be limits to whatever they might do, says Arthur Caplan, a professor emeritus of population health and bioethics at New York University. The White House would still exert control over federal agencies and departments, and the Supreme Court, which has often ruled in the administration’s favor, is dominated by a conservative majority. But a stronger political opposition in Congress could lead to more dealmaking, he says.

“It’s not just [that the Democrats are] going to come in and say, ‘Your science policy has been retrograde; we hate it. We don’t agree with all this diversity, equity and inclusiveness censorship; we don’t agree with many of your appointments,’” he says. “But you then are in a position to barter and bargain to get what you want because you have the purse strings and are willing to use them.”

Science funding rarely surfaces as a major issue for voters. But Collette Delawalla, founder and CEO of the science advocacy group Stand Up for Science, says there are ample science-based issues on the ballot this year that could prove pivotal. Health care costs are one of the top issues that voters are considering while voting, one recent poll found. Delawalla adds that many voters may also be worried about public health, particularly given the ongoing measles crisis and the summer’s cyclosporiasis outbreak.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “People are concerned about the food system not being safe,” she says. “They’re concerned about rollbacks at the [Environmental Protection Agency] and their water not being safe to drink or data centers polluting their air around them.”

While the Trump administration has scrapped or weakened several climate-related laws, including the recent decision to roll back methane gas limits, Delawalla acknowledges that climate change isn’t an issue that has received much attention during the campaign—but gas prices are focusing attention on fossil fuels.

“I don’t think it’s clean energy for clean energy’s sake” that may be motivating voters, she says, “as much as it is: gas prices are really high, and people are absolutely looking for alternatives. And obviously, the alternative is green energy.”

The election could prove pivotal for several pieces of pending science legislation. In September Congress passed a stopgap funding bill that didn’t include a proposed rule change to put political appointees in charge of awarding science grants—that pause is set to expire in December. There is also the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), which was recently introduced to the Senate and has drawn fire for promoting fossil fuels at the expense of renewable energy. These and other questions, such as future budgets for NASA and other critical science agencies, will likely be settled after the winning lawmakers are sworn in in January 2027.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “I think there’s a lot of potential in a new Congress to reimagine what we can do there,” Goldman says, “to think about new policy ideas to take different pathways if there’s a different political makeup.”

articles.title: Self-flying cargo planes are coming. Can they be safe with no one aboard?

paras.en: Back in August I took my first Waymo. Whizzing up and down the hills of San Francisco, I was at once mesmerized by the steering wheel turning on its own and a bit scared of the occasional jerk and sudden stop. But even as robotaxis lurch into the mainstream, some technologists are trying to empty a loftier seat: the pilot’s.

In some ways, flying a plane is easier than driving a car, at least as far as automation is concerned. Unlike on roads, there are no surprise closures, no fallen trees and no running kids in the sky. In fact, autopilots already do much of the flying. On the other hand, the solutions have to be more delicate. As Robert Rose, chief executive officer of Reliable Robotics, points out, planes don’t have the easy out of “if something happens, slam on the brakes.”

In mid-October Reliable’s software taxied, took off and landed a Cessna Grand Caravan, a single-engine turboprop plane, at Albuquerque’s main airport while a pilot supervised from company headquarters in California, more than 700 miles away. (A safety pilot rode along as a backup.) Days later, the company announced new funding that brought its valuation to more than $1 billion. The flights were part of a new Federal Aviation Administration program to figure out how autonomous aircraft can fit into the nation’s airspace.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

Reliable’s eventual goal is a fleet of cargo planes with no pilots aboard during takeoff, flight or landing, and it isn’t alone. In September Joby Aviation flew its own self-piloting Caravan coast-to-coast without its safety pilot touching the controls. Boston-based Merlin is putting another autonomous Caravan through certification with regulators in New Zealand and the U.S. Reliable has been working toward certification, a deliberately slow process, for years and expects to start earning the FAA’s okay for some of its systems by the end of 2027, according to TechCrunch.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Certification hinges on testing that shows that a critical failure happens only in an extremely tiny fraction of cases—less than one time in a billion flight hours. According to Rose, today’s autopilots clear that bar only because a human pilot is there to take over when needed, so his pitch is to make the autopilot even more, well, reliable.

Ella Atkins, a professor of aerospace engineering at Virginia Tech, doubts that reliability alone keeps people in the cockpit. “If you look at what pilots actually do, they follow checklists,” she says. “It’s very rare that someone goes completely off-script and saves the day.” She points to two other holdups flying without a pilot aboard: People may not feel comfortable, and it’s harder to assign blame when something goes wrong. “Every company is less liable for costs after a crash if they can point to a pilot and say it was pilot error,” Atkins says.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Plenty of aircraft fly themselves today. “We’ve been flying unmanned air vehicles, or drones, of reasonably large size. We’ve been flying those for a while,” says R. John Hansman, a professor of aeronautics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Anything plane-sized needs to be far more dependable, he says, because a crash could be much more catastrophic: “A small quadcopter drone doesn’t have to have the level of redundancy that a large vehicle that could hurt people on the ground or carry people needs.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Self-driving car companies stress their use of artificial intelligence to detect and perceive the world around them, but Rose wants no part of it, at least not the neural network kind. “You lose the explainability or traceability for why various functions exist,” he says. “Frankly, there’s no way to get it certified.”

Instead Reliable Robotics uses the fountains of data that spring from aviation’s heavy regulation. The FAA publishes precise, regularly updated runway locations, and planes already broadcast their positions through the Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast, or ADS-B, system. Reliable’s software runs those and various other measurements through specialized algorithmic filters to pin down exactly where its own plane is and adapt accordingly. Atkins cautions against completely rejecting modern technologies in design, though she notes that the “nearly century-old technology gap” plagues the entire aviation industry.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The company plans to roll out its automation in steps. First up is approval just for automated takeoff, landing and taxiing, considered some of the most difficult parts of flying planes today. According to research by Boeing, about 70 percent of fatal accidents involving commercial jets happen during takeoff and landing. These stages are also the parts where human pilots currently have the most control. “Our normal navigation systems take you automatically to about 200 feet above the ground, and then typically the pilots see the runway and they land,” Rose says.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: To get around this, Reliable designed its navigation system to handle takeoff and landing, too. Some previous computer-assisted landing systems have used radarlike radio beams to help track the plane through landing. The result is a semiautomated system that Rose says makes it “arguably easier to hand land the plane than configure all the automation.” He claims his system requires no extra infrastructure at the runway or airport.
After that, Reliable aims to take the safety pilot out of the cockpit altogether, a step that’s still years off. Even then, Hansman says, “there will always be some level of human supervision.”
But if the test flights in Albuquerque keep going well, airline passengers could someday soon look out airport windows to see roboplanes taking to the skies, with no one looking back.

articles.title: New York’s first measles death in 30 years is an omen of worse to come

paras.en: A child in upstate New York died on Monday after contracting measles. This marks the state’s first death from the disease in 30 years, as the outbreak continues to spread across the country.

In a statement, New York governor Kathy Hochul said she was “heartbroken” and that the death reflected a crisis of government and public health. Hochul declared measles a statewide disaster last month.

With fewer immune protections, children are especially at risk for measles and its more dangerous effects. And as the outbreak surges, doctors are becoming increasingly concerned about congenital measles. If a pregnant woman has measles, there’s a 25 to 30 percent chance her child will also acquire measles, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics. Congenital measles is not tracked by the Center for Disease Control and Prevention—the condition had become exceedingly rare, but rising rates are raising fears about its potential effects once more.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

As of October 29, the CDC had confirmed 4,852 measles cases across the U.S. so far this year. New York State has had a total of 178 confirmed cases, mainly concentrated in the central part of the state. According to officials, the recent death in New York occurred in Lewis County, which is northeast of Syracuse and has seen 16 cases in 2026.

It is representative of a worsening national picture. The U.S. is currently in the thick of the worst measles outbreak since 1991. Case numbers this year have already doubled those of 2025—previously the worst year for the disease since 1991. (The U.S. was declared measles-free in 2000.) Technically, the country still holds its measles-free status, a title that is marked by 12 months without continuous local transmission, although experts expect that may change soon. Officials are set to meet in the next few weeks to determine whether that status—hailed for years as a symbol of excellence in public health—should be revised or eliminated.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: As of October 30, the CDC has reported three deaths from measles nationally—although some states have reported deaths that have been disputed by the CDC—and an 11 percent hospitalization rate. In its milder forms, the disease can cause an itchy rash and fever, but it can also cause pneumonia and severe brain inflammation, which, without treatment, can prove fatal or disabling. The measles virus is the most contagious virus known—but it is not impossible to contain. Vaccines, particularly the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) combined shot, had helped measles fade because of herd immunity. But dwindling vaccination rates are helping the disease break through, with dire consequences.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The MMR jab offers 97 percent protection for life after two doses given in childhood and was the major factor in eradicating measles in the U.S. But with higher levels of vaccine skepticism among the public and the upper echelons of the Trump administration, fewer children are receiving the vaccine: in the past 10 years, MMR vaccination rates among kindergarteners have fallen from 94 percent to 92.4 percent. (A 95 percent vaccination rate is the critical number to ensure community or herd immunity.) Of the cases reported by the CDC this year, 96 percent were among people who were unvaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown. It’s unclear whether the child that died on Monday was vaccinated.

articles.title: NASA’s Swift telescope will face a fiery demise after a failed rescue
articles.author: Meghan Bartels

paras.en: For two decades, when the high-energy universe called, NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has answered. But now, the spacecraft’s science tenure is ending, just when its skills might be more valuable than ever. The Swift spacecraft is falling uncontrollably, destined to burn up in Earth’s atmosphere in just a few days.

The telescope launched in 2004, tailored to reveal the secrets of gamma-ray bursts. These outbursts are the most powerful kind scientists have ever seen, but they often faded before earlier telescopes could respond. Swift took its name from its ability to jump to work when a flash went off. That talent both illuminated these elusive bursts and made the observatory a cornerstone of modern astronomy for far longer than scientists ever dreamed.

“This was designed to be a two-year mission,” says astrophysicist Brad Cenko of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md. “We’re coming up on year 22. We are so fortunate to have had the opportunity to do all the things that we have.”

Over the decades, the spacecraft has lost about half its original altitude as it constantly slammed into molecules in the atmosphere. Those minuscule impacts infinitesimally slowed the observatory, pushing it closer to Earth. The sun’s relatively high activity in recent years has accelerated the process, leaving the spacecraft unable to continue into the 2030s as engineers hoped. A spacecraft commissioned by NASA to loft Swift out of danger launched in early July, but by late August, technical issues made a boost attempt impossible.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Swift is doomed — with nothing lined up to replace its unique capabilities.

When scientists dreamed up the Swift mission, the massive energy and elusive nature of gamma-ray bursts made them one of the most tantalizing phenomena out there. Astronomers desperately wanted to understand how they worked.

Swift was equipped with three instruments. Its Burst Alert Telescope gave scientists eyes on gamma-ray emissions from up to half the visible sky, with the resolution to pinpoint where light is coming from. The agile spacecraft could then swing itself and its other instruments — one tuned to X-rays and the other to visible and ultraviolet light — to quickly give scientists a view of a patch of sky across a swath of types of light. It was a combination unlike any observatory before or since.

“It’s such a unique telescope,” says astrophysicist Wen-fai Fong of Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill., who is not part of the mission team. “It has all these views of the universe, all in one observatory, which by itself is rare, but it can also rapidly point any of these instruments.”

Swift’s roster of accomplishments speaks to the power of that recipe. “Almost immediately after launch, Swift started discovering things,” says astrophysicist Lynn Cominsky of Sonoma State University in Rohnert Park, Calif. That’s not an exaggeration: One record-breaking observation, taken just the month after launch, revealed that stellar corpses with powerful magnetic fields undergo outbursts that create a distinct kind of gamma-ray signature.

That observation pushed back against scientists’ existing categorization of gamma-ray bursts. Before Swift, the bursts fell into two buckets. Long gamma-ray bursts lasted as long as minutes, and scientists believed they stemmed from exploding stars triggering supernovae. Short gamma-ray bursts, in contrast, lasted less than two seconds and were believed to originate in merging neutron stars, the superdense remains of a star large enough to explode but too small to create a black hole.

Swift confirmed this basic sketch, but also complicated it by finding bursts that didn’t cleanly fit into this binary. “The more data you get, the more confused you get,” Cominsky says. Other notable bursts the telescope observed included the brightest (gamma-ray burst) of all time, nicknamed BOAT, the highest-energy photons from such a burst, and multiple claimants to the title of most distant burst.

Notably, all of Swift’s data was public right away, even as team scientists were still working to understand what the telescope had seen. “That was very new,” Fong says, crediting the mission with inspiring other observatory teams to follow suit.

As other astronomers heard about Swift’s work, they realized how powerful the observatory might be for their own interests as well. As Swift’s tenure unfolded, astronomers started asking to borrow the nimble observatory to study a whole range of objects changing on the sky.

“With scientists, if you give them a tool to do something, they will other find other things that you can do with that tool,” says astrophysicist Phil Evans of the University of Leicester in England. In its later years, Swift observed between five and 10 “targets of opportunity” most days, tallying hundreds or even thousands in a year.

Perhaps its most ground-breaking collaborations were partnerships with observatories hunting for ghostly neutrinos that travel nearly as quickly as light but don’t interact often, and for gravitational waves, the ripples in spacetime triggered by massive objects. In 2017, Swift participated in back-to-back discoveries: the unique explosion caused by two neutron stars merging, then the first neutrino traced back to its origin.

Since then, all efforts to observe light affiliated with a neutrino or gravitational-wave signal have come up empty. “We had these two really close together and then nothing since,” Evans says. “Which is frustrating, but also kind of fun.”

A range of current and future observatories will be able to take over some of Swift’s work, but not all of it. Even during the six months this year when Swift paused operations to prepare for the boost attempt, scientists felt its loss, says astrophysicist Judith Racusin of NASA Goddard. Racusin worked with Swift during its early years before turning her focus to NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, which launched in 2008 but boasts different strengths than its colleague. “We’re going to miss out,” she says of Swift’s loss. “Not just on the common events we have thousands of, but the really rare, unusual ones, which are often the ones we learn the most from.”

paras.en: Mission personnel had Swift cram in as much science as possible as its demise approached. After the boost attempt was called off, the team turned Swift’s instruments back on for a scientific swan song. That included technical observations to ensure the utility of all its recent data, as well as indirect observations of Earth’s atmosphere at lower altitudes than many spacecraft are able to withstand. Swift even caught glimpses of a comet in its final weeks.
And, of course, there were gamma-ray bursts. One particularly intriguing burst came in late September and was rather far away but remarkably energetic.
“It feels a little bit like a last hurrah of Swift,” Racusin says of the event. “It’s a burst that we’ll be studying for some time, so I’m really glad we got Swift data on it while we could.”

articles.title: ‘Exhumed’ recounts the true story of America’s first vampire
articles.author: Anna Mattson

paras.en: October is my favorite month. I love when the leaves change colors and the air gets brisk. My hunger for media that sends a shiver down my spine is at an all-time high. This spooky season, I found satiation in Exhumed, a new book by historian Aaron Mahnke.

Mahnke draws on rich science-based history and folklore to show how fear of the unknown has shaped culture throughout history, even into the present day. He cites Taylor Swift, Twilight and other pop culture phenomena in his analysis — a choice that injects fresh air into the otherwise miasmic atmosphere. And thanks to Mahnke’s gripping prose, I felt like I was in the middle of the action. It was hard to lay the book down.
Exhumed kicks off with the true story of America’s first “vampire.”

Walk with me for a moment back in time to Exeter, Rhode Island in 1892. Rampant tuberculosis is killing scores of people, including three members of the Brown family: matriarch Mary and her daughters, Mary O. and Mercy L. Then a son, Edwin, falls ill with the same symptoms — sparking concern that one of the women is an undead vampire who is sucking his life away. The town exhumes the bodies.

Mercy is surprisingly well-preserved. Her hair and nails appear longer and blood dribbles from her skin when it is pierced, “evidence” that confirms everyone’s worst fear: Mercy is indeed a vampire. (Nevermind that she perished in the dead of winter, when temperatures were probably cold enough to substantially slow decomposition.) The town burns Mercy’s heart, though it doesn’t save poor Edwin. These events helped inspire Bram Stoker’s Dracula, which was published five years later.

Interestingly, the cause of tuberculosis — a bacterium — was discovered a full decade before Mercy’s story unfolded. But news doesn’t always travel fast and entrenched beliefs can be difficult to change, even in the face of hard evidence. Exhumed explores this idea far beyond Mercy’s tragic tale.

Fear has led people to do some extremely odd things by today’s standards: burning hearts to kill “vampires,” setting boobie-traps in graves to prevent the dead from rising or drinking the blood of freshly hanged men to “cure” epilepsy. Without modern science to explain the unexplained, people often filled in the blanks with stories, Mahnke explains.

He implores readers to withhold judgement. After all, storytelling is one of the main ways that humans make sense of the world. “All of us, both then and now, are simply making the best of what we have, trying to find a way to improve our lives,” Mahnke writes.
Perhaps this practice continues today in different shades.

At one point, eating mummies, or “mumia,” was considered cure-all for most ailments —headaches, stomach troubles and general sickness. Is it too far from the expectations some people have of buying a “health shot” from Whole Foods? Not really!

More than a century after Mercy Brown’s heart was incinerated, we’re still clinging to stories and rituals that offer us a sense of control over the thing we fear most: death. Exhumed makes it clear that we haven’t outrun this instinct, we’ve just given it different packaging.
If you are the type of person who has 50 tabs open at any given moment, then you will appreciate Exhumed’s myriad quirky facts. Here are three of my favorites:

- Leonardo da Vinci was a fan of corpse medicine, the practice of reusing body parts from dead people for medicinal purposes. Like many of his peers, da Vinci believed the human body contained “vital spirits.” When someone died, there’d be leftover spirits for the living to make use of.

- In 17th century Europe, the tomato was known as the “poison apple.” Many people became sick after eating tomatoes and some even died. For two centuries, society wrongly blamed the fruit. The real killer turned out to be lead leached out of pewter dishes by tomatoes’ acidic juice.

- The spinning red, white and blue poles on barbershops were born out of the business’ former specialty, bloodletting. Red stripes stand for blood, blue for veins and white for the rags used for clean-up. The ball on top is said to represent the bowl that captured the blood. And the pole itself represents the wand patients squeezed during the procedure. Feeling sick in 1705? Head to the local barber with the spinning pole outside.

articles.title: How hawkmoths turned their genitals into bat-busting weapons
articles.author: Elie Dolgin

paras.en: When a bat closes in, some hawkmoths fight back with their genitalia. By rasping specialized scales on their sex organs against structures on their abdomens, the moths unleash bursts of ultrasound that can scramble the sonar a hungry bat uses to lock onto prey.

But this acoustic counterattack is no evolutionary one-off. Relentless pressure from predators has pushed these otherwise tasty insects to reinvent this defensive tactic up to seven times throughout their evolution, with separate lineages arriving at distinct anatomical solutions to the same threat, researchers report November 4 in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B.
The findings suggest that the high-frequency acoustic skirmishes playing out overhead each night, beyond the range of human hearing, may be far more varied than scientists realized.

“Clearly the hawkmoths as a whole have more tricks up their sleeve,” says Marc Holderied, a sensory biologist and bioacoustics researcher at the University of Bristol in England who was not involved in the study.

The discovery builds on more than a decade of research by sensory ecologist Jesse Barber, now at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, and entomologist Akito Kawahara of the Florida Museum of Natural History in Gainesville. Those scientists’ earlier work showed that moths across multiple families, from tiger moths and fruit-piercing moths to geometer moths and jewel caterpillar moths, produce ultrasound in response to bat attacks. Other insects, including some beetles and fireflies, do too.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But among the most striking defenders are hawkmoths, a family of some 1,600 mostly nocturnal, torpedo-shaped speedsters, also known as sphinx moths, that hover at flowers like hummingbirds. Many fend off bats by scraping their genitalia like a fingernail dragged along a comb, producing ultrasonic clicks that can disrupt the predators’ sonar.

The anatomical diversity of these sound-producing systems, however, and how they evolved remained poorly understood. So Barber, Kawahara and their team, including Florida museum colleague and evolutionary biologist Paul Masonick, combined audio recordings of male hawkmoths responding to bat calls with high-resolution imaging of preserved specimens from overlapping species. Although some females also produce ultrasound, the researchers focused on males because female sound creation remains too poorly documented for systematic analysis.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Among the 143 species tested, 77 produced ultrasound. They did so in three distinct ways. All three rely on a patch of enlarged, football-shaped scales on the male’s genital valves, which are paired structures used to clasp females during mating. But what those scales scrape against varies.

Some rub the scales against a row of corresponding scales near the rear of the abdomen. Others drag them across stiff spines jutting from the abdomen’s edge. Still others rasp them over a field of microscopic bumps on the insect’s underside, a previously unidentified part of the sound-making apparatus.

These mechanical differences are reflected in the sounds themselves. Moths that scrape their genital scales against spines or tiny bumps tend to make more continuous noise, with greater potential to jam bat sonar. Those that scrape scales against other scales produce irregular bursts, which may startle attackers or mimic the warning calls of foul-tasting prey.

Notably, moths that scrape against the newly identified bumpy surface have the broadest acoustic repertoire, with even close relatives sounding quite different. That flexibility could give them more options for evolving new defenses against bats, notes Nick Dowdy, an evolutionary biologist at the Milwaukee Public Museum who was not involved in the research. Other groups, by comparison, may be more constrained by their anatomy, he says, leaving them “locked into certain strategies.”

The authors estimate that genitalia-enabled ultrasound production evolved independently at least four and as many as seven times between roughly 5 million and 30 million years ago. According to Masonick, it is a vivid example of convergent evolution in which the same predatory menace repeatedly drove the moths to adapt similar behaviors through different anatomical routes.

But the evolutionary arms race was not a one-way street, he points out. Several hawkmoth lineages that shifted toward twilight or daytime activity subsequently lost their specialized sound-producing machinery.
“It goes to show how intense bat predation is on insects,” Masonick says. “It’s been a major driver of insect evolution.”

articles.title: Moths Keep Evolving Their Genitals Into Anti-Bat Weapons, Again And Again
articles.author: Michelle Starr

paras.en: Some evolutionary innovations are so useful that nature keeps on making them.

There's the crab; everyone knows nature keeps making crabs. There's the ability to fly, whether by feathers, membranes, or chitin. And, of course, there's the indispensable trick of using one's genitals to scramble the sonar of hunting bats.
No, your eyes are not deceiving you. Some moths have evolved the ability to make noise at bats using their genital structures.
And apparently it's so useful that this ability has emerged, separately, again and again in different species of hawkmoths.

According to new research, these moths have evolved the ability to scream at bats using their genitals independently as many as seven times over 30 million years – and at least three distinct anatomical mechanisms have emerged, producing different kinds of potentially sonar-jamming ultrasound.

"Collectively," writes the team in a study led by entomologist Paul Masonick of the Florida Museum of Natural History, "our findings deepen our understanding of defensive bioacoustic adaptations in this iconic predator-prey system."

The relationship between predator and prey is one of nature's most powerful drivers of evolution. The constant threat of death from a particular source – a predator on the prowl for snacks – creates pressure to find ways to avoid ending up on the menu.

We see it time and again – an evolutionary arms race in which predators and prey continually evolve new ways to outwit each other, driving adaptations such as camouflage, toxicity, spikes, armor, and ways to look much bigger and tougher than the reality might be.
For hawkmoths harried by hungry bats, producing sounds that confuse the echolocation their predators use to locate flying prey in the darkness has the potential to be a powerful survival strategy.
But moths don't have larynxes. So they have to get a little bit more creative.

The trick is a process called stridulation – producing sound by rubbing two body parts together, like the chirps of crickets rubbing their wings, or the hissing of spiders rubbing their legs against each other.

In male hawkmoths, the instruments are specialized scales on a pair of genital structures called valvae. By moving these structures against modified surfaces on their abdomens, the moths can produce bursts of ultrasound.
And, as the researchers discovered, there is more than one way to make genital music.
Masonick and his colleagues examined the genital structures of male hawkmoths from across the family, using detailed imaging to identify the surfaces responsible for producing their ultrasonic calls.

In some species, specialized scales on the genital structures scrape against other scales on the abdomen. In others, they rub against tiny spines. And in a third group, the scales scrape across little bumps called nodules.

Each mechanism produces its own distinctive ultrasonic sounds – a tiny percussion band that's beyond the range of human hearing – but when slowed down to bring them into the audible range, they resemble a series of rapid clicks, buzzes, or trills.
The scale-on-scale mechanism tends to produce shorter, more intermittent bursts of ultrasound, while scale-on-spine moths produce longer, more sustained emissions.
The scale-on-nodule moths, meanwhile, seem to have the most varied repertoire, producing sounds that differ considerably even between closely related species.
And, amazingly, these three distinct mechanisms for yelling from the gonads weren't all inherited from a single, acoustically gifted ancestor.

When the researchers mapped the sound-producing structures and behaviors onto the hawkmoth family tree, they found that the ability to sing an ultrasonic genital song in response to hunting bats appears to have repeatedly evolved independently, as many as seven times over the past 30 million years.
Which raises the question: If nature kept reinventing the screaming willy, just how useful is it?
Surprisingly, the answer is: not consistently – at least, maybe not in the way you might expect.
The researchers analyzed recordings of the moths' ultrasonic performances, measuring how long each burst lasted, its frequency, and how much time the moths spent making noise.
They then compared these measurements with what previous experiments had revealed about the kinds of sounds that can interfere with bat echolocation.
And not all the strange moth songs were up to the task.
The more sustained sounds were most likely to have the acoustic characteristics associated with disrupting bat sonar in a way that could help the moth evade a toothy capture.
But even the shorter bursts may have their uses.

Some hawkmoths have hearing organs that allow them to detect the ultrasonic calls of approaching bats, giving them time to respond with a barrage of noise. That's when it would be useful to mess with echolocation.
Others, however, are deaf. They can't hear the bats coming, so they can't respond to approaching predators in the same way. However, they can still produce ultrasound when touched.

The researchers suggest that shorter bursts might startle a bat as it closes in for the kill, potentially giving the moth a chance to escape. Well, and it would, wouldn't it? Imagine going in for a tasty snack, and its genitals start yelling at you. You'd back right the hell off.

Another possibility is acoustic mimicry. Some moths use ultrasonic signals to warn bats that they're toxic or otherwise unpleasant to eat. Hawkmoths, which are generally palatable to bats, may be jumping on the warning bandwagon by making similar sounds.
And there might be another, more appropriate use for the genital sounds, at least in some species.
The variety of sounds produced by the scale-on-nodule mechanism raises the possibility that the sounds could also help moths recognize members of their own species during courtship.
This remains to be tested, but nature is very good at finding new uses for old tricks.
So there you have it – if you can't avoid turning into dinner, maybe at least you can get a little romance before you go.
The research has been published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences.

articles.title: Medieval Humans Partly Caused Two Catastrophic Lake Tsunamis, And We Could Easily Do It Again, Scientists Warn
articles.author: Jess Cockerill

paras.en: Tsunamis are not exclusive to the ocean: with the right conditions, they can happen in lakes, too.
At Lake Iseo in northern Italy, medieval humans set the scene for two such catastrophic wave events, and researchers are warning that it could easily happen again.

In a paper published in Nature Communications, an international team has brought together data from sediment cores, seismic profiles, a medieval manuscript, archaeological records, and the modern-day lake itself.
This range of sources helped them recreate the unusual medieval disasters via computer models.

Lake Iseo is downstream of the Italian Alps, from which it receives a regular supply of water via snowmelt. The same tectonic activity that helped to form the Alps also brings the occasional earthquake to the region.
Two thousand years of intensifying land use changed the way sediment settled in the delta, making its sides steeper.

Before the Middle Ages, the Oglio River delta was surrounded by forest. When it rained, loose sediment would flow downhill, but its passage was slowed by the dense networks of tree roots and fungi that held the soil together.
Underwater, the delta's slopes were gentle, gradually tilting towards the lake's deepest point, which is around 250 meters.
But things rapidly changed around the fall of the Roman Empire.

In the centuries that followed, more and more forests that once surrounded the delta were removed for pasture and mining; the human population grew; and three times more sediment was flushed into the lake each year on average.
More and more sediment accumulated at the lake's northern end, creating precariously steep underwater banks just waiting to crash.
And that's exactly what happened, twice.
The natural shape of the delta could handle some seismic activity from time to time without necessarily flooding the surrounding towns.

But when the violent 1117 CE Verona Earthquake shook the lake's steepened banks, they collapsed in an underwater landslide, displacing a massive amount of water that, according to the researchers' modeling, would have flooded large sections of the shores of Lake Iseo without a minute's warning.

"Our simulations reveal that the medieval delta collapses in Lake Iseo generated some of the largest subaquatic landslide-induced tsunamis ever inferred in a lacustrine setting," the study's authors write.
By their calculations, waves in the northern part of the lake would have exceeded 50 meters, inundating nearby shores in less than a minute, with water reaching up to 2.7 kilometers inland.
A 12th-century manuscript now held at the Vatican Library describes the catastrophic event in vivid detail that matches the modeling well. The passage is translated to English as follows:

"The lake overflowed so much that very few of the inhabitants of the nearby villages escaped this danger. Many castles and fortresses also collapsed miserably, with the destruction of their inhabitants."

But alas, medieval folks are not especially known for their scientific inquiry – disasters like this were more likely seen as a message from God. They rebuilt, and resumed the practices that had led to the first fatal tsunami.
Just over a century later, a second earthquake hit: the 1222 CE Brescia earthquake.
Another large tsunami ensued in Lake Iseo, with waves peaking at around 13 meters, and water rushing up to 1 kilometer inland.

"Both tsunamis propagated rapidly across Lake Iseo and were strongly influenced by Monte Isola, the central island, which acts as a natural barrier, splitting the waves and partially shielding the cities behind it," the authors explain.

"Despite this protection, areas such as [the town of] Iseo still experienced significant impacts, with maximum wave heights of ~5.5 meters (1117 CE) and ~2 meters (1222 CE), arriving ~7 minutes after the landslides."
Lake Iseo now has the most densely built shores of any lake in the Italian Alps. Meanwhile, more than eight centuries' worth of sediment has built up since the 1222 CE collapse.

"A tsunami comparable in magnitude to the catastrophic events that struck Lake Iseo during the medieval period would cause severe devastation today, given the region's dense population and shoreline development," the authors write.

"A global lake synthesis showed that human-driven erosion has reached its highest levels since the Industrial Era, progressively overloading deltas worldwide; thus, similar catastrophic failures may become more likely in the future."
The research has been published in Nature Communications.

articles.title: Almost 75% of Deceased NFL Players Had Degenerative Brain Disease, Major Study Estimates
articles.author: Peter Dockrill

paras.en: In 2017, a bombshell discovery rocked the world of American football.

Alarmingly, scientists found that 99 percent of examined brains from deceased NFL players bore signs of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative neurological condition linked with repeated blows to the head.
In the years since, studies have revealed numerous sports increase the risk of brain injuries from repetitive head trauma, including soccer and rugby.

In the case of CTE among former NFL players, though, it's been difficult to identify just how common the brain disease is, but a new study appears to give us the most accurate assessment yet, suggesting about three-quarters of professional players had the condition when they died.
"Current knowledge regarding CTE neuropathology in American football players is derived from autopsy-based studies," researchers report in a new paper published in JAMA Network Open.
"Autopsy studies are inherently susceptible to registry bias, which may distort estimates of both disease prevalence and associations of exposures with outcomes."
In other words, when scientists study the post-mortem brains of ex-NFL players that have been donated to science, their results are limited to those specific donations.
For example, the landmark 2017 study found signs of CTE in 110 out of 111 (99 percent) of brains studied – but that doesn't mean that 99 percent of all NFL players would develop the disease.

That's because players who experience cognitive, mood, or behavioral symptoms would be expected to be more likely to participate in brain donation, resulting in a form of selection bias (aka 'registry' bias in this context).
In August this year, researchers published a study that took some preliminary steps to account for that bias, identifying all 1,712 former NFL players who died during the years 2008–2021.
Of that group, 338 had donated their brains for study, and 315 of them had a diagnosis of CTE.

But because most of the former deceased players had not donated their brains for study, all researchers could conclude was that CTE prevalence at death ranged somewhere between 18.5 percent and 98.7 percent – or between 24.5 percent and 97.7 percent for players who died between 2016 and 2021.

In the new study, several members of the same research team refined these estimate ranges by combining data from the UNITE brain bank with population-level mortality records for all deceased NFL players identified through the National Death Index (NDI).

After modeling the selection bias effect – estimating that players with cognitive symptoms were approximately five times more likely to have their brains donated for study – the researchers calculated what they claim is the first estimate of population-level prevalence of CTE neuropathology among former NFL players at the time of their death.
It's a breakthrough. But for the NFL community, it's an undeniably grim statistic.

"After adjusting for this selection process, we estimated that approximately 74.5 percent of deceased former NFL players had CTE neuropathology at death between 2008 and 2023," the team explains in their study, led by biostatistician Julia Gallini from Boston University.

While the findings are certainly concerning, they don't mean that three-quarters of former NFL players are destined to develop dementia, says study co-author and neuroscientist Daniel Daneshvar from Harvard Medical School.

"In our clinic with former players, particularly those in midlife, we have had success improving cognitive symptoms, mental health and quality of life through both targeted treatments and proactive brain health strategies," Daneshvar explains.
"While we cannot yet treat the underlying CTE pathology, our goal is to bend the curve of brain aging, extend brain healthspan and help players feel and function better throughout their lives."

In terms of next steps, the researchers say it will be important to estimate the prevalence of CTE in football players at lower levels of play (high school and college), to help define the scope of this public health concern, but they note the lack of data may make that difficult.
Aside from the statistical challenges, they say we need more research into the mechanisms, clinical manifestations, and prevention of CTE across all levels of play.
The findings are reported in JAMA Network Open.

articles.title: A hidden star is plowing through Betelgeuse’s atmosphere, new evidence suggests

paras.en: A hidden star is plowing through Betelgeuseâs atmosphere, new evidence suggests

- Something mysterious is disturbing Betelgeuse, and astronomers believe they have identified the culprit: a hidden companion star called Siwarha. New radio observations reveal that the smaller star may be plowing through Betelgeuseâs enormous atmosphere, creating disturbances that subtly stretch and distort the red supergiantâs shape.

Something unusual is happening inside the enormous atmosphere of Betelgeuse, one of the most recognizable stars in the night sky. Astronomers have detected subtle changes in the star's shape that suggest something is moving through its outer layers, disturbing the surrounding gas like an unseen visitor making noise inside a house. (Metaphorically speaking.) New observations point to a likely culprit: Siwarha, a recently discovered companion star that appears to be traveling through Betelgeuse's atmosphere.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Betelgeuse is a massive red supergiant located in the constellation Orion, where it forms the famous hunter's shoulder. Although the star has fascinated astronomers for generations, it attracted worldwide attention in late 2019 and early 2020 when its brightness unexpectedly plunged to its lowest recorded level in more than 100 years. The event, known as the Great Dimming, raised questions about what was happening inside the aging star.

Now, observations from the U.S. National Science Foundation's Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (NSF VLA) and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) reveal that Betelgeuse's vast outer atmosphere has largely returned to normal. More intriguingly, the measurements provide new evidence that a nearby companion star is physically disturbing the giant star's atmosphere.

The research was led by Dr. Lynn D. Matthews, Principal Research Scientist and Assistant Director at MIT Haystack Observatory, working with scientists from the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, the University of Manchester, and the European Southern Observatory. The team analyzed observations gathered between 2021 and 2026 at seven radio frequencies ranging from 22 GHz to 485 GHz.

Different radio frequencies allow astronomers to examine different depths within a star's atmosphere. By combining the observations from both telescopes, the researchers reconstructed the structure of Betelgeuse's outer layers, beginning just above its visible surface and extending outward to several times its radius.

"It was the combination of the incredible data from the NSF VLA and ALMA that gave us a convincing result here," said Matthews. "The fact that we can use these facilities to actually resolve the disks of nearby stars is amazing."
Betelgeuse Recovers From Its Mysterious Great Dimming

The latest measurements also help scientists understand how Betelgeuse has changed since its extraordinary fading episode. Several months before the Great Dimming (when Betelgeuse ejected a billion tons of solar material, partially blocking our view), an earlier investigation led by Matthews detected unusually low temperatures in the star's atmosphere at radio wavelengths.

At the time, researchers suggested that turbulent convection deep inside Betelgeuse may have generated a shock wave that traveled outward and disrupted the surrounding gas. That disturbance could have helped trigger the enormous release of material that later formed dust and obscured part of the star's light.

The new observations indicate that the atmosphere has since warmed to temperatures more typical of Betelgeuse. At a distance of approximately 2.7 times the star's radius, the gas now has a measured brightness temperature of about 3,500 Kelvin (comparable to Betelgeuse's own surface temperature).
Astronomers Discover an Unexpectedly Cold Atmospheric Layer

The researchers also confirmed a feature that scientists had suspected existed for years: a region of unusually cool gas between Betelgeuse's visible surface and its higher atmospheric layer, known as the chromosphere.

Using ALMA at its highest observed frequencies, the team was able to probe closer to the star's surface than previous radio measurements had allowed. The results revealed temperatures falling to approximately 2,200 Kelvin, more than 1,000 degrees below the temperature of the visible surface, or photosphere.

This cool region corresponds to the "MOLsphere," a layer containing molecular gas that astronomers had previously identified primarily through infrared observations. The new radio measurements provide a much more direct examination of this elusive part of Betelgeuse's atmosphere and confirm the long-suspected "temperature minimum."
A Hidden Companion Star May Be Distorting Betelgeuse

One of the most intriguing discoveries involves Siwarha, the smaller star believed to orbit extremely close to Betelgeuse. Astronomers first proposed the companion's existence in 2024 as a possible explanation for a puzzling cycle in which Betelgeuse's brightness changes approximately every 2,100 days. Subsequent direct imaging and spectroscopic observations have provided additional support for the companion's existence.
The name Siwarha reflects its relationship with Betelgeuse. The giant star's name comes from the Arabic expression meaning "the hand of al-Jawza," while Siwarha means "her bracelet."

Unlike a planet or star traveling far from its host, Siwarha is believed to follow an orbit that takes it directly through Betelgeuse's extended atmosphere. Its estimated orbital distance is only about twice the red supergiant's radius.
"This companion is orbiting so close to the star that it actually passes through its extended atmosphere," Matthews explained.

As Siwarha moves along its orbit, it may push through the surrounding gas much like a fast boat cutting through water. The resulting wake could disturb the atmosphere, producing changes that astronomers can detect even though the smaller star itself remains invisible in the radio observations.

In fact, the researchers calculated that Siwarha is likely tens to hundreds of times too faint to be detected directly with the radio measurements they collected. Instead, they searched for indirect evidence of its presence by studying the shape of Betelgeuse's atmosphere.
Betelgeuse's Changing Shape Reveals New Clues

The scientists discovered that Betelgeuse does not always appear perfectly round at radio wavelengths. Its atmosphere sometimes develops a slightly stretched, oval appearance, and the timing of these changes appears to match the expected position of Siwarha.
To investigate this connection, the team measured the atmosphere's departure from a circular shape ("ellipticity") across observations taken at different times.

They found that Betelgeuse tends to look more elongated when Siwarha is expected to be at its greatest apparent separation from the giant star. When the companion is predicted to pass in front of or behind Betelgeuse from our perspective, the atmosphere appears rounder.
This relationship provides compelling evidence that the smaller star may be influencing the shape of Betelgeuse's outer layers through gravity and its physical passage through the gas.

The effect resembles noticing ripples spreading across a pond without being able to see what caused them. Although Siwarha remains too faint to identify directly at radio wavelengths, the changing shape of Betelgeuse's atmosphere may reveal its movement around the larger star.
Future Observations Could Reveal More About Betelgeuse

Despite the promising results, astronomers emphasize that additional observations are necessary to confirm the connection between Siwarha's orbit and the atmospheric distortions. Measurements covering more of the companion's orbital cycle, particularly at radio frequencies that have not yet been studied extensively, could help establish how strongly the smaller star affects Betelgeuse.

More advanced instruments may eventually provide an even clearer picture. The Next Generation Very Large Array, an observatory currently under development, is expected to make detailed studies of nearby stars and their atmospheres much easier.

Such observations could reveal not only how companion stars influence their massive neighbors, but also how aging red supergiants lose material as they approach the final stages of their lives. Understanding these interactions may help astronomers better explain the complicated processes that shape the evolution of enormous stars like Betelgeuse.

The findings were published in The Astronomical Journal in a paper titled "New Spatially Resolved Observations of Betelgeuse from the VLA and ALMA: Evidence for Atmospheric Perturbations from a Close Companion."

- L. D. Matthews, A. K. Dupree, A. M. S. Richards, W. R. F. Dent. New Spatially Resolved Observations of Betelgeuse from the VLA and ALMA: Evidence for Atmospheric Perturbations from a Close Companion. The Astronomical Journal, 2026; 172 (3): 184 DOI: 10.3847/1538-3881/ae953d

articles.title: Scientists trick cancer cells into making the drugs that kill them

paras.en: Scientists trick cancer cells into making the drugs that kill them

- Scientists have developed a promising new cancer-fighting strategy that uses carbon monoxide naturally produced by tumor cells to manufacture powerful drugs inside the cancer cells themselves. Early laboratory experiments suggest the technique could selectively attack cancer while sparing healthy cells, potentially paving the way for safer chemotherapy alternatives.

Researchers in Japan have developed an innovative way to turn a chemical produced by cancer cells into a weapon against them. Instead of delivering toxic drugs throughout the body, their experimental approach uses carbon monoxide released by cancer cells to manufacture anticancer compounds directly inside the cells themselves.

The research, led by Katsunori Tanaka at the RIKEN Pioneering Research Institute (PRI) in Japan, was published in Nature Communications. In laboratory experiments, the team demonstrated that a specially designed compound could trigger drug production inside cancer cells without generating the same toxic substances in healthy cells. Although the technique is still at an early stage, it could eventually provide a way to attack tumors while reducing the harmful side effects associated with conventional cancer treatments.

paras.en: Turning Cancer's Own Toxic Gas Against It

One of the greatest challenges in cancer treatment is destroying malignant cells without damaging healthy tissue. Traditional chemotherapy can cause serious side effects because its toxic effects are not always limited to tumors. Tanaka and other researchers are investigating more selective strategies that could make cancer treatments safer.

Their long-term goal is to replace the direct delivery of toxic drugs with relatively harmless compounds that become active only after entering cancer cells. These compounds would use substances already present inside tumors to generate therapeutic drugs exactly where they are needed.

Carbon monoxide offers an intriguing opportunity for this approach. Although best known as a poisonous gas produced by sources such as gasoline engines, carbon monoxide is also generated naturally by many types of cancer cells. Because tumors can produce unusually high amounts of the gas, it may serve as a useful biological marker for identifying cancer cells, provided it can be detected.

Scientists in RIKEN's Biofunctional Synthetic Chemistry Laboratory investigated whether they could exploit this difference. Their strategy involved delivering a metal catalyst into cells and using the excess carbon monoxide in cancer cells to drive a chemical reaction that produces a toxic compound. In principle, the reaction would occur primarily in cancer cells, where enough carbon monoxide is available, while sparing normal cells.
Protecting the Catalyst Inside Cancer Cells

To make the system work, the researchers turned to a class of compounds known as palladacycles. These metal-containing compounds can react with carbon monoxide to produce an organic molecule called phenanthridinone. Certain derivatives of phenanthridinone are toxic to cells and have already been incorporated into anticancer drugs.

However, there was a major obstacle. When palladacycles are introduced directly into cells, substances such as glutathione rapidly deactivate their central palladium catalyst. Without an active catalyst, the reaction cannot produce the desired drug.

Tanaka's team addressed this problem by building on its previous work using metal catalysts to carry out chemical reactions in living systems. The researchers enclosed a palladacycle within albumin, a protein commonly found in blood. This protective protein carrier allows the complex to travel through the bloodstream while shielding the palladium catalyst from substances that would otherwise deactivate it after entering cells.
Laboratory Tests Reveal Selective Drug Production
The scientists evaluated their system through a series of experiments. They began by testing different palladacycles to identify which one could generate the greatest amount of phenanthridinone.

Next, they exposed cultured human liver, cervical, breast, and lung cancer cells to the albumin and palladacycle complex for 48 hours. They also tested the compound on a noncancerous cell line to determine whether the same chemical reaction would occur in healthy cells.

After 48 hours, the researchers detected phenanthridinone in the cancer cell lines but not in the normal cells. The findings indicated that the albumin carrier successfully protected the catalyst from glutathione and that the chemical reaction occurred selectively in the cancer cells under the conditions tested.

The team then refined the system so that the newly formed compound could separate from the carrier and move freely throughout the cell. Additional modifications allowed the reaction to generate a particularly toxic phenanthridinone derivative already used in anticancer drugs.

When the researchers introduced this modified system into cultured liver cancer cells, they observed the anticancer compound forming inside the cells. The cells subsequently showed signs of damage caused by the toxic drug, providing proof that the approach could generate a cancer-fighting substance directly within its intended target.
Why the Experimental Drug Did Not Form in Blood

An important safety concern involved carbon monoxide already present in the bloodstream. If that gas triggered the chemical reaction before the compound reached cancer cells, the resulting drug could damage blood cells instead of its intended target.

Fortunately, laboratory testing showed that the toxic drug was not produced in blood. The researchers believe this is because carbon monoxide in the bloodstream is largely attached to hemoglobin, the protein responsible for transporting oxygen. In this bound form, the gas appears to be unavailable for the reaction needed to manufacture the drug.

The finding suggests that the system may be able to travel through blood without prematurely generating harmful substances, although further studies will be needed to establish its safety in living organisms.

"This work represents an important advance in therapeutic in vivo synthetic chemistry," says Tanaka. "In our therapeutic strategy, molecules naturally present or generated within the body -- including disease-associated metabolites -- are used as endogenous chemical feedstocks to synthesize therapeutic molecules directly at the site of disease."

The researchers now plan to move beyond cultured cells and test the approach in animal models. If future experiments are successful, the technology could help establish a new class of cancer treatments that exploit the chemistry of tumors to produce drugs directly at the disease site, potentially limiting damage to healthy tissue.
